a16_0085634.speaker: Peterson
a16_0085634.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a16_0085634.speaker: Duke
a16_0085634.text: Okay, Pete. I take that back. You can see a little of it as the particles stream off. When they get out into the Sun, you can see them. And it looked like they have the same trajectory as the other ones, but it's very few right now.

a16_0085634.speaker: Peterson
a16_0085634.text: Roger. Kind of going out the top center, slightly right center of the picture?

a16_0085634.speaker: Duke
a16_0085634.text: Yeah, that's about right. Yeah.

a16_0085634.speaker: Peterson
a16_0085634.text: Rog.

a16_0085634.speaker: Peterson
a16_0085634.text: Ken, can we roll to get this area back in the sunlight where we could have a better look at it? [Long pause.]

a16_0085634.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0085634.text: Okay, Pete. We're just about ready to maneuver. We are maneuvering.

a16_0085634.speaker: Peterson
a16_0085634.text: Okay. I guess you'll want to go back the way you came and go back to that attitude where you had good sunlight on it.

a16_0085634.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0085634.text: Okay, that's the P23 attitude.

a16_0085634.speaker: Peterson
a16_0085634.text: Roger.

a16_0085634.speaker: Young
a16_0085634.text: Okay, and ever so often, I see a particle come out from that region at some accelerated velocity, like it's leaving the spacecraft.

a16_0085634.speaker: Peterson
a16_0085634.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a16_0085634.speaker: Duke
a16_0085634.text: Okay, Pete, for my edification, were all the - the PAD, the blanket pressures, the helium tanks looking okay on the RCS?

a16_0085634.speaker: Peterson
a16_0085634.text: Affirmative. They were, Charlie. [Long pause.]

a16_0085634.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0085634.text: This is Apollo Control, the picture we're getting right now is the interior of the Command Module. All three crewmen back in the Command Module, now. And after the look we got at the Lunar Module, on the telemetry data, everything appeared to be normal. We've had a group of very interested engineers and project management people here in the control center, looking at the television picture. And can see very clearly the panel which had the shredded appearance what Charlie Duke described earlier as appearing like shredded wheat.

a16_0085634.speaker: Peterson
a16_0085634.text: Charlie, we - just as a point of verification here, did you have floodlights when you went into the LM? We didn't show any - any current drain when you went in there.

a16_0085634.speaker: Duke
a16_0085634.text: Yes, sir. Just like the refrigerator, it came right on, with the hatch about a quarter of the way open. And when I went to All, we had all the floodlights.

a16_0085634.speaker: Peterson
a16_0085634.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a16_0085634.speaker: Duke
a16_0085634.text: But you can see a lot better over here when you take your shades off.

a16_0085634.speaker: Peterson
a16_0085634.text: Rog [laughter]. [Long pause.]

a16_0085634.speaker: Duke
a16_0085634.text: And, Pete, every time the - one of the Command Module, Service Module, RCS plus-X jets fires towards that - that one over the hatch here, it really blows that stuff off.

a16_0085634.speaker: Peterson
a16_0085634.text: Roger; copy.

a16_0090324.speaker: Young
a16_0090324.text: Okay, Houston. As of this moment, that area is completely free of particles. It wouldn't do you any good to show you any TV of it, because it's not doing anything.

a16_0090324.speaker: Peterson
a16_0090324.text: Roger; copy. [Long pause.]

a16_0090324.speaker: Peterson
a16_0090324.text: Okay, John. I guess that's about all the data we're going to get. We're going to have to think that over a while, so we'll go ahead and stow the TV camera and get back to the Flight Plan.

a16_0090324.speaker: Young
a16_0090324.text: Yes, sir. It's certainly an unusual thing; and, furthermore, it's very strange how this upper surface here has flaked off behind the - behind the - docking target, which I guess you - you can't see that on the TV. I couldn't see it on the monitor. Can you see it on the TV?

a16_0090324.speaker: Peterson
a16_0090324.text: We get a pretty good look at a portion of it. Looks like a lot of, like Charlie said, shredded wheat.

a16_0090324.speaker: Young
a16_0090324.text: Yeah, it looks like about a half - a half inch or an inch of grass growing out of the - of the surface there.

a16_0090324.speaker: Peterson
a16_0090324.text: Yeah, we got a pretty good look at that.

a16_0090324.speaker: Young
a16_0090324.text: Okay.

a16_0090324.speaker: Peterson
a16_0090324.text: I don't think we know what it means yet, but we did get a good look at it.

a16_0090324.speaker: Young
a16_0090324.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a16_0090324.speaker: Young
a16_0090324.text: Charlie might say that looks Ba-a-ad.

a16_0090324.speaker: Duke
a16_0090324.text: You're right [laughter]. [Long pause.]

a16_0090324.speaker: Duke
a16_0090324.text: Did you have a TV picture of the cockpit there? [Pause.]

a16_0090324.speaker: Peterson
a16_0090324.text: Affirmative; real briefly there.

a16_0090324.speaker: Duke
a16_0090324.text: [Laughing] That's what I was afraid of. [Long pause.]

a16_0090324.speaker: Peterson
a16_0090324.text: Okay, 16. We'd like to get the Waste Stowage Vent valve, Open, again now. [Long pause.]

a16_0090324.speaker: Duke
a16_0090324.text: And, Pete, the Lunar Module looks very clean. There was very few particles in it, and that's just about it. Over.

a16_0090324.speaker: Peterson
a16_0090324.text: Roger; understand. And, Char - Charlie, we'd like to go into the Flight Plan here at 12:15 and delete closing the Vent - Waste Stowage Vent valve, and move that to 13:15.

a16_0090324.speaker: Duke
a16_0090324.text: Okay; we're moving it to 13:15.

a16_0090324.speaker: Peterson
a16_0090324.text: Roger.

a16_0090324.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0090324.text: This is Apollo Control at 9 hours, 8 minutes. Again, to recap the situation after having the crew get in, power up the Lunar Module and taking a look at the external area where the material on the skin was shredding, particles were coming out. We can find nothing obviously wrong and that's obviously reassuring to have all of the data on the propellant tanks, and the pressures and quantities looking normal. At the present time, the thing that we're looking into is the possibility of an unusually large number of jet firings at some point from the Command Module Reaction Control System thrusters

a16_0090324.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0090324.text: At the point the crew will pick up their Flight Plan, they'll be about one hour, perhaps a little bit more, behind where they would have been had this problem not cropped up. This is, however, a relatively slack period in the Flight Plan. We would expect them to be able to make up the time without a great deal of difficulty. They're scheduled to be taking some navigation sightings through the Command Module optics system. These will be used to update the onboard guidance system's knowledge of its position and trajectory.

a16_0090324.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0090324.text: This is Apollo Control. As a point of interest, that entire exercise in the Lunar Module took about one hour. We reached the conclusion here in the Control Center that we were going to ask the crew to enter the LM at about 8 hours, 13 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. A couple of minutes after that John Young came up with a further report of what appeared to be particles venting from the LM which reinforced and further confirmed the decision to go into the Lunar Module. The crew, Young and Duke, to our best estimate were in the LM by 8 hours, 30 minutes Ground Elapsed Time and spent about 16 minute

a16_0091825.speaker: Peterson
a16_0091825.text: 16, for your information, we're not going to do Midcourse Correction l, and we're looking at about 12 feet per second on Midcourse Correction 2.

a16_0091825.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0091825.text: And CapCom Don Peterson has just advised the crew that Midcourse Correction Number 1 will not be required. That opportunity for the midcourse is scheduled at 11 hours, 39 minutes. And by the time we get around to the opportunity of Midcourse Correction Number 2, the amount of velocity change it appears would be required at somewhere on the order of 12 feet per second. By dropping Midcourse Correction 1, of course, that will give the crew a bit of help in making up the time that was lost in going into the Lunar Module and we would expect that they would have most of that time made up by the tim

a16_0092401.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0092401.text: Don, do you anticipate any significant change in the Verb 49 maneuver angles due to our slip in time?

a16_0092401.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0092401.text: This is Apollo Control at 9 hours, 58 minutes. We've had virtually no conversations with the crew since they completed the exercise in checking out the Lunar Module, some 45 minutes or so ago. And it's been relatively quiet here in the Control Center. We've had no further discussions of the problem, or apparent lack of a problem with Lunar Module. The situation, to recap, began prior to this shift's coming on, shortly after the Translunar Injection with a crew report of particles apparently coming off the Lunar Module. And at the time it was not known where they were coming from or what the na

a16_0095800.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0095800.text: Okay. Hey, let me give you a couple of comments here in real time so you can write them down. Yeah, one of the things that had been mentioned was this business about reflections in the sextant when you're doing P23s, and I've got a - gee it's a beautiful picture of the Earth's horizon; the optics are just super, and we've got a - got a - what looks like an inverted - sort of like a mirror image - in the opposite side away from the horizon. It's really quite obvious...

a16_0095800.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0095800.text: ...and you can just see the bright areas.

a16_0095800.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0095800.text: And it's about - yeah, it's just in the sextant, and it's about - oh, I don't know how to give you a percentage of the intensity, but it is much less intense than - than the thing in the Earth. That's - that's very bright. And the star is - gee, the match between the Earth horizon as seen through the fixed line of sight and the star line of sight is just perfect. It's really nice. The only thing I can't see as well as I'd like is the crosshairs, and with the illumination turned up to full bright, they just don't stand out when the old Earth is in the field of view. When I get them down against

a16_0095800.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0095800.text: And, as you probably noticed there, we used that little adaptive short P23 erasable program, which is really swift; that thing just fires these things off, and I don't feel like in any way we're having to take short cuts on the pointing accuracy. The only time it takes now is to dress up the substellar point on initial acquisition. That's what we're doing now, and it seems to take quite a while.

a16_0095800.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0095800.text: Next time we design a spacecraft, Don, we should remember not to put the optics in the kitchen.

a16_0095800.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0095800.text: That was Ken Mattingly giving a subjective evaluation of the optics and the program used in computing these midcourse navigations. Mattingly noted that there was a reflection in the CSM sextant, the optical device that he was looking through in lining up a star, in this case over the Earth horizon. Once the star is lined up in the proper position, Mattingly pushes a button and the computer automatically notes the time and the angle between the star and the Earth horizon. And from this computes and updates its knowledge of the spacecraft position's trajectory. Mattingly noted that the - there d

a16_0101638.speaker: Young
a16_0101638.text: That's the first Mark, isn't it? I think he cycled on it. [Long pause.]

a16_0101638.speaker: Young
a16_0101638.text: Yes, he's been taking a little bit longer each one.

a16_0101638.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0101638.text: This is Apollo Control. Ken Mattingly is still involved in taking the midcourse sightings through the CSM sextant. On completing that activity the Flight Plan becomes relatively unencumbered. We don't have very many additional scheduled activities and we expect that the crew will be able to make up the hour that was lost in getting into the Lunar Module and checking - checking out what appeared to be a possible problem resulting from - noting that the - one of the skins on the Lunar Module was peeling and the material flaking off and the possibility that something underneath - one of the tanks

a16_0101638.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0101638.text: This is Apollo Control at 10 hours, 57 minutes. The Flight Activities Officer has just reported that the crew is completing the midcourse navigation exercise using Program 23. After that, they will align the spacecraft guidance platform which is used as an attitude reference. Flight Activities Officer said that they will be back on the normal Flight Plan prior to the time that they're scheduled to begin their rest period. There's been no further discussion here in the Control Center of the peeling thermal skin on the Lunar Module. The data that we saw when John Young and Charlie Duke entered t

a16_0105632.speaker: Peterson
a16_0105632.text: Rog; we are going to dilute - delete that maneuver to thermal attitude that's coming up in the Flight Plan at about 9:30 - in the Flight Plan. And also, when you get a chance, we want you to zero Noun 26, because there's a possibility that if you hit a Noun 30 with what you got in Noun 26 now, you'll get a transfer to a wrong place in the program. [Pause.]

a16_0105632.speaker: Young
a16_0105632.text: Boy, you guys are reading our minds up there, or down there. [Pause.]

a16_0105632.speaker: Young
a16_0105632.text: What do you want to do? Just go right into PTC?

a16_0105632.speaker: Peterson
a16_0105632.text: Negative; we're going to do the P52 that's at - down around 10:40 in the Flight Plan.

a16_0105632.speaker: Young
a16_0105632.text: Understand. And then go to PTC, huh? [Pause.]

a16_0105632.speaker: Peterson
a16_0105632.text: Negative; we got some UV photos at 12:20 that have to be done at 12:20. [Long pause.]

a16_0111341.speaker: Peterson
a16_0111341.text: 16, you can go ahead and torque them.

a16_0111656.speaker: Peterson
a16_0111656.text: 16, we got a state vector update, if you'll go to Accept. [Pause.]

a16_0111656.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0111656.text: Rog; you've got P00 and Accept.

a16_0111656.speaker: Peterson
a16_0111656.text: Roger. [Pause.] And, also if you can copy, we've got a change to the G&C Checklist, Page 9-4. [Long pause.]

a16_0111656.speaker: Peterson
a16_0111656.text: Roger; under Baker, column Baker, line 4, change from 11522 to 13353, and, on line 5, change 13000 to 00041. [Pause.]

a16_0111656.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0111656.text: Okay, I'm on Page G/9-4, column Bravo, line 04 is 13353; that replaces 11522. Line 05, 00041 replacing 13000.

a16_0111656.speaker: Peterson
a16_0111656.text: And, 16, you can have the computer. [Pause.]

a16_0111656.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0111656.text: Don, you folks ready for a little fuel cell purge?

a16_0111656.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0111656.text: Don, fuel - Fuel Cell 1 purge, O 2 purge is in progress.

a16_0112519.speaker: Peterson
a16_0112519.text: 16, Houston. We're looking at an O 2 flow of less than one pound per hour, and we'd like to know if you have closed the waste storage vent valve.

a16_0112922.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0112922.text: Houston, do you want us to dump the waste water down to about 10?

a16_0114017.speaker: Peterson
a16_0114017.text: 16, let's terminate the charge on Battery Bravo.

a16_0114017.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0114017.text: Okay, we're showing about 29 percent on our waste water, Don. How does that look with what you all have on the ground?

a16_0114017.speaker: Peterson
a16_0114017.text: We're looking at about 30.5 percent now.

a16_0114017.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0114017.text: Okay, so you want us to terminate ours at 10 percent; our gauge reading of 10 percent will be good enough?

a16_0114330.speaker: Young
a16_0114330.text: Okay, we've terminated the waste dump.

a16_0114747.speaker: Duke
a16_0114747.text: Houston, we vented the batteries and it went to 0.4, looks - maybe 0.2 now.

a16_0114747.speaker: Peterson
a16_0114747.text: Charlie, did you get a reading on that battery before you vented it?

a16_0114747.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0114747.text: This is Apollo Control at 11 hours, 59 minutes; and it's continued rather quiet here at Mission Control. We've had relatively few conversations with the crew aboard Apollo 16 in the last 45 or 50 minutes. The activities aboard the spacecraft have been primarily housekeeping sorts of things. Dumping the waste water; these tanks gradually fill up from excess water produced by the fuel cells and at a given level, they are dumped back down to about ten percent of their capacity. The crew has aligned the guidance platform used as a reference for attitude. They'll be changing out the lithium hydroxi

a16_0115841.speaker: Peterson
a16_0115841.text: 16, could you give us a reading on LM/CM Delta-P? [Long pause.]

a16_0115841.speaker: Young
a16_0115841.text: Rog. LM/CM Delta-P is 0.2, which is what it was in the altitude chamber, and that apparently zero on our gauge.

a16_0115841.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0115841.text: And the pressure equalization valve is verified closed.

a16_0121006.speaker: Peterson
a16_0121006.text: 16, Houston. On this UV photography, we want to be sure we go Mode, Free. I think last time, we didn't get that.

a16_0121006.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0121006.text: No, we did get it last time. [Long pause.]

a16_0121006.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0121006.text: Pete, on the last sequence, we did go Free.

a16_0121006.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0121006.text: I said, on that first UV sequence we had, we did go Free.

a16_0122213.speaker: Peterson
a16_0122213.text: 16, when you finish the UV photos, we'd like you to go on and start the PTC right away, if you concur with it. [Pause.]

a16_0122213.speaker: Peterson
a16_0122213.text: Rog; and, in connection with that, we'll ask you to stow the High Gain prior to going into PTC. [Long pause.]

a16_0123204.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0123204.text: Hey, Don, you really can get some pretty stable initial conditions.

a16_0124045.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0124045.text: It looks - it looks to me like we've used a - a lot more RCS propellant than I would have guessed. Is it just our onboard readings or is that a fact? [Pause.]

a16_0124045.speaker: Peterson
a16_0124045.text: We're seeing apparently some biases in the P - in the RCS sensors up there. [Pause.] Stand by - wait one. We'll get you some readings, Ken.

a16_0124754.speaker: Peterson
a16_0124754.text: 16, prior to entering PTC, go Manual and Wide on the High Gain and minus 52 and 270. [Pause.]

a16_0124754.speaker: Young
a16_0124754.text: Okay; you got Manual and Wide, minus 52 and 270.

a16_0125325.speaker: Peterson
a16_0125325.text: 16, Houston. We're going to have to delay going into the PTC until after we close the Waste Stowage Vent valve at 13:50. [Pause.]

a16_0125325.speaker: Young
a16_0125325.text: Okay. We're supposed to wait 20 minutes for the rates to damp anyhow, huh?

a16_0125325.speaker: Peterson
a16_0125325.text: Ken, on the RCS quantities, I've got some numbers for you here. [Pause.]

a16_0125325.speaker: Peterson
a16_0125325.text: Roger. The - Quad A is reading 1.5 low. All the rest of them are - are reading high. Quad Bravo is 0.6, Charlie is 5.7, and Delta is 5.6. [Pause.] And our Delta on the Flight Plan is a plus 5 total right now. [Long pause.]

a16_0125325.speaker: Young
a16_0125325.text: Okay, is that - is that pounds, or percent, or degrees, or what? Over.

a16_0125325.speaker: Peterson
a16_0125325.text: The - the total of 5 pounds is pounds.

a16_0125325.speaker: Peterson
a16_0125325.text: 16, Houston. We're starting to see a high temperature in the subsatellite battery in the SIM bay, so what we'd like to do is go ahead and close the Waste Stowage Vent valve now and get into PTC as soon as we can.

a16_0125325.speaker: Young
a16_0125325.text: Roger. Waste Stowage Vent going Closed now. [Long pause.]

a16_0125325.speaker: Peterson
a16_0125325.text: Stand by one, and we'll take a look. [Long pause.]

a16_0125325.speaker: Peterson
a16_0125325.text: The rates look good and you can go ahead into PTC.

a16_0125325.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0125325.text: This is Apollo Control at 13 hours. Apollo 16 will shortly be going into its Passive Thermal Control mode with the spacecraft rotating at about the rate of three revolutions per hour to maintain proper temperatures. And we do have from the Flight Dynamics Officer now a preliminary estimate on the time and location that the Saturn third stage, the S-IVB, will impact the Moon. This event is tentatively now expected to occur at 75 hours, 6 minutes, 28 seconds. And the preliminary target point - we expect that this will change somewhat as we get additional tracking on the Saturn stage - is latitud

a16_0130000.speaker: Peterson
a16_0130000.text: 16, we're going to let you get in - well into the PTC here. And monitor - the primary loop rad out temps and let it stabilize, and then it may be necessary to go down to Panel 382 and adjust it again to try to keep that temperature at about 45 degrees Fahrenheit.

a16_0130000.speaker: Peterson
a16_0130000.text: And, Ken, if we have to do that, we'd suggest you mark a place down there so that, during the subsequent, PTCs you can just set the thing to that mark.

a16_0130000.speaker: Peterson
a16_0130000.text: 16, go Omni Bravo and we'll take over switching it for you. [Pause.]

a16_0131051.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0131051.text: You would really love this sight. We're - as we rotate around now, we've got the - the Earth out the window Number 1, and it's about - oh, almost - not quite down to half. And you can see India and the continent, and it's covered with clouds, and no photograph can ever describe the way it looks. It's really super.

a16_0131051.speaker: Peterson
a16_0131051.text: It really sounds fantastic. Wish I were there.

a16_0131051.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0131051.text: Yes, sir. You would love it.

a16_0131051.speaker: Young
a16_0131051.text: You can see all of Australia, too. It's really something else.

a16_0131051.speaker: Peterson
a16_0131051.text: About what size does the Earth look from where you are? [Long pause.]

a16_0131051.speaker: Young
a16_0131051.text: Looks like it's about - it's approximately 4000 miles in radius.

a16_0131051.speaker: Peterson
a16_0131051.text: Hey, that's a pretty good estimate.

a16_0131051.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0131051.text: No, it's - it didn't quite fill the window. Well, I'm not - I'm about - I'm about three - my eyes are about three feet from the window, and it didn't quite fill it.

a16_0131051.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0131051.text: You know, a sight like that goes a long ways to make tomato soup taste good.

a16_0131051.speaker: Peterson
a16_0131051.text: Yeah, that's what I've heard. [Long pause.]

a16_0131051.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0131051.text: I hate - Don, I hate to belabor the point, but I would appreciate it if the guys that are working on the RCS budgeting and all could take a look and - and see if they could determine if there was any place where we were going over more than what they might have expected for that phase.

a16_0131051.speaker: Peterson
a16_0131051.text: Okay; we'll have them take a look. [Long pause.]

a16_0131051.speaker: Peterson
a16_0131051.text: Okay, Ken; for your info, they said you were slightly ahead following LM extraction and apparently we used a little excess during the P23s.

a16_0131051.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0131051.text: Okay; that - that - that stands to reason; that not being able to see the reticle on there is a real nuisance. You can do it, and it's - I guess there is also a certain amount of getting used to the knack of flying that thing around. It's - for some reason, it seems a little bit different to find the attitude than it was in the simulator; but the biggest nuisance was the inability to see the reticle, but if that's where we used our extra, that's fine.

a16_0132250.speaker: Peterson
a16_0132250.text: And, 16, I've got P37 block data for about four different times for you when you're ready to copy. [Long pause.]

a16_0132250.speaker: Young
a16_0132250.text: Okay; we'll get it in a few minutes.

a16_0135921.speaker: Peterson
a16_0135921.text: 16, Houston. We're standing by on this P37 block data PAD anytime you're ready.

a16_0135921.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0135921.text: This is Apollo Control at 14 hours and we're in the process of a shift handover here in Mission Control. Flight Director Gerry Griffin and his team of flight controllers coming on now to relieve the Pete Frank team. And we do expect to have a change of shift press briefing. That will begin in about 15 minutes and will be held in the MSC News Center Briefing room. Apollo 16 at the present time is 66,450 nautical miles [123,065 km] from Earth and the spacecraft velocity is 6,990 feet per second [2,130 m/s].

a16_0140234.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0140234.text: Roger. We just changed over down here. How're things going?

a16_0140234.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0140234.text: Ah, this is really a ball, Henry. [Pause.] Hey - much as I hate to say it, this PTC doesn't look so red hot to us. Can you give us any clues whether it's gonna hack it or not?

a16_0140234.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0140234.text: 16, Houston. We don't see anything down here that's causing it divert - to diverge, but it does look marginal. We're gonna keep an eye on it. [Pause.]

a16_0140834.speaker: Young
a16_0140834.text: Roger. We just cycled the H 2 fans as per presleep checklist. And Fan number 3 was still in Auto. Do you want to leave it in Auto tonight? Over.

a16_0140834.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0140834.text: That is affirmative. Leave it in Auto.

a16_0140834.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0140834.text: Apollo 16, Houston. The block data - P37 block data for the updates book whenever you're ready.

a16_0141223.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0141223.text: Okay, that's four - four blocks. I'll just read them in succession: 025:00, 4907, minus 165, 070:45; 035:00, 7454, minus 165, 070:13; 045:00, 5857, minus 165, 094:31; 055:00, 4879, minus 165, 118:41 and these all assume no Mid-Course 2. [Pause.]

a16_0141223.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0141223.text: Apollo 16, Houston. We want to still keep working on this SPS gauging problem. We'd like to get a readout if we could on your SPS fuel and oxidizer pressures. [Pause.]

a16_0141223.speaker: Young
a16_0141223.text: Okay, that fuel pressure is reading right now 168. Oxidizer pressure is in the green, and it's reading 1 - 186 or 87.

a16_0141223.speaker: Young
a16_0141223.text: That's affirm, isn't it? And we were told this morning before launch that that was nominal.

a16_0141223.speaker: Young
a16_0141223.text: Because - because of a bias in the gauge. So we're probably gonna need some kind of a - another Delta-P figure to go on our LOI card - I mean our midcourse card.

a16_0141223.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0141223.text: That's affirmative, and it's in work.

a16_0141223.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0141223.text: And I think I show we have just at 15 percent waste water, but we are gonna go ahead and chlorinate unless you think the EECOMs don't want that. [Pause.]

a16_0141223.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0141223.text: 16, Houston. We're - we're not sure we understand your question here. If you're asking if it's okay to chlorinate the potable, that's - that's good.

a16_0141223.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0141223.text: Okay. Just wanted to make sure if you ever need a waterboiler, people don't like to put the chlorine in there, so I just thought I'd check with you before I did it. [Pause.]

a16_0141223.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0141223.text: Okay, I copy now. [Pause.] They say still press ahead, Ken.

a16_0143021.speaker: Young
a16_0143021.text: Okay, Houston. We'll run the cabin pressure up to 5.7 as per this presleep checklist.

a16_0143021.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0143021.text: 16, Houston. When you changed the lithium hydroxide canister, we noted a small drop in the suit compressor Delta-P down here. Did you change any of the configuration in the suit loop at the time you did that? [Pause.]

a16_0143021.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0143021.text: Well, Henry, sometime back there during the day, I opened up the flow line to my hoses that had been turned off and laid them around to try and get some better ventilation in here. But I don't remember whether that was about the same time or not.

a16_0143021.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0143021.text: Okay. We're not concerned; we're just trying to answer the question. That's probably what it was.

a16_0143021.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0143021.text: This is Apollo Control. The change of shift press briefing momentarily to begin in the small briefing room in the News Center; any air-to-ground conversation from Apollo 16 will be recorded for playback at the conclusion of the Press Conference. At 14 hours, 32 minutes Ground Elapsed Time, this is Apollo Control.

a16_0143850.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0143850.text: Thank you, folks. Ready for a Verb 74?

a16_0144246.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144246.text: Apollo 16, Houston. We're showing your cabin pressure up around 5.9. Recheck your O 2 flow.

a16_0144246.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0144246.text: This is Apollo Control. During the - just completed press conference some minute and half of tape from the air-ground from Apollo 16 was accumulated. We'll play back that tape at this time and rejoin any subsequent conversation prior to the time the crew goes into their eight-hour rest period. At 14 hours, 43 minutes; playing back tape and going live, this is Apollo Control.

a16_0144808.speaker: Young
a16_0144808.text: Houston, 16. Over.

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: Go ahead.

a16_0144808.speaker: Young
a16_0144808.text: Roger. We gonna turn the voice off - per the presleep checklist. Okay?

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: Will you stand by just a minute, 16? [Pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: 16, Houston. Do you have your O 2 heaters configured? [Pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Young
a16_0144808.text: That's affirm; 1 and 2 is Off, 3 is in Auto, and the [pause] H 2 Heaters are both in Auto.

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: Apollo 16, Houston. This is for Ken. Do you have anything to report on your film status? [Pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0144808.text: That's in work, Henry.

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0144808.text: Gee, Henry, on 16-millimeter magazine Alpha Alpha, we have approximately 20 percent remaining. [Pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: Copy. [Long pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0144808.text: On magazine November November, that's a 70 millimeter, we're up to frame 33. [Pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0144808.text: And on Oscar Oscar, it's frame 18. [Pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: Roger, 18. [Long pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0144808.text: And, Henry, we are going without (garble) what do you think about PTC?

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: Roger. The - your first part of your transmission was blocked out. We had a antenna switch. However, on the PTC, guess he thinks it will go throughout the sleep period, and then we'll reinitialize after you wake up. But he doesn't think it'll go a full 16 hours, but it's good for the sleep period. [Pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0144808.text: Okay. The first thing you said was we'll go without the tone booster. We'll go with normal comm delay.

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: Okay.

a16_0144808.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0144808.text: That's for caution and warning part. [Long pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: And, Ken, did you use anything out of mag Juliet Juliet?

a16_0144808.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0144808.text: That's negative.

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0144808.text: Okay, Henry. Are there any onboard read-outs that you folks would like to have?

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: Negative, Ken, I think we're all in good shape here. Everything looks good at this point. You got anything else for us? [Pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0144808.text: No, I'm just looking ahead, and I've got five and a half minutes to go to sleep.

a16_0144808.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_0144808.text: Rog. Why don't you take that? Y'all did a real good day's work. Only two things left to do are those two comm switches, the Squelch and the Normal Mode Voice. Get a good night's sleep, and we'll see you tomorrow. [Pause.]

a16_0144808.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0144808.text: And the communications officer here in Mission Control has reported that the crew has indeed turned off the voice switch onboard the spacecraft, and are settling in for a night's sleep. The spacecraft analysis status report, dated at 14 hours Ground Elapsed Time, less than an hour ago; most of the entries state no change or performance is normal. For example, in propellant usage on the CSM Reaction Control System propellants, they are now 349 pounds [158 kg] over the predicted budget for this time in the flight. Fuel cells are working normally. All the cryogenic tankage are in normal condition

a16_0144808.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0144808.text: This is Apollo Control, 16 hours and 1 minute Ground Elapsed Time. Crew of Apollo 16 having some 6 hours, 58 minutes remaining in their programmed sleep period. About 20 minutes ago, the Flight Surgeon reported that, from his biomedical telemetry, that none of the crew was asleep at that time and that apparently Mattingly, because of a somewhat higher heart rate, was probably doing some exercising. For those persons who are interested in numbers and statistics, the halfway point in distance for Apollo 16, that is from surface to surface, Earth-Moon, will take place at a Ground Elapsed Time of

a16_0144808.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0144808.text: This is Apollo Control at 17 hours, 1 minute Ground Elapsed Time; slightly under six hours remaining now in the Apollo 16 crew rest period. Spacecraft is now 77,898 nautical miles [144,267 km] out from Earth. Velocity now 6,288 feet per second [1,916 m/s]. In a continuing refinement of the predicted S-IVB impact statistics, we have yet another set of numbers. The lastest predicted impact for the S-IVB stage on the lunar surface is at 0.93 north latitude by 22.35 west longitude at a Ground Elapsed Time of 75 hours, 6 minutes, 22 seconds. These figures likely will be updated as more tracking is

a16_0144808.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0144808.text: This is Apollo Control, 19 hours and 1 minute Ground Elapsed Time into the mission of Apollo 16. Apollo 16 presently 84,895 nautical miles [157,225 km] out from Earth. Velocity 5,920 feet per second [1,804 m/s], continuing to decelerate. While it may be a little premature, the space flight meteorology group here in Mission Control is already forecasting that the splashdown weather conditions, some 12 days away here, are going to be good. Possibly a few rain showers in the area near Christmas Island. Some four hours remaining in the crew's sleep period. Spacecraft still in the Passive Thermal C

a16_0144808.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0144808.text: This is Apollo Control, 20 hours and 1 minute Ground Elapsed Time in the mission of Apollo 16. Some 3 hours remaining in the scheduled sleep period for the crew. Spacecraft is now some 88,262 nautical miles [163,461 km] distant from Earth. Velocity now 5,755 feet per second [1,754 m/s]. The numbers for the predicted S-IVB impact continue to vary as the tracking is further refined. The latest numbers from the Flight Dynamics Officer gives an estimate of impact at 2 degrees, 16 minutes north latitude by 23 degrees, 11 minutes west longitude with an impact time of 75 hours, 7 minutes and 4 second

a16_0144808.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0144808.text: This is Apollo Control; 21 hours, 1 minute Ground Elapsed Time into the mission of Apollo 16. The Apollo 16 spacecraft is now 91,524 nautical miles [169,502 km] out from Earth. Velocity now 5,602 feet per second [1,707 m/s]. Apollo 16 crew at this time apparently all sleeping rather well. They signed off just before 3 am CST for the scheduled eight-hour sleep period. According to flight surgeon Dr. Sam Pool, Young and Mattingly were awake for perhaps an hour past the signoff time and Duke still an hour beyond that. Only two of the crewmen are hooked up to the biomedical telemetry, but as Dr. P

a16_0144808.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0144808.text: This is Apollo Control; 22 hours, 1 minute Ground Elapsed Time in the flight of Apollo 16. Here in Mission Control, the flight control team of Gene Kranz is being briefed for the next eight-hour shift, as Gerry Griffin's Gold Team plans to - makes preparations for retiring 'til tomorrow morning. There will not be a change of shift press briefing with the Gold Team Flight Director and as much as the entire shift with the exception of about the first 30 minutes have been - has consisted of the crew being asleep. Distance at this time: Apollo 16 is 94,738 nautical miles [175,455 km] out from Eart

a16_0144808.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0144808.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 22 hours, 28 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. The handover in Mission Control between the two Flight Control teams has been completed. The team of flight controllers headed by Gene Kranz are now all onboard. Our CapCom for this shift will be astronaut Tony England. We presently show Apollo 16 at an altitude of 96,103 nautical miles [177,982 km] from Earth and travelling at a velocity of 5,399 feet per second [1,646 m/s]. Our clock in Mission Control shows that we're approximately 31 minutes away from time of crew wakeup. At 22 hours, 28 minutes continuing to moni

a16_0230300.speaker: Young
a16_0230300.text: Go ahead there, Houston. How you doing?

a16_0230300.speaker: England
a16_0230300.text: Hey, you sound good. Good morning up there. How are you doing?

a16_0230300.speaker: England
a16_0230300.text: Good show. Everything looks fine up there from down here.

a16_0230300.speaker: England
a16_0230300.text: [Chuckle, pause.] How are your comrades doing? [Pause.]

a16_0230300.speaker: Young
a16_0230300.text: Oh, they're just starting to stir. [Long pause.]

a16_0230300.speaker: England
a16_0230300.text: I'd hum something for you to wake you up, but I got a tin ear. [Pause.]

a16_0230300.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0230300.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 23 hours, 9 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 16 presently 98,222 nautical miles [181,907 km] away from the Earth. The velocity now reading 5,309 feet per second [1,618 m/s].

a16_0230300.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0230300.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 23 hours and 16 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 16 now 98,558 nautical miles [182,529 kilometres] away from the Earth and traveling at a speed of 5,295 feet [1,614 metres] per second. Very little conversation with Apollo 16 thus far, however, the wakeup call has been placed and we'll standby and continue to monitor. We're at 23 hours, 16 minutes at Ground Elapsed Time and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a16_0232526.speaker: Duke
a16_0232526.text: Okay. For Ken, he had from Meal C everything but the pecans, and he ate his sandwich and his orange juice. His PRD is 15030. Six hours in an 8-hour period; he was awake every - once every hour. Okay. Excuse me.

a16_0232526.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0232526.text: We're switching Omnis at this time. That is Charlie Duke with the post-sleep report.

a16_0232526.speaker: Duke
a16_0232526.text: Okay, Tony. Had one more than 41 and he let some of them off, and 13 ounces total intake. [Long pause.] Okay...

a16_0232526.speaker: England
a16_0232526.text: Okay, Charlie ... Charlie, could you say the voids again?

a16_0232526.speaker: England
a16_0232526.text: Could you say the voids again on Ken?

a16_0232526.speaker: Duke
a16_0232526.text: One was timed 41 - 41 seconds; the other one was lost due to a malfunctioning bag. And we got on me now - for my meal, I had the sandwich and the orange juice that was in the suit. For Meal C, I had half the spaghetti, all the ambrosia, and the cocoa. My PRD is 21040. I got about 5 hours sleep; got two voids of 20 and 25 with about a 20-ounce fluid intake. Over.

a16_0232526.speaker: England
a16_0232526.text: Okay. I got it all. Sounds like you all slept pretty good. [Pause.]

a16_0232526.speaker: Duke
a16_0232526.text: Well, it was off and on for me. I must have been... [Long pause.]

a16_0232526.speaker: England
a16_0232526.text: I tell you, I'd be so excited, I wouldn't sleep at all.

a16_0232526.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0232526.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 23 hours, 32 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 16 now 99,379 nautical miles [184,050 km] away from the Earth. Now traveling at a speed of 5,261 feet per second [1,603 m/s].

a16_0233200.speaker: Duke
a16_0233200.text: Houston, we're charging Battery A. [Pause.] And on that food, Tony, add my apricot cubes, I just ate them. [Long pause.]

a16_0234103.speaker: England
a16_0234103.text: Charlie, Houston.

a16_0234103.speaker: Duke
a16_0234103.text: Go ahead

a16_0234103.speaker: England
a16_0234103.text: Okay. On that fluid consumption there, the numbers you gave were in ounces. Could you verify that's ounces and not bags? [Pause.]

a16_0234103.speaker: Duke
a16_0234103.text: Say that again, Tony.

a16_0234103.speaker: England
a16_0234103.text: In the fluid you've consumed - the drinks, you gave the numbers in ounces, and I guess the blank here is listed in number of bags and partial bags, and they just want to verify the fact that the number you have was in ounces and also to check and see what unit you want to use for the rest of the mission on that so everybody will have it straight.

a16_0234103.speaker: Duke
a16_0234103.text: Okay, we'll use - we'd like to use ounces, and that's what we'll go with.

a16_0234103.speaker: England
a16_0234103.text: Okay.

a16_0234103.speaker: Duke
a16_0234103.text: That's what I read.

a16_0234103.speaker: England
a16_0234103.text: Okay. Understand. Thank you. [Pause.]

a16_0234103.speaker: Duke
a16_0234103.text: Tony, the - the menu side of it, the things that are in the menus are in, of course, bags.

a16_0234103.speaker: England
a16_0234103.text: Okay, we understand.

a16_0234103.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0234103.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 23 hours, 42 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. That was Lunar Module Pilot Charlie Duke talking to CapCom Tony England here in Mission Control clarifying one point in the post-sleep report. We presently show Apollo 16 at a distance of 99,923 nautical miles [185,057 km] from the Earth, and traveling at a speed of 5,238 feet per second [1,596 m/s].

a16_0234103.speaker: Young
a16_0234103.text: Okay. We can see the Earth out there, and it's getting a good deal smaller. It's about the same size as the Moon almost, out the other window. And Africa is clear this morning - at least the part that we can see, which is what's usually clear, right around from the Canaries on.

a16_0234103.speaker: England
a16_0234103.text: Very good. We've got you about a little over - well, you just passed 100,000 miles [185,200 kilometres] on our chart here.

a16_0234103.speaker: Young
a16_0234103.text: I would guess we're about 100,000 miles out. Yes.

a16_0234103.speaker: England
a16_0234103.text: Well, sounds like a milestone. [Long pause.]

a16_0234103.speaker: England
a16_0234103.text: [Laughter.] They say you're only 14 miles off, John. You're going to have to recalibrate your eyeball. [Long pause.]

a16_0234103.speaker: Young
a16_0234103.text: Okay. From our point of view, you only got a little more than half an Earth.

a16_0234103.speaker: England
a16_0234103.text: Oh, that's right. We forgot; you're kind of handicapped.

a16_0234103.speaker: Young
a16_0234103.text: Right.

a16_0234103.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0234103.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 23 hours, 51 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 16 now 100,355 nautical miles [185,857 km] away from the Earth, and now traveling at a speed of 5,220 feet per second [1,591 m/s]. It's been a very quiet day thus far for the crew of Apollo 16. We've heard from them with their post-sleep report, and aside from a brief commentary by John Young on his view of the Earth, we've heard little else at this point, but we'll stand by and continue to monitor. This is Apollo Control, Houston at 23 hours, 52 minutes Ground Elapsed Time.

a16_0240107.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0240107.text: Okay, can we stand by awhile?

a16_0240107.speaker: England
a16_0240107.text: Okay, just give me a call when you're ready.

a16_0240107.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0240107.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 24 hours, 5 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 16 now 101,035 nautical miles [187,117 km] away from the Earth. Velocity now reading 5,193 feet per second [1,583 m/s]. During this period of relative calm and quiet, we'll pass along a brief update to our status on the crew report of last night of a - of particles emitting from the Lunar Module in the vicinity of the aluminum closeout panel which covers the Mylar insulation over the RCA [sic] system number - or System A. The panel in question is 50-56 aluminum .004 inches thick [0.1 millimetres] with a 0.001 [i

a16_0240107.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0240107.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 24 hours, 14 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 16 now 101,502 nautical miles [187,982 km] away from the Earth and traveling at a speed of 5,173 feet per second [1,576 m/s]. We presently show the spacecraft weight at 103,078 pounds [45,848 kilograms]. We'll stand by and continue to monitor any conversations that might take place between the crew of Apollo 16 and our CapCom in Mission Control, Tony England. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a16_0241400.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0241400.text: Hey, Tony.

a16_0241400.speaker: England
a16_0241400.text: Ah, go ahead, Ken. [Pause.]

a16_0241400.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0241400.text: Okay. I'm about to finish up on my coffee here. If it's something I don't need to write down, I'll just listen to what you have to say as you - as you read it off.

a16_0241400.speaker: England
a16_0241400.text: Okay. That sounds good. [Pause.] On the systems status, the RCS - everything looks fine. You're 27 pounds [12.2 kg] ahead on your usage. Must have a pretty light hand on the throttle there. [Long pause.]

a16_0241400.speaker: England
a16_0241400.text: Okay, and on the ECS, the failure mode's probably in the control electronics. The valve was driving at a max rate - that's 12 seconds, full open to full close, and they saw that on TM by the flow rate. I don't recommend making any sensor changes since that doesn't seem to be the problem, and thermal runs are being made here at this time to determine the setting for lunar orbit. They don't anticipate any problems with it. [Pause.]

a16_0241400.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0241400.text: Okay. I - I kept watching it since we've set it. We haven't touched that thing now for a long time, and maybe I just haven't caught any of the extremes, but it looks like it's been holding nicely between about 45 and 50.

a16_0241400.speaker: England
a16_0241400.text: Right. We concur. We - we don't think you're gonna have to touch it until you go to the dark side. [Long pause.] Okay, and on the SPS - normally during SPS cooldown during translunar coast, the helium in the SPS oxidizer tanks is absorbed by the oxidizer, causing a decrease in oxidizer tank pressure. Your transducer hasn't indicated this, and there - there may be a problem with that transducer. We've got a procedure change that I'll give to you later in your Flight Plan update, prior to the Midcourse 2, that will allow them to check that transducer. [Pause.]

a16_0241400.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0241400.text: Okay, Tony. And is there any change in the Midcourse 2 time, or is it going to be like the Flight Plan?

a16_0241400.speaker: England
a16_0241400.text: Right now, it looks as per Flight Plan. [Pause.] Okay. And on your DSE tape, Hank had a chance to take a look at it. Sounded - said it sounds fine. Dick will be in a little later and listen also, so everything looks Go for - for the operations in lunar orbit. [Pause.] And everything else looks great. It's kind of nice not to have much to say here. Sure isn't like the sims. [Pause.]

a16_0241400.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0241400.text: Yeah, I hope we've [garble] the last sim [laughter].

a16_0241400.speaker: England
a16_0241400.text: Right. I got a little...

a16_0241400.speaker: Duke
a16_0241400.text: ...You said it all.

a16_0241400.speaker: England
a16_0241400.text: That's right. I went through the news. I don't know whether you guys, over your coffee, would like to read the newspaper, but I've got all the news that's fit to print, and I really don't have much to say. A great piece here is in the world of art. One of Vincent Van Gogh's best was stolen from the San - San Diego Art Gallery as part of a display that was named "Out of Sight." And I've got an input from Dottie here for Charlie. [Pause.]

a16_0241400.speaker: Duke
a16_0241400.text: I'm all ears.

a16_0241400.speaker: England
a16_0241400.text: Okay. She says your - your five bird eggs have hatched, and so you've got five new, healthy neighbors. [Pause.]

a16_0241400.speaker: Duke
a16_0241400.text: Oh, great; thank you [laughter].

a16_0241400.speaker: England
a16_0241400.text: You're welcome. [Long pause.]

a16_0241400.speaker: England
a16_0241400.text: Okay. And on the Flight Plan update, we have five items, and there's no hurry to get them up there. Whenever you're ready to take them and - and can write the stuff down, I'll send them on up.

a16_0241400.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0241400.text: Okay. Why don't you give us another ten minutes or so?

a16_0241400.speaker: England
a16_0241400.text: Okay, that'll be fine. [Long pause.]

a16_0241400.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0241400.text: Tony, you'd enjoy seeing this place. After all the things you had to go through to keep the cockpit nice and clean out there, you'd never recognize it. [Pause.]

a16_0241400.speaker: England
a16_0241400.text: Ah, it probably looks like any - any bachelor's pad.

a16_0241400.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0241400.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 24 hours, 22 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 16 now 101,860 nautical miles [188,645 km] away from the Earth, and traveling at a speed of 5,159 feet per second [1,572 metres].

a16_0242650.speaker: Duke
a16_0242650.text: Okay, Houston. You speak with the Flight Plan update.

a16_0242650.speaker: England
a16_0242650.text: Okay. Stand by a second, Charlie.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Charlie, Houston.

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Go ahead.

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Did you want the Flight Plan or the Update Book?

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay. This will be in the Update Book, this first one. [Long pause.]

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Okay, go ahead.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay. Go to the section on "Flight Plan Updates." It has the EMP programs. [Pause.]

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Okay.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay, we'd like you to add a last step to each of the four EMP probe procedures. That would make a fourth step on the "Shortened P23" and a seventh step on "Manual range input," et cetera.

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Okay. Stand by, Tony. They must had a hand over. You were cut out. Start over again, please.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay, understand. All right. In the "Flight Plan Update" section, on the four EMP programs, we'd like you to add a fourth - correction, a final termination procedure to each of the four programs. So on the "Shortened P23," we'd have a Step 4, which reads "Verb 25 Noun 26 Enter," and then the "Four registers, Enter all balls" - correction, "Three registers, Enter all balls." [Long pause.]

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Okay, copy. Four step for P23 is "Verb 25 Noun 26, Enter all balls in all registers."

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay. And on the next program, the "Manual range input," Step 7 would be the same thing. [Long pause.]

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Copy. "Manual range input," Step 7 to "Verb 25 Noun 26, Enter all balls."

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay. And on the "Optics angle to body angles," we'll add a Step 7, and it would be the same as before. [Long pause.]

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Okay. Copy all balls.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay. And on the "Jet monitor" program, it'll be a Step 6, the same thing. [Long pause.]

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Okay. Go ahead.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay. The purpose for these were - was to protect the E-memory from other programs.

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Okay...

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: ...Okay. The next change is to your "SPS burn rules." So if you can get that card. [Long pause.]

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Go ahead.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay. On the fuel to oxidizer pressure, [pause] it should read - or it does read "Greater than 115." Will you change it to read "124 for oxidizer, 110 for fuel." [Long pause.]

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Okay. "Pressure greater than 115" is changed to "124, oxidizer; 110, fuel."

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: That's correct. And in the "Fuel to oxidizer Delta-P," it reads "Less than 20 psi." We'd like to change that to "35 psi oxidizer greater than fuel, or 5 psi oxidizer less than fuel." [Long pause.]

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Okay; copy "35 oxidizer greater than fuel; 5 oxidizer less than fuel."

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay. And the final part of that is in the "Tight constraints" there in the box, [pause] it says "Greater than 160, and greater than 80." We'd like to change that to "Greater than 168 oxidizer, and greater than 153 fuel." [Pause.]

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Okay. "Greater than 168 oxidizer; 153, fuel." [Pause.]

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: And I guess on that "Tight constraints" also, it's the - the chamber pressure says "Greater than 80" for the "Tight constraints." [Pause.]

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Okay.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay. And that's the end of that procedure. A note here that this assumes a - a good oxidizer transducer, and there may be a - a problem that it's hung up. And we'll have a - a little later change in the Midcourse 2 burn procedure. And from this, we'll be able to tell what - what - where the problem is. I'll get that up to you as soon as they've sorted it out here. [Pause.] Okay, and there are two notes here. [Pause.] For Ken, a reminder to watch the UV film consumption magazine Oscar Oscar. He's right on the budget now, and there's no pad.

a16_0242833.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0242833.text: Rog. And there's no way to cut a film out.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: I understand.

a16_0242833.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0242833.text: Now, we're - we're aware of it being tight, Tony. If you see us slip behind - I - I guess I don't know what to do about it. You'll have to come up with a recommendation of what - what other photo to delete.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay. Well, we just thought we'd let you know that you had a two-frame pad, and we've already used it.

a16_0242833.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0242833.text: You mean we've taken two frames we weren't supposed to?

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: I don't understand the note here. That was the note I got. Maybe it was used up before - before they loaded it or something. I'll find out.

a16_0242833.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0242833.text: As far as I know, Tony - Yeah, yeah, I just want to make sure that there's no misunderstanding on our part about what it is we're supposed to do, because we took only those frames that were selected, because we are aware of the tight budget.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay; understand.

a16_0242833.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0242833.text: And we might be off a little bit on the numbers we gave you, because, you know, that counter's kind of gross, and it's easy to get off by a - by a number or so, particularly when you start at the low end.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: All right; understand. I'm just off that more than a number. Okay, and a last note. We'd like you to take a look when you get a chance at that - the LM thermal surface, and see if you notice any changes or can give us any more words on it. We really don't anticipate a problem there. It turns out in looking back, there was a history of one batch of bad paint, and they sort of think it's just the paint blistering up. And it doesn't seem to be on a...

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: All right...

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: ...on the surface that'll give us a real bad problem.

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: Okay. We're ready to bring up the High Gain if you've got some angles for us.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay. I'll get them.

a16_0242833.speaker: England
a16_0242833.text: Okay. We'd like you to stand by for ten minutes on that High Gain. [Pause.]

a16_0242833.speaker: Duke
a16_0242833.text: All right.

a16_0242833.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0242833.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 24 hours, 39 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 16 now 102,739 nautical miles [190,273 km] away from the Earth, and traveling at a velocity of 5,123 feet per second [1,561 m/s].

a16_0244514.speaker: England
a16_0244514.text: Okay, on the High Gain, we'd like you to select Pitch, minus 40; Yaw, plus 90; and the Beam width in Narrow. And we'll give you a cue to switch over to the High Gain. [Long pause.]

a16_0244514.speaker: Duke
a16_0244514.text: Okay. You've got them selected. You going to cue us, you say?

a16_0244514.speaker: England
a16_0244514.text: That's affirmative. We'll give you a cue.

a16_0244514.speaker: England
a16_0244514.text: Okay. We'd like you to go Reacquisition now, and we'll command. [Pause.]

a16_0244514.speaker: England
a16_0244514.text: We'd like you to go Reacquisition now. [Pause.]

a16_0244514.speaker: Duke
a16_0244514.text: Okay. You've got Reacq and High Gain.

a16_0244514.speaker: Young
a16_0244514.text: Okay, Houston. To discuss that thermal layer of grass that we got [pause] growing on the - growing just outside the docking target, it's thinned out a pretty good bit since last night. I think it's gone somewhere, but there're a lot of these little square - rectangular strips about - up to two inches long; I see one that must be three inches long, and they're just sort of - look like they're glued - somebody glued a bunch of strips of grass onto that thermal shield, but most of them have gone. Where it was 100 percent coverage before, it looks like it's about 50 percent coverage now. [Pause.]

a16_0244514.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0244514.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 24 hours, 48 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. That was John Young describing the current status of the particles on the Lunar Module. We show Apollo 16 at 103,197 nautical miles [191,120 km] away from the Earth, traveling at a speed of 5,106 feet per second [1,556 m/s].

a16_0244514.speaker: England
a16_0244514.text: Okay, we'd like you to go ahead on the film cycling down to the MSFN cue and then call us back.

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: Okay, Houston. How about a cue? [Long pause.]

a16_0245220.speaker: England
a16_0245220.text: Okay. Stand by a second. [Long pause.]

a16_0245220.speaker: England
a16_0245220.text: Okay, Ken. Go on, then, with your procedure.

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: Okay, I'll read these out as I go through them.

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: John, would you switch - why don't you put me on vox?

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: And the only thing that looked a little different is when I got down to the step where it said "Pan Camera Mode to Standby," it already was. I guess that's just an oversight.

a16_0245220.speaker: England
a16_0245220.text: Okay. Okay, that's no problem. [Long pause.]

a16_0245220.speaker: Young
a16_0245220.text: You want to be on vox?

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: Yeah. No, that's top switch, top left, all the way down.

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: I - Okay, Tony. Can you read me now? I'm on vox.

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: All righty. Mapping Camera is coming On. Stand by.

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: You like to have the Pan Camera Self Test simultaneously, or would you like to do it sequentially?

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: Okay; Pan Camera to Self Test, getting Self Test.

a16_0245220.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0245220.text: You can hear Command Module Pilot Ken Mattingly checking out the Pan Camera and the Mapping Camera onboard with the Mission Control Center in Houston. This is Apollo Control, Houston at 24 hours, 55 minutes Ground Elapsed Time.

a16_0245220.speaker: Young
a16_0245220.text: Hope so. I wouldn't be talking to anybody if it wasn't on.

a16_0245220.speaker: Young
a16_0245220.text: Ken, you what to try the...

a16_0245220.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0245220.text: Apollo Control, Houston at 24 hours, 56 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 16 now 103,540 nautical miles [191,756 km] away from Earth.

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: Okay, I've got the gray flag on the Pan Camera Mode talkback, and that took about 45 seconds, as opposed to a minute.

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: Okay. So I'm going to go ahead and take the Pan Camera Power to Off.

a16_0245220.speaker: Young
a16_0245220.text: If you're gonna oxidize your Delta-Ps, you're in - That's really a pain. How you gonna monitor something with that kind of an attitude?

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: Okay, I'm getting ready to take the Mapping Camera to Off, center.

a16_0245220.speaker: England
a16_0245220.text: Okay, I've got two minutes here.

a16_0245220.speaker: England
a16_0245220.text: Right. It's a Mickey special. [Long pause.]

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: Take the SM/AC Power Off. [Pause.] Man, that's what you call good timing. [Pause.]

a16_0245220.speaker: Duke
a16_0245220.text: Okay, Tony. We're going to Omni Bravo, and selecting is returned to High Gain.

a16_0245220.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0245220.text: Yes, please, John; back to PTT Intercom. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a16_0245220.speaker: Young
a16_0245220.text: That was our big thing for today, wasn't it?

a16_0245220.speaker: Duke
a16_0245220.text: Okay, Tony, we got a Delta - LM/CM Delta-P of 0.8...

a16_0245220.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0245220.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 24 hours, 58 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. The crew of Apollo 16 following very closely the timeline in the Flight Plan. Apollo 16 Commander John Young has just donned a biomedical harness as reported by Lunar Module Pilot Charles Duke. At 24 hours, 59 minutes; Apollo 16 is 103,686 nautical miles [192,026 km] away from the Earth.

a16_0250637.speaker: England
a16_0250637.text: Hey, John, you're giving us some great TV there. [Long pause.]

a16_0250637.speaker: Young
a16_0250637.text: What did you say? What did you say, Tony?

a16_0250637.speaker: England
a16_0250637.text: I said we're getting some great TV down here. Looks good.

a16_0250637.speaker: Young
a16_0250637.text: Was that one of your tapes?

a16_0250637.speaker: England
a16_0250637.text: Ah so, that's a tape. Sorry about that.

a16_0250637.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0250637.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 25 hours, 7 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. That exchange between Tony England and Apollo 16, the reference was to a replay which is taking place in the Mission Control Center of the tape of yesterday evening's television. This picture's being studied by some of the flight controllers here who had not had an opportunity to see it before along with Dr. Robert R. Gilruth who was the former director of the Manned Spacecraft Center. We're at 25 hours, 8 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 16 now 104,125 nautical miles [192,839 km] away from the Earth and traveling a

a16_0250637.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0250637.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 25 hours, 11 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Very little conversation taking place between our CapCom Tony England and the Mission Control Center and the crew of Apollo 16. It is during this time frame however that the crew of Apollo 16 should be performing the electrophoresis demonstration. During this demonstration, the crew will attempt onboard to prove the higher purity of particle migrations in zero g. Three Mylar tubes containing microspheres are used for this activity. The tubes are positively and negatively charged at either end. The movement of the micr

a16_0251807.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0251807.text: Okay, Tony. We're on the electrophoresis now, and we're now - just about to - to hook up the power cable and turn the power on, and it says at that point "Hold for instructions from Houston."

a16_0251807.speaker: England
a16_0251807.text: Okay [laughter], instructions I have there are to press on through that hold and go on down to just before starting the camera and then hold again and give us a call.

a16_0251807.speaker: England
a16_0251807.text: Okay. At your convenience, when you get a chance, we'd like you to read out all quads of the RCS propellant quantity for correlation with the TM.

a16_0251807.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0251807.text: Okay. A is 90; B is 96; C is 96; D is over 100, about 101 or 2.

a16_0252354.speaker: Young
a16_0252354.text: Houston.

a16_0252354.speaker: England
a16_0252354.text: Go ahead, Charlie.

a16_0252354.speaker: Young
a16_0252354.text: Houston, we're - we're down to the step - before Ken turns on the electrophoresis fire. Where do you want us to hold that? Over.

a16_0252354.speaker: England
a16_0252354.text: Okay, we'd like you to hold just prior to starting the camera. [Pause.]

a16_0252354.speaker: Young
a16_0252354.text: Okay, just prior to starting the camera.

a16_0252354.speaker: England
a16_0252354.text: Rog. On the next page.

a16_0252354.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0252354.text: Okay; how about telling us where we're going here, because...

a16_0252354.speaker: England
a16_0252354.text: Okay...

a16_0252354.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0252354.text: ...I've got to turn this thing on, and I'd like to have it in my mind what it is we're going to do.

a16_0252354.speaker: England
a16_0252354.text: Rog. It's no big deal. The note here was, at that point, you're supposed to observe the current meters, and if there's no indication of a current flow in any tube, you tap the box gently along the - the axis, parallel with the face, and then you allow the whole se - the whole unit to lie motionless for additional three to five minutes before proceeding. They're afraid there may be a bubble in one of the tubes, and you don't get a current.

a16_0252354.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0252354.text: Okay. Well, actually, there's a bubble in each tube.

a16_0252354.speaker: England
a16_0252354.text: Say that again.

a16_0252354.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0252354.text: Actually, there's a bubble in each tube. And it's - each tube has a bubble. They are in exactly the same place. They're lined up in a row, and they are directly over meter Number 3. And the bubbles are about - oh, one-eighth of an inch in diameter. [Pause.]

a16_0252354.speaker: England
a16_0252354.text: Okay, the PI says that's okay, and we should go ahead and proceed.

a16_0252354.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0252354.text: Okay. Now, the question that you had for me was that if - if any of the meters do not go into the green, we turn the power on. Did you want me to tap the box, and then do what?

a16_0252354.speaker: England
a16_0252354.text: Okay. The instructions were to tap the box gently, allow the unit to remain motionless for an additional three to five minutes, and then proceed.

a16_0252354.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0252354.text: Okay; and this time, if we don't get the meters into the green, we proceed anyhow; is that correct?

a16_0252354.speaker: England
a16_0252354.text: According to the instructions, that's correct.

a16_0252354.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0252354.text: All righty.

a16_0252354.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0252354.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 25 hours, 27 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. That was Ken Mattingly, Command Module Pilot of Apollo 16, discussing procedures for the electrophoresis demonstration with CapCom Tony England here in Mission Control. We now show Apollo 16 at the 105,057 nautical miles [194,566 km] away from the Earth and traveling at a speed of 5,032 feet per second [1,534 m/s].

a16_0252354.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0252354.text: Okay, Tony. It turns out that meter Number 1 is just barely into the red; meter Number 2 didn't come up quite into the red; meter Number 3 is about a needle width below the red. [Pause.]

a16_0252354.speaker: England
a16_0252354.text: Okay. We'd like you to go on with the experiment. [Pause.]

a16_0252354.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0252354.text: Okay, I've jiggled it a little bit and I'm gonna let it settle here for a second, and then we'll start. We'll give you a mark when we start.

a16_0252354.speaker: England
a16_0252354.text: Roger, we concur.

a16_0253016.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0253016.text: Okay, Houston; we have started the experiment. And as soon as we got it rotating - got it running, and I turned according to the decal on the box, which is counterclockwise, half rotation; and, soon as I did, the orange film disappeared and - I see white particles coming through - coming through as a stream. It looks much like a - a - it looks like latex. [Pause.]

a16_0253016.speaker: England
a16_0253016.text: Okay. We copy that. Any difference in rates between the different tubes? [Pause.]

a16_0253016.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0253016.text: Yeah. The first thing that happened, as soon as I opened it, I got a big blob of this stuff inside of the - it looks like the inside of the window here between where it shows - the decal on the outside says "Sample 1 and 2." it's got a big - couple of big blobs in there [garble under radio static] the Number 1 sample is approaching it. The Number 3 sample is about halfway between ring 2 and 3. Also have current meter Number 1 is in the green, current meter Number 2 is in the green, and Number 3 is still about a needle width below the red line and didn't move at all. The bubbles are moving at a

a16_0253016.speaker: England
a16_0253016.text: That's affirmative. The white material in the fastest tube.

a16_0253016.speaker: England
a16_0253016.text: And we had some bad comm right there in the middle when you were describing the rates and the difference in the three tubes of the white material. If you could say a little bit of that again, it might help.

a16_0253016.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0253016.text: Okay. It's moving much more rapidly than I had anticipated it would, Tony. Right now, the Number 2 sample is leading by about a nose. It's just crossed the one - two - three - four - fifth ring inscribed on that center tube. The Number 3 sample has just crossed the fourth one; the Number 1 sample has just crossed the fifth one now; and Number 2 is about halfway between five and six. Number 3 sample is maintaining a very cohesive shape and looks like a little cylinder with a pointed nose on it, and it's maintaining its white consistency. And it's going in - I can guess that the length of the -

a16_0253016.speaker: England
a16_0253016.text: Okay. You say there is no difference in diffusion between 1 and 2?

a16_0253016.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0253016.text: Well, there wasn't when we started, now - well, now that we've hit the Reversal Switch [laughter], I guess all bets are off. The - [laughter] they've just really - really broken up in Number 2 and in - Number 1 is holding together a little better. They really looked very, very similar; except that just as it crossed the last ring before the yellow ring, Number 2 started to get an elongate nose on the point, and it was starting to twist - I say it was looking like a corkscrew. And then about the same time, when - just about the time I hit the Reversal Switch, the sample in Number 1 did the same

a16_0253016.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0253016.text: And we're about to approach the original end. Do you want me to reverse it again, or what do you suggest at this point? [Pause.]

a16_0253016.speaker: England
a16_0253016.text: Yeah, Ken. We'd like you to reverse it again.

a16_0253016.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0253016.text: Okay, and I'll do that when the first large portion of the sample reaches the Lexan manifold; is that okay? That's - some of the diffused material will already coincide.

a16_0253016.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0253016.text: Apollo Control, Houston, that is Ken Mattingly describing the movement inside the three tubes for the electrophoresis demonstration. We're at 25 hours, 37 minutes into the mission. Apollo 16 now 105,559 nautical miles [195,495 km] out from the Earth.

a16_0253016.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0253016.text: Okay, I've reversed it, and I reversed it when the pointed end of sample Number 3 reached the first marked ring before reaching the Lexan manifold.

a16_0253016.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0253016.text: And it's starting to snake now. I - These - these little blobs don't seem to take this reversal so well. Another thing that was a little different on that first - when I - after I reversed it, sample Number 1, I mentioned that all three had bubbles who were right together when we started. The bubble on - on them all passed over to the extreme right end, except that Number 1, when we reversed the samples, it remained over in the right end, and Numbers 2 and 3 traveled with the material.

a16_0254008.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0254008.text: Okay, Tony, Number 2 has reached the end again. I'm going to reverse it for the last time.

a16_0254008.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0254008.text: It's reversed at this time. Mark it.

a16_0254008.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0254008.text: Number 2 is completely - looks like a - an emulsion. Number 1 still has a central core that's holding together, and Number 3 is doing a good job of staying together. It's diffused very little.

a16_0254008.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0254008.text: Okay, and at the end of this - it looks to me like it's so diffused that at the end of this run when we get it back, I'll just go ahead and secure it.

a16_0254237.speaker: England
a16_0254237.text: Yeah, Ken, I think they're gonna have fun analyzing that one.

a16_0254237.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0254237.text: I think they've got their work cut out for them. [Pause.] Are there any questions that you might want to get resolved that maybe I - were obvious to me but weren't obvious to you [laughter] before we put it all away? We're going to be closing down here in a couple of minutes.

a16_0254237.speaker: England
a16_0254237.text: Okay. The PI is back there, and hopefully he's working on some questions.

a16_0254237.speaker: England
a16_0254237.text: Okay. One, you said you - you tapped the box there at the beginning to try to get rid of the bubbles. How long did you wait before you started? I know you gave a mark, but we'd like to verify that.

a16_0254237.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0254237.text: Between the time we tapped the bubbles and the time we started the experiment?

a16_0254237.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0254237.text: Is that the time frame you - ? Okay. That time frame was - I would guess it was about a minute, Tony. Because when I tapped it, I just couldn't get them to move. I had already - I had already tapped that thing once before, for the bubbles, and - because when - as soon as we unpacked it, we saw the bubbles out there, and I banged it a little bit to try and see if I could get them to move and didn't have any luck at all. So we didn't wait any three or five minutes, it - it was about two minutes, I guess.

a16_0254237.speaker: England
a16_0254237.text: Okay, we copy that; two minutes. And on the Tube 1, did you notice any separation of the two sizes?

a16_0254237.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0254237.text: Not unless that's what this diffuse and central feature turns out to be. But the dark - oh, let me rephrase that, the higher concentration of material that makes it look more solid - if that's a large particle and the diffuse material is the finer particles, then I would say that perhaps there was a separation of small particles from larger ones in tube Number 2 just about the time I reversed it, just starting to show up, and Number 1 perhaps the same. And Number 3, I would say, if that's the proper interpretation, that there was no appreciable separation of any kind. And I'm not sure that Num

a16_0254237.speaker: England
a16_0254237.text: All right, we copy that. We - I sort of expected from the information we got here that [Number] 1 would be the one that split up into two sizes, but I guess we'll have to look at that later.

a16_0254237.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0254237.text: Okay. Again, I'm not sure what this little burst of material that got out on the window might be. Maybe we lost some of the stuff from one of them.

a16_0254237.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0254237.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 25 hours, 48 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. We've had a continuing discussion with Command Module Pilot Ken Mattingly on the electrophoresis demonstration. We now show Apollo 16 at 106,097 nautical miles [196,492 km] out from the Earth and traveling at a velocity of 4,992 feet per second [1,522 m/s].

a16_0255022.speaker: Young
a16_0255022.text: Houston, did you get that? That was magazine UU up to Frame 55 on that experiment.

a16_0255536.speaker: England
a16_0255536.text: Okay. At your convenience, we've got the change to your SPS burn procedure. [Pause.]

a16_0255536.speaker: Young
a16_0255536.text: Okay, you've got to stand by on that one. Things are kind of busy right now.

a16_0255536.speaker: England
a16_0255536.text: Right, understand. No hurry at all.

a16_0255536.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0255536.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 26 hours, 13 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Literally no conversation with the crew of Apollo 16 during a good part of this shift thus far.
