We now show Apollo 16 at 107,262 nautical miles [198,649 km] away from the Earth. Velocity now reading 4,947 feet per second [1,508 m/s]. Apollo 16's present weight 103,026 pounds [46,732 kilograms]. This is Apollo Control, Houston; continuing to monitor at 26 hours, 13 minutes since lift-off.

a16_0255536.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0255536.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 26 hours, 33 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. We presently show Apollo 16 at a distance of 108,209 nautical miles [200,403 km] away from the Earth. Velocity now reads 4,912 feet per second [1,497 m/s]. We're standing by continuing to monitor in the event we have any conversation with the crew of Apollo 16, but it's been a very quiet shift. We're at 26 hours, 33 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a16_0263300.speaker: Duke
a16_0263300.text: Houston, 16.

a16_0263300.speaker: England
a16_0263300.text: Go ahead, Charlie.

a16_0263300.speaker: Duke
a16_0263300.text: Tony, you just went by my window, and that half-Earth, man, is a spectacular sight.

a16_0263300.speaker: England
a16_0263300.text: I bet it is. I tell you, I'm green with envy. [Pause.]

a16_0263300.speaker: Duke
a16_0263300.text: Well, I don't want to trade with you.

a16_0263300.speaker: England
a16_0263300.text: [Laughter, pause.] You say the world looked pretty good when it went by?

a16_0263300.speaker: Duke
a16_0263300.text: How far out are we now, Tony?

a16_0263300.speaker: England
a16_0263300.text: 108,285.1 [nautical miles - 200,538.4 kilometres].

a16_0263300.speaker: Duke
a16_0263300.text: Say again. You were broken up.

a16_0263300.speaker: England
a16_0263300.text: Okay; 108,285.1. Change to point 6.

a16_0263300.speaker: Duke
a16_0263300.text: Okay, thank you. [Long pause.]

a16_0263300.speaker: Duke
a16_0263300.text: I think one of the most impressive sights, Tony, is the cloud formations you can see and the polar icecap.

a16_0263300.speaker: England
a16_0263300.text: Very good. Have you had a chance to look long enough to see your - see the dynamics at all?

a16_0263300.speaker: Duke
a16_0263300.text: Negative. We just now took the shade down on my side. That's the first view I've had all morning.

a16_0263300.speaker: England
a16_0263300.text: Very good.

a16_0263300.speaker: Duke
a16_0263300.text: There was that awful big storm up off the coast of Alaska in the Bering Sea, I guess it was yesterday. I can't see that now, though. I think you all are in the dark. [Long pause.]

a16_0263300.speaker: England
a16_0263300.text: I guess our weather chart doesn't go up that high. I was going to see what we've got there now, but it only includes your recovery areas. [Long pause.]

a16_0263300.speaker: England
a16_0263300.text: We were reviewing that film that you took - that TV that you took last night. And there are a lot of sparklies out the window. Were those all just loose particles floating around?

a16_0263300.speaker: Duke
a16_0263300.text: Yes, the LM was really shedding on that one panel there, Tony, and, in fact, we've still got quite a few particles floating along with us right now.

a16_0263300.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0263300.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 27 hours Ground Elapsed Time. We presently show Apollo 16 at a distance of 109,490 nautical miles [202,775 kilometres] from Earth and traveling at a speed of 4,864 feet [1,482 metres] per second. Meanwhile in the Mission Control Center, we do presently plan for Apollo 16 to perform midcourse correction Number 2. This would be at the normal Flight Plan time; 30 hours, 39 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. And the MCC-2 burn would have a Delta-V of 12.6 feet per second [3.84 m/s], and this would be a burn of a two-second duration performed with the Service Propulsion

a16_0263300.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0263300.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 27 hours, 8 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. During this quiet period in the Mission Control Center we are replaying the launch television on one of the large screens. This was the team of flight controllers that was on station during launch, and quite frankly very few had the opportunity to follow the sequence during the - visually during the actual launch. We presently show Apollo 16 at an altitude of 109,854 nautical miles [203,450 km] and a velocity of 4,850 feet per second [1,478 m/s].

a16_0272909.speaker: Duke
a16_0272909.text: Houston, 16.

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: Go ahead, Charlie.

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: Oh...

a16_0272909.speaker: Duke
a16_0272909.text: Stand by one. Ken wants to - Stand by.

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a16_0272909.speaker: Duke
a16_0272909.text: Okay, Tony. Go ahead.

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: Okay, this isn't the burn rules. It's a discussion of procedures for Midcourse-2 only. And a change could be noted in your cue card - SPS cue card - or the G&C Checklist G/5-2, but you might want to hear the whole thing before you write it down. Okay, at burn minus 6 minutes, the line that reads "SPS Helium Valve, two, to Auto" should be changed to "SPS Helium Valves, two, to Manual for 10 seconds." And "After 10 seconds, SPS Helium Valves, two, to Auto." And then they'd remain in Auto for the burn. And we have a couple of notes to that. First...

a16_0272909.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0272909.text: You're talking about going to On when you say "Manual." And you don't want us to stay there ten seconds if it exceeds 200, do you?

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: That's right. If it exceeds 210, we want you to turn them off. And we'll do the burn with them off - because if it went to Auto during the burn, we'd go right back into the problem.

a16_0272909.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0272909.text: Okay.

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: Okay. That was one of the notes, and you just anticipated it there. The other note is, you may, if - if we've diagnosed the transducer problem correctly, you'll probably get an SPS Pressure light. That will go on at 201 pounds. [Long pause.]

a16_0272909.speaker: Duke
a16_0272909.text: Okay.

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: Right now, they're anticipating that, by the time of the burn, that transducer will be biased about 15 pounds high. [Pause.]

a16_0272909.speaker: Duke
a16_0272909.text: Okay; that's the oxidizer side?

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: That's affirmative.

a16_0272909.speaker: Duke
a16_0272909.text: Okay. What is - what do you think's wrong with that transducer?

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: Right now, the note is that the comparison chamber, which should be at about atmospheric pressure, has leaked. And the leak is just making up for the normal absorption of helium, so the gauge is reading about constant. Eventually, that comparison chamber will leak down to zero, and then you'll be comparing - instead of comparing to 14.7, you'll be comparing to zero, and it will read 15 pounds high. [Long pause.]

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: We're reading about 11 pounds high now. [Pause.]

a16_0272909.speaker: Duke
a16_0272909.text: Okay; our gauge has been constant since lift-off.

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: Right. We can read the pressure farther on down the line; and, in the fuel side, the tank pressure and the pressure down the line are tracking right along, and they should be on the oxidizer side. But on the oxidizer side, the tank's staying constant and the one down the line is dropping down as it should. So either the one in the tank is just locked up or the leak out of the comparison chamber is just making up the difference. [Pause.]

a16_0272909.speaker: Duke
a16_0272909.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a16_0272909.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0272909.text: Apollo Control, Houston at 27 hours, 34 minutes. Apollo 16 now 111,051 nautical miles [205,666 km] away from the Earth. Velocity now reads 4,806 feet per second [1,465 m/s].

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: Charlie, Houston.

a16_0272909.speaker: Duke
a16_0272909.text: Go ahead.

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: Just so there is no misunderstanding here, I'd like to verify this up - this - procedure. We're going to Manual for 10 seconds at six minutes before the burn, and then, nominally, we'll go back to Auto even if you get a - a caution. The only point where we'd go to Off would be if it went above 210. [Pause.]

a16_0272909.speaker: Duke
a16_0272909.text: Okay, copy. At six minutes, Helium Valves go to Manual for 10 seconds, then to Auto. If pressure goes to greater than 210, go to Off.

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: That's affirmative.

a16_0272909.speaker: Duke
a16_0272909.text: If we get a caution light, but less than 210, we still stay in Auto.

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: That's right.

a16_0272909.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0272909.text: Apollo Control, Houston at 27 hours, 37 minutes into the mission. That was CapCom Tony England updating the crew of Apollo 16 the procedures for the Midcourse Correction Number 2 burn, which is ... MCC2 scheduled for 30 hours, 39 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. That would be a 12.6 foot per second [3.84 m/s] burn with a duration of two seconds using the Service Propulsion System engine. We're 27 hours, 38 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 16 now 111,245 nautical miles [206,026 km] away from the Earth. Velocity continuing to decrease and now reading 4,799 feet per second [1,463 m/s].

a16_0272909.speaker: Duke
a16_0272909.text: Houston, 16. Do you guys feel like that your transducers are good on the... [Pause.]

a16_0272909.speaker: Duke
a16_0272909.text: What I mean to say is, do you feel like your telemetry's good on the SPS tank pressure? [Pause.]

a16_0272909.speaker: England
a16_0272909.text: Stand by one, Charlie.

a16_0274029.speaker: England
a16_0274029.text: Okay, the telemetry here - the telemetry is good. And we can read from the transducer that you're reading your oxidizer tank pressure; we can also read from the inlet pressure transducer, which you can't read on board. The inlet pressure transducer indicates that nominal decay and pressure due to helium absorption by the oxidizer. And this looks just like all the other flights. The other one is the one that you're reading, and it looks like it's locked up. The reason for the procedure that we've sent up is to make sure that the - we know the pressures in the lines before this burn, which will

a16_0274029.speaker: Duke
a16_0274029.text: Well, okay. That's what had us a - talking in here about how we're going to monitor the LOI.

a16_0274029.speaker: England
a16_0274029.text: Right. That's our concern, too. And what we're trying to do is get enough unknowns out of this Midcourse so that we can have a good handle on the LOI.

a16_0274029.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0274029.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, at 28 hours, 4 minutes into the mission. We presently show Apollo 16 at the distance of 112,448 nautical miles [208,253 km] away from the Earth and now traveling at a speed of 4,755 feet per second [1,449 m/s]. We're standing by continuing to monitor any conversation which has been quite sparse through the past several hours of the flight, but we'll continue to do that and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a16_0281001.speaker: Young
a16_0281001.text: Roger. The bias test is completed at the end of a minute, 40 seconds. We got 102.0 on our Delta-V counter.

a16_0281001.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0281001.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 28 hours, 10 minutes. That was Apollo 16 Commander John Young reporting that the EMS bias check was completed. We presently show Apollo 16 at 112,740 nautical miles [208,794 km] away from the Earth and now traveling at a speed of 4,744 feet per second [1,446 m/s]. Thus far, during this shift, the White Team of flight controllers; it's been very straight forward, by the books. Very little conversation between Mission Control and the flight crew. We're standing by and continuing to monitor at 28 hours, 11 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Apollo 16, Houston. [Long pause.]

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Go ahead.

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Okay, Tony; go ahead.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay. Last night during the TV show, the lighting wasn't ideal. Maybe you have observed something that we couldn't see in the tapes here. Okay, that panel behind the docking target - was it completely covered with the shredded material? There's an access panel right in the middle of that - of the overall panel there - and we're curious to know if it was just in the access panel, or the whole panel. [Pause.]

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Okay, Tony, it was on the whole panel.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay, how about any other panels around? It looked like on TV there might be some on that panel just to the right. And, if so, do you have any words on any other panels?

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Okay, it's on that whole section there, Tony. There's two triangular panels, one on each side of this rectangular pattern which is right below the docking target. That whole section that is parallel of the Plus-X [axis], below the docking target, the two triangular panels and the rectangular panel, all are shredded.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay, we copy that.

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: [Garble.]

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Say again? [Pause.]

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Was there any gold Mylar, Kapton visible on the panel behind the docking target?

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Negative. It's - it's - apparently just a black surface now, most of the white-looking paint, or whatever it is, is all - most all gone now. There's just a - oh, I'd say maybe a ten percent of the surface is now covered with this shredded white stuff.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: The origin of that question was there was some question whether the panel may not have come off entirely and, underneath that, is some of that Mylar stuff.

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Well, the panel is still on, in fact, you - you can't even see the Mylar - the - the - below it is a black surface that looks much like the top of the ascent prop - propellant tank.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay, and I guess you mentioned last night there was some streaming of the paint as it was coming off. Was there a preferred direction - or what was it?

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Yeah, radially - well, from us, it was radial to the X-axis. Almost right out over the ascent module - out the Y-axis. [Pause.]

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Was it independent of your jet firings?

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: When Ken fired the jets, it really blew it off then.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Uh-huh. In the same direction?

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: No, it made it go the other way down towards - the - the legs of the LM.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay, and, without the RCS then, it was almost at right angles to the panel and, otherwise, it was going down towards the legs?

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Yes, and it looks like - like John said, right now, Tony, as we come around into the Sun, there's some particles coming out - off now more towards Quad 2. And it looks like it's on the underside of this panel as we cannot - we cannot see it, and - but it's between Quad 3 - 2 and the APS propellant module - correction - the APS propellant tank.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay, we're looking at the drawing here and see where you mean.

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Say again?

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Roger; we copy that, Charlie. What we're searching for on this direction of flow is if you think there's any - anything in the area that might cause it to stream out like some - a leaky tank or anything of that sort, or whether it just seems to be almost random.

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Say again Tony, you cut out after - all after 'What we're searching for.'

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay, what we're searching for here is just - We don't think there is any leak over there or anything of that sort. but, if there is a preferred direction of flow, we're looking for any indication of what it might be so we'll know where - where the flow is coming from.

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Tony, please, you're - for some reason, you weren't up-linking, and we've had all after 'What - what we're searching for.'

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay; stand by a second, Charlie. I'll be back with you in a minute. [Long pause.]

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay, Charlie; Houston. How do you copy now? [Pause.]

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: You're five by.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay, we were just searching around here a little bit - Far-out possibility might be that we had a small leak in there or something and it was causing the peeled paint to flow off in a particular direction; and we were just wondering if you had any indication that that might be the case, or whether it's just flying off at right angles? [Pause.]

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Well, when - when we first saw it, that was our opinion also, but now that most of it's gone - is - it - it's sort of just coming off in different directions. Over.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay, we copy that.

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: And, Tony, the stuff that - is really not white; it's more of - now it's more of a gold-looking color or sandy color now.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay. That's the shredded stuff you're talking about?

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: That affirmative.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: All right, the thermal people aren't - aren't upset about this at all. They don't think it will give us any constraint. Evidently, that surface was only on there for the very high-Sun case. [Pause.]

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Okay. Well, the panel is intact underneath that paint job, whatever it was. The panel apparently is intact.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay, Charlie, I guess that's the whole set of questions here. Everybody is very happy with - with what we're hearing. [Long pause.]

a16_0282456.speaker: Duke
a16_0282456.text: Tony, that panel that shredded - the ones we were telling you about are - have some more pronounced wrinkle ridges in them than any of the other panels.

a16_0282456.speaker: England
a16_0282456.text: Okay, we copy that, Charlie. We'll find out what that means.

a16_0282456.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0282456.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 28 hours, 36 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. We presently show Apollo 16 at 113,903 nautical miles [210,948 km] away from the Earth and traveling at a speed of 4,703 feet per second [1,433 m/s]. The exchange that you heard between Charlie Duke, the Lunar Module Pilot aboard Apollo 1,6 and CapCom Tony England dealt, of course, with the particles that were sighted first yesterday evening. The Grumman thermal people who operated one of the staff support rooms, here have identified it as not being a problem, and here in Mission Control we're attempting to acquire mo

a16_0282456.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0282456.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 28 hours, 52 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Our displays presently show Apollo 16 at a distance of 114,597 nautical miles [212,234 km] away from the Earth. Velocity now reads 4,678 feet per second [1,426 m/s]. We're at 28 hours, 52 minutes and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a16_0282456.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0282456.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 28 hours, 57 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 16 now 114,858 nautical miles [212,717 km] away from the Earth, and now traveling at a speed of 4,669 feet per second [1,423 m/s]. In the Mission Control Center we're in the process of a shift changeover. This being the Orange Team of flight controllers replacing the White Team of flight controllers. And we're at 28 hours, 58 minutes into the mission. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a16_0291128.speaker: Duke
a16_0291128.text: Okay, did you read John there?

a16_0291128.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0291128.text: Okay, we're exiting PTC and going to the far-UV attitude.

a16_0291128.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0291128.text: This is Apollo Control at 29 hours, 14 minutes. We've completed our shift handover in Mission Control. Flight Director Pete Frank has been checking with his flight controllers. He'll being going around the room shortly and getting a status and briefing for the things that will be going on during this shift. We will have a change of shift press briefing. That is scheduled to begin in about ten to 15 minutes and will be in the News Center Briefing Room. Participants in the briefing will be Flight Director Gene Kranz, and Flight Surgeon Dr. Royce Hawkins. That again will be in about ten to 15 min

a16_0292138.speaker: Peterson
a16_0292138.text: 16, we've got a state vector and a target load whenever you're ready to accept. [Pause.]

a16_0292138.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0292138.text: How long you been down there?

a16_0292138.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0292138.text: How's the weather down there today, Pete?

a16_0292138.speaker: Peterson
a16_0292138.text: And, Charlie, you're right over the Gulf of Mexico.

a16_0292138.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0292138.text: [Garble] looked out his window and said that you guys are still there.

a16_0292138.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0292138.text: Looks like you guys are still there.

a16_0292138.speaker: Duke
a16_0292138.text: What did you say about the Gulf, Pete?

a16_0292138.speaker: Peterson
a16_0292138.text: Yeah, you should be right directly over the Gulf of Mexico. [Long pause.]

a16_0292138.speaker: Duke
a16_0292138.text: Yeah, I was thinking the same thing - that we could see it, anyway.

a16_0292138.speaker: Peterson
a16_0292138.text: And, 16, you can have the computer. [Pause.]

a16_0292138.speaker: Young
a16_0292138.text: Thank you. Do you want us to go to Delta now, or you guys going to hang on to the antennas? [Pause.]

a16_0292138.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0292138.text: This is Apollo Control. We are ready to switch now to the MSC News Center Briefing Room for our change of shift press briefing.

a16_0293921.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0293921.text: Houston, do you have the angles?

a16_0293921.speaker: Duke
a16_0293921.text: Okay, Houston. Go ahead with your PAD.

a16_0293921.speaker: Peterson
a16_0293921.text: Okay, MCC-2: SPS/G&N; 66768; plus 1.24, minus 0.11; 030:39:00.01; Noun 81 is plus 0008.9, minus 0001.1, plus 0008.9; 094, 354, 010; Noun 44s are NA; Delta-V T , 0012.6, 0:02, 0008.3; sextant star, 40, 256.4, 30.3; rest of the PAD is NA. Set stars are Sirius and Rigel; 219; 166; 313; ullage, none; LM weight, 36258.

a16_0293921.speaker: Duke
a16_0293921.text: Okay, we copy MCC-2, SPS slash G&N; 66768; plus 1.24, minus 0.11; 030:39:00.01; plus 0008.9, minus 0001.1, plus 0008.9; 094, 354, 010; NA; NA; 0012.6, 0:02, 0008.3; 40, 256.4, 30.3; rest of the PAD is NA. Sirius and Rigel; 219; 166; 313; no ullage; LM weight, 36258.

a16_0293921.speaker: Peterson

a16_0294550.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0294550.text: This is Apollo Control at 29 hours, 52 minutes into the flight of Apollo 16. During our change of shift press briefing, the crew aboard the spacecraft has been completing preparations for their first Midcourse Correction on the translunar leg of this flight. That midcourse coming at the second opportunity, at a Ground Elapsed Time of 30 hours, 39 minutes. And they have now completed aligning the guidance platform which is used as an attitude reference for the maneuver. The burn will be performed with the Service Propulsion System engine in the Service Module and will be a 12.6-foot-per-second

a16_0295641.speaker: Young
a16_0295641.text: Houston, can we do this waste water dump now, or do you want us to wait closer in?

a16_0295641.speaker: Peterson
a16_0295641.text: Stand by a minute, John; we'll check it. [Pause.]

a16_0295641.speaker: Peterson
a16_0295641.text: John, we'd prefer you wait until after the sextant star check.

a16_0295641.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0295641.text: I'll tell you one thing about that - that sextant business, Don. We got so many particles off the LM out there that I don't believe you could recognize a star pattern - in the telescope ever, but they show up just perfect in the sextant.

a16_0295641.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0295641.text: Sure makes you appreciate one of these nondrifting platforms.

a16_0295641.speaker: Peterson
a16_0295641.text: Rog. Ken, in view of that, you can do that water dump any time you want.

a16_0295641.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0295641.text: Oh, we'll go ahead and do that. Do you have any objections to our going ahead and going to the attitude?

a16_0295641.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0295641.text: Looks like we're really crowding the length of time it's going to take to dump the water - up against the burn time.

a16_0295641.speaker: Peterson
a16_0295641.text: Yeah, you can go ahead - you can go ahead to attitude, or do the water dump whichever you want.

a16_0295641.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0295641.text: Okay, we'll - we'll go ahead and go to attitude and see what we have for time.

a16_0295641.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0295641.text: I'd like to - We'll get the star check off in the first priority.

a16_0300248.speaker: Duke
a16_0300248.text: Pete, we go to stop charging Bat A now?

a16_0300248.speaker: Peterson
a16_0300248.text: And, 16, you can delete charging Battery A after the burn; it's charged sufficiently.

a16_0300248.text: 16, I've got some gyro drift updates and PIPA bias for you, when you're ready to copy. [Long pause.]

a16_0300248.speaker: Peterson

a16_0300248.speaker: Peterson
a16_0300248.text: That's affirmative. And on the PIPA bias, the address is 1456, 76747. [Pause.] Omni Alpha, 16.

a16_0300248.speaker: Peterson
a16_0300248.text: That's affirmative, and did you copy Omni Alpha?

a16_0300248.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0300248.text: This is Apollo Control at 30 hours, 11 minutes. We're now about 28 minutes away from the scheduled ignition, for the midcourse correction; the first to be performed on this leg of the flight to the Moon. That maneuver again will be performed with the spacecraft Service Propulsion System engine. It will be a burn of about two seconds duration, providing about 12.6 feet per second [3.84 m/s] in velocity change.

a16_0301100.speaker: Young
a16_0301100.text: Pete, you're on the High Gain. Do you want Reacq and Narrow?

a16_0301100.speaker: Peterson
a16_0301100.text: Just a moment. Reacq and Narrow, Charlie.

a16_0301100.speaker: Young
a16_0301100.text: Okay, the star check checks out good. It's right in the middle, and the waste water dump is in work.

a16_0301100.speaker: Peterson
a16_0301100.text: Say, again, John; I didn't copy that.

a16_0301100.speaker: Young
a16_0301100.text: Star checks good; it's right in the middle, and the waste water dump is in work.

a16_0302257.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0302257.text: Don, could you tell us if - if the Delta-V C number you gave us includes any kind of a bias to compensate for the minute of EMS on time prior to ignition?

a16_0302257.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0302257.text: Yeah, I'm not asking for one; I'm just asking if that's in there.

a16_0302257.speaker: Peterson
a16_0302257.text: Okay, stand by while I check it. [Long pause.]

a16_0302257.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0302257.text: Okay. We're terminating the waste water dump now.

a16_0302257.speaker: Peterson
a16_0302257.text: Ken, the PAD does take that into account. [Pause.]

a16_0302257.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0302257.text: This is Apollo Control at 30 hours, 29 minutes. We're now about ten minutes away from the scheduled ignition time for the midcourse correction maneuver to be performed with the spacecraft Service Propulsion System engine, a very short burn of about two seconds duration. This maneuver will change the point of closest approach to the Moon from it's present value of about 117 nautical miles [217 km] down to the desired altitude of 71 nautical miles [131 km] at which point the Lunar Orbit Insertion maneuver would be performed placing the spacecraft in the nominal 58 by 170-nautical-mile [107 by 31

a16_0303304.text: Okay, we've pressurize the - the - pressure in the SPS now.

a16_0303304.text: Helium Valves. You got two in Auto, right?

a16_0303304.text: [Garble] have to go without that TVC Servo Power, AC1 and AC...

a16_0303304.speaker: Young
a16_0303304.text: Okay. Then RA - RHC number 2 to AC.

a16_0303304.speaker: Young
a16_0303304.text: You have Spacecraft Control to SCS.

a16_0303304.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303304.text: Main A? Here we go; one.

a16_0303304.speaker: Young
a16_0303304.text: Okay. Verify trim control and set. Verify...

a16_0303304.speaker: Duke
a16_0303304.text: Okay, Houston. I'm looking at oxidizer pressure of just about 210. We're going to leave the valves in Auto.

a16_0303304.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303304.text: Pitch is good. Yaw is good.

a16_0303304.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303304.text: [Garble] feel that baby this time. Okay, going to CMC.

a16_0303304.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303304.text: MTVC is good in pitch, good in yaw. Back to neutral. They go back to zero, back in CMC. Key Release. Pro.

a16_0303304.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303304.text: All right. Want me to get - let me get the atti - We're still oscillating. Let me get that squared away before I go back to...

a16_0303304.speaker: Young
a16_0303304.text: Okay, let's Enter on that, okay?

a16_0303304.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303304.text: But don't Pro yet. Okay, got that.

a16_0303304.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303304.text: Sure does. Plus 2. Minus 2. Boy, did that thing pulse on zero. Trim. Looks good.

a16_0303304.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303304.text: Okay. Scale is 5/1. Going to Rate, High. Wait for 59. I got Delta-V, 8.3. You're gonna need Bank A.

a16_0303304.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0303304.text: This is Apollo Control. We're now about three minutes away from the ignition of this midcourse correction. Everything continues to look good. The spacecraft is in the proper attitude, the SPS tanks are pressurized. And we're now two minutes, 35 seconds from ignition.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: [Garble] this way. Turn her off at three seconds, or if you holler.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: Okay. Did the pressure stop going up?

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: Okay. But - but it stopped on its own. It wasn't because you let go.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: Okay. That was all I wanted. All righty.

a16_0303605.speaker: Duke
a16_0303605.text: Fuel side went up to about 175.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: Okay. Okay, [garble] I what there was about that Delta-P? We haven't made such an issue of the Delta-P before.

a16_0303605.speaker: Duke
a16_0303605.text: See that? We said fuel and Ox greater than the Delta-P - greater than 35, Ox greater than fuel. That's what we got right now. Man, I thought I burned them all.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: Okay. Coming up on - coming up on a minute. Still have no thrust light on. I have no translation control power on because we don't have any - don't have any ullage.

a16_0303605.speaker: Duke
a16_0303605.text: Well, if you want to trim, you got plenty.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: We'll get this one right on time. See if their bias looks good. Oh.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: Mark it. The Delta-V in Normal. The light is still out. I 'm bringing on Delta-V Thrust Switch A. Stand by.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: Yeah. Nothing more to do but monitor and shut down an overburn.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: [Garble] flashing. Okay. That doggone EMS isn't even going anywhere.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0303605.text: Coming up on ten seconds to ignition.

a16_0303605.speaker: Young
a16_0303605.text: Have you seen the SPS Thrust light? [Laughter.] Okay.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: I don't know, John. I really don't.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0303605.text: And our Guidance officer reports the burn is complete. It was scheduled to be a two second burn with a change in velocity of 12.6 feet [3.84 metres] per second.

a16_0303605.speaker: Young
a16_0303605.text: Well, the old burn's complete, Houston. It's a big boot.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: Okay. You want that to go to translation - we take that to 0.2, right?

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: Okay. No weight to make. I'll let you -

a16_0303605.speaker: Duke
a16_0303605.text: Delta-V C was plus or minus 3.17

a16_0303605.speaker: Duke
a16_0303605.text: Okay, what was our trim attitude?

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: Okay, you got these? Okay, just hit [garble].

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: Let - let's get some gimbals off.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0303605.text: Servo Powers are Off. Got the residuals killed.

a16_0303605.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0303605.text: And we're still waiting for the preliminary numbers on that burn. First reports from the Guidance officer...

a16_0304106.speaker: Duke

a16_0304106.speaker: Duke
a16_0304106.text: Okay, Delta-T IG was 0. Burn time was, on my watch, 2.1. We got trim within an attitude of 094, 352, 008; plus 0.1; minus 0; plus 0.1; Delta-V C , minus 3.1. Fuel's reading 010, and Ox, 010; no unbalance.

a16_0304106.speaker: Duke
a16_0304106.text: And on board, our fuel - Okay, Pete, and on board, the fuel pres - during the burn, the fuel pressure dropped to 170 and the oxidizer dropped to 200.

a16_0304106.speaker: Young
a16_0304106.text: Okay, Houston, our LM/CM Delta-P is 0.8. You want to go ahead and do the Tunnel Vent to Vent until greater than 2.7, right?

a16_0304607.speaker: Peterson
a16_0304607.text: Stand by 1. I'll get you a number. [Pause.] They're saying an hour and 50 minutes.

a16_0304607.speaker: Young
a16_0304607.text: That's about what we - that's about what it looks like to me.

a16_0304607.speaker: Peterson
a16_0304607.text: John, you using Charlie's wristwatch to get that number? [Pause.]

a16_0304607.speaker: Young
a16_0304607.text: No, I was just remembering how small that tunnel venthole is.

a16_0304607.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0304607.text: This is Apollo Control at 3 hours - at 30 hours, 52 minutes. It'll probably be on the order of 2 to 2½ hours from now before the Flight Dynamics Officer has sufficient tracking data to confirm that the midcourse correction had the desired effect; that being to lower the point of closest approach to the Moon from the value that we had prior to the maneuver of 117 nautical miles [217 km] down to the desired altitude of 71 [nautical miles - 131 km] and also to place the spacecraft arrival time at the desired Flight Plan time. The preliminary numbers however did appear to be normal and we'l

a16_0305200.speaker: Peterson
a16_0305200.text: 16, would you verify H 2 Tanks 1 and 2 Heaters, Off, and H 2 Tank 3 Fan, Auto?

a16_0305200.speaker: Young
a16_0305200.text: Oh, oh, we got Tanks 1 and 2 Heaters in Auto, and - and Fan 3 in Auto. I'll turn H 2 Heaters 1 and 2, Off.

a16_0315311.speaker: Young
a16_0315311.text: Okay, Houston. We're up to 2.1 on the LM/CM Delta-P gauge now.

a16_0315311.speaker: Peterson
a16_0315311.text: Roger. Copy 2.1. [Pause.] And while I'm talking to you on this oxygen-tank pressure gauge, it's starting to look like there's a bias in there of about 14.7 [psi - 101 kilopascals] due to the fact that the reference chamber has apparently leaked its 1 atmosphere reference value down to probably vacuum. And that, coupled with a 5-psi [35 kilopascals] meter bias, should give you a total bias of about 20 psi [138 kilopascals] on the oxygen-tank pressure. But the gauge seems to be working okay except for that bias, so we're going to continue to follow it so we can give you a - maybe a better number

a16_0315311.speaker: Peterson
a16_0315311.text: It's doing the same thing as the - as the panel we were - we looked at last night, huh?

a16_0315311.speaker: Duke
a16_0315311.text: That's affirm, except for - It - it's not nearly as bad, and it's just primarily on the inboard side, but it is beginning to get the shredded wheat appearance like the other one. Over.

a16_0315311.speaker: Duke
a16_0315311.text: Pete, on the outboard side [clears throat] right out near the quad - or right above the quad - on that same panel, it - it seems to me it's beginning - it looks like it starts out with a very fine, shaggy-grass-type stuff, and then slowly peels up into the shredded-wheat type. Over.

a16_0320306.speaker: Peterson
a16_0320306.text: 16, Houston. When you get a minute, we've got a - an addition to the Flight Plan at 32:48. [Long pause.]

a16_0320306.speaker: Young
a16_0320306.text: Roger. Go ahead with your 32:48 addition.

a16_0320306.speaker: Peterson
a16_0320306.text: Okay. We want to add a note to read the LM/CM Delta-P. [Pause.]

a16_0320306.speaker: Peterson
a16_0320306.text: And we want to get that prior to that CM/LM pressure equalization decal. [Pause.]

a16_0320306.speaker: Peterson
a16_0320306.text: And, Ken, that - we've made an ink correction on the back of that AOS/LOS Sun-wheel aid there. When you getting around to digging that out, I can give it to you, or I can pick it up later. [Pause.]

a16_0320306.speaker: Young
a16_0320306.text: Ken's busy right now. Say again. Over.

a16_0320306.speaker: Peterson
a16_0320306.text: Okay, on the back of the Sun wheel - the AOS/LOS Sun wheel - we've entered an ink note to account for the fact that we change REFSSMAT in the middle of his work there. We made an error on it. We've got to change the note now, and sometime when he's got that wheel out, I can read him up the correction.

a16_0320306.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0320306.text: This is Apollo Control at 32 hours, 5 minutes. A few minutes ago, Charlie Duke reported additional paint apparently peeling from another of the aluminum skins on the Lunar Module, and from Duke's description this appeared to be one of the surfaces in the area of Quad 1 on the Lunar Module. This would be the quad adjacent to the Commander's station in the crew compartment. And Duke said that there were about three square feet of surface area involved. He described the appearance of the surface about as the other surface which had also peeled. Ranging from what he said was a kind of a sprouting

a16_0320306.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0320306.text: This is Apollo Control at 32 hours, 26 minutes. Here in the Control Center the Lunar Module Control officer has replayed the tape of Charlie Duke's description of the additional surface of the LM that appeared to be peeling - where the paint was peeling, similar to the way panels below the docking target were reported peeling yesterday. From Duke's description, we were not able to pin point the precise panels involved although it is obviously very close to the area that was reported peeling previously, and appeared much the same from Duke's description. The paint which is painted on the very t

a16_0323141.speaker: Young
a16_0323141.text: Okay, Houston. We're maneuvering to the attitude.

a16_0324300.text: Okay, Houston, we're going to come on with the direct O 2 and pump up the cabin.

a16_0325200.speaker: Duke
a16_0325200.text: Okay, we copy. We'll go to 3.4. [Long pause.]

a16_0325703.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0325703.text: This is Apollo Control at 32 hours, 58 minutes. The LM cabin has now been vented down to the desire - desired pressure level and the crew will shortly begin repressurizing the cabin to about 5 to 5½ pounds per square inch. Following that, they will be preparing to enter the Lunar Module. I expect that will require about five to ten minutes. The Flight Plan calls for them to be in the LM by about 33 hours and five minutes or about seven or eight minutes from now. They will have to remove the tunnel hatch, the probe and drogue assembly, and then crawl through the tunnel into the Lunar Mod

a16_0330734.speaker: Duke
a16_0330734.text: Okay, Houston, we're about ready to remove the hatch.

a16_0330734.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0330734.text: That was Charlie Duke reporting that the crew is about ready to remove the hatch allowing them to get into the LM tunnel, remove the probe and drogue assembly which will clear the tunnel and allow them to enter the Lunar Module.

a16_0331413.speaker: Young
a16_0331413.text: [Faint.] Charlie's floating on over there now.

a16_0331413.speaker: Young
a16_0331413.text: Houston, Charlie's floating on over to the Lunar Module now - to check on old Orion.

a16_0331413.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0331413.text: That was John Young reporting Charlie Duke, as he put it, "floating over to the Lunar Module now." That report came at 33 hours, 14 minutes, and we expect that Young will be following shortly.

a16_0331413.speaker: Young
a16_0331413.text: Houston, that docking tunnel index, minus 3.5.

a16_0331413.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0331413.text: This is Apollo Control. We're awaiting the first bits of data from the Lunar Module as Young and Duke begin partially powering the vehicle up. The Flight Dynamics Officer just reported that, as a result of the midcourse correction performed at 30 hours, 39 minutes, the spacecraft appears to be on the desired trajectory and will be approaching the Moon at an altitude of about 71 nautical miles [131 kilometres] at its closest point prior to the Lunar Orbit Insertion maneuver. This is the preplanned value. We also have an update on the predicted impact point for the Saturn third stage, the S-IVB.

a16_0332110.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0332110.text: Rog, Don. Did you guys get the tunnel index? [Pause.]

a16_0332110.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0332110.text: And, Don, I'm holding off on the oxygen heaters. I'm keeping them all three in Auto until we get the surge and repress tanks built back up. That okay? If you would like for me to turn them off, I can reconfigure now; otherwise, I would like you to help me remember not to leave them on.

a16_0332110.speaker: Peterson
a16_0332110.text: Roger, we concur, Ken. [Pause.] We'll remind you.

a16_0332110.speaker: Mission Control
a16_0332110.text: This is Apollo Control, at 33 hours, 47 minutes. We've heard nothing from John Young and Charlie Duke, since Young reported about 30 minutes ago that they were entering the Lunar Module Orion. The crew is scheduled to be stowing items that they've carried over from the Command Module and then we'll begin powering up the Lunar Module, according to checklists that they will be carrying on with them. And shortly after they begin the partial power up, we should see telemetry data of most of the critical systems aboard the Lunar Module.

a16_0335357.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0335357.text: Hey, Don, can I talk to you about the docking latch?

a16_0335357.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0335357.text: You all set, or do you want me to wait a minute?

a16_0335357.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0335357.text: You weren't on board at the time, that's right, we were talking to Gordy...

a16_0335357.speaker: Mattingly
a16_0335357.text: But that's one of the things we reported and the plate that goes over the bungee fairing is cocked slightly. And now that we've got everything cleaned out of the tunnel, I can look in here. It's real obvious that the bungee hasn't fired completely. It's down; the top of the bungee is recessed about a half of an inch down. It looks like it just hadn't triggered and, as a matter of fact, I'm looking at the latch and, by golly, I can see between the latch and the total ring, so it didn't even pull down against that. And I really obviously don't have any concern for it; except I'm - I've never see

a16_0335357.text: Casper, we capt - we got all the data we need and we're going to take a look at it. We do not want you to recock and fire the thing manually and we'll get back to you later.

a16_0335831.text: And, Houston, Casper turned over the power supply to Orion at 33:58. [Pause.]

a16_0335831.speaker: Peterson
a16_0335831.text: Roger, Casper.

a16_0335831.text: With Ken Mattingly's report that he'd turned over power to the LM; which came at 33 hours, 58 minutes; we would expect shortly to begin seeing telemetry data from the Lunar Module. Also Mattingly commented on a problem that had been reported previously and that is that one of the 12 docking latches on the Command Module apparently had not latched firmly around the docking ring of the Lunar Module, as would normally be expected.
