a16_1030500.speaker: Young (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: What I haven't been able to figure out is whether it's a.m. or p.m.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: p.m.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: You can feel those thrusters burn.

a16_1030500.speaker: Young (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Yeah.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Okay, 35 minutes, the Ascent Bats are coming On. They're On - at 103:42.

a16_1030500.speaker: Young (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Okay, if we're 66,000 feet, we're probably gonna have 10 or 15 or 20 feet a second more to start with.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Yeah. Okay; Throttle Control we got. LMPs we got.

a16_1030500.speaker: Young (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Yeah.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Rate Scale, 25 Degrees per Second?

a16_1030500.speaker: Young (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Go.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Att/Translation, 4 Jets?

a16_1030500.speaker: Young (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: 4 Jets.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Okay. Check DCS [sic] - DPS, APS, RCS. Let's go look at the DPS. Okay. APS - was okay. Okay. Okay, there we go. Press l, Press 2. Pressure's coming down. It must be cooling off. Supercrit [garble] - but that ambient's okay. Okay. Okay?

a16_1030500.speaker: Young (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: The switch guards are checked.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Okay. ECS looks good.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Bias my gages, and EPS.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Okay? The Commander's Bus, Inverter 1.

a16_1030500.speaker: Young (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Inverter 1 is closed, Charlie.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Okay; going Descent 1.

a16_1030500.speaker: Young (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Okay; we've still got the S-band antenna open.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: That's okay. That's just the high gain; and we're not using that,

a16_1030500.speaker: Young (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Okay.

a16_1030500.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16_1030500.text: Coming up at AOS in a moment - at six minutes.

a16_1030500.speaker: Young (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: See my - It's shedding.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: It is? Yeah, I know. Uh-huh. Right out front.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: I wish I had a drink of water.

a16_1030500.speaker: Young (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: I don't know what that noise is, but it really is something.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: It sure is.

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Man, that really is something. We don't even have VHF Ranging on. Well, we got it on, but Ken's not locked up.

a16_1030500.speaker: Young (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: That Moon is really some kind of place!

a16_1030500.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1030500.text: Yeah.

a16_1034900.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1034900.text: Okay, it's gonna be almost - by - let's see, we're six hours late and it's three degrees - about a 15-degree Sun angle, John.

a16_1034900.speaker: Duke (LM comm)
a16_1034900.text: We'll be having AOS here, momentarily.

a16_1034900.speaker: Mission Control
a16_1034900.text: This is Apollo Control; 103 hours, 49 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Less than two minutes before Apollo 16's spacecraft, Orion and Casper, come around on the 16th revolution. Some 27 minutes away from ignition for the powered descent and subsequent landing which should take place around 8:23 pm Central Standard Time. Ignition for the descent to the lunar surface is now programmed for a Ground Elapsed Time of 104 hours, 17 minutes, 23 seconds. As Casper comes around the corner it should have circularized its orbit around the Moon with the burn maneuver for circularization having taken place at 1

a16_1034900.speaker: Mattingly
a16_1034900.text: Hello, Houston. Casper did it this time.

a16_1034900.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_1034900.text: Hey, good show, you want to give us a report?

a16_1034900.speaker: Mattingly
a16_1034900.text: Okay. Okay, the burn was on time and for the right duration. And the residuals were plus 0.2, plus 0.2, and 0. That was after a trim: and the attitude for those residuals was 161.38, 132.96, and 0.12. Delta-V C was minus 8.5; the oxidizer is 32; the fuel is 34; and the decrease-increase is pegged at decrease, probably because of the short duration. The burn required a trim. The original residuals were plus 1 and plus 0.6 and plus 0.7. So I had to roll in order to take out the Z-components.

a16_1035315.speaker: Irwin
a16_1035315.text: Orion, this is Houston. How do you read?

a16_1035315.speaker: Young (LM)
a16_1035315.text: Loud and clear, Jim.

a16_1035315.speaker: Irwin
a16_1035315.text: Okay. I have a couple of comm procedures for you...

a16_1035315.speaker: Young (LM)
a16_1035315.text: Okay. Jim, I...

a16_1035315.speaker: Irwin
a16_1035315.text: ...on Panel 12, will you get the Function switch to Range; and on Panel 11, Updata Link circuit breaker closed. [Pause.]

a16_1035315.speaker: Young (LM)
a16_1035315.text: Updata Link is closed, Function switch to Range.

a16_1035315.speaker: Irwin
a16_1035315.text: Roger. And I'm standing by for your report.

a16_1035315.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_1035315.text: Roger; and would you give us the trim attitude again, please.

a16_1035315.speaker: Duke (LM)
a16_1035315.text: And, Jim - Okay, we got the Ascent Bats On at 103:42. The ED bats are Go at 37 volts.

a16_1035315.speaker: Irwin
a16_1035315.text: Roger; copy. The Ascent Bats 103:42, and ED bats are good. [Pause.] And I have a PDI ephem update...

a16_1035315.speaker: Mattingly
a16_1035315.text: Okay, I'll give you again the trim attitude, and this is for these 210 residuals. That's after trimming, that was 161.38, 132.96, and 0.12.

a16_1035315.speaker: Young (LM)
a16_1035315.text: And we were on Inverter 2 for a while.

a16_1035315.speaker: Irwin
a16_1035315.text: Copied. You were on Inverter 2.

a16_1035315.speaker: Duke (LM)
a16_1035315.text: Go ahead.

a16_1035315.speaker: Young (LM)
a16_1035315.text: Go ahead.

a16_1035315.speaker: Hartsfield
a16_1035315.text: Roger; copy.

a16_1035315.speaker: Irwin
a16_1035315.text: Okay...

a16_1035315.speaker: Young (LM)
a16_1035315.text: Just for a little while.

a16_1035315.speaker: Irwin
a16_1035315.text: ...India, 104:17:24.66; DEDA 231, plus 56990. Over. [Pause.]

a16_1035315.speaker: Mattingly
a16_1035315.text: And, Hank, I did complete the fuel cell purge.

a16_1035315.speaker: Irwin
a16_1035315.text: Good readback. [Long pause.]

a16_1035315.speaker: Mattingly
a16_1035315.text: Standing by.

a16_1035315.speaker: Duke (LM)
a16_1035315.text: Hey, was that 56991 or [5699]0, Jim?

a16_1035315.speaker: Duke (LM)
a16_1035315.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a16_1035315.speaker: Duke (LM)
a16_1035315.text: Do we have an up-link, Jim?

a16_1035315.speaker: Irwin
a16_1035315.text: Roger. If - You have P00. If you go to Data, we'll send you some up-links

a16_1035315.speaker: Mattingly
a16_1035315.text: Okay. That's 104:19:11; 24:01; 25:41; and 26:29; north 3 miles.

a16_1035315.speaker: Duke (LM)
a16_1035315.text: Okay. You have it, P00 and Data.

a16a1044126.text: This is Apollo Control and Orion is safely on the ground at Descartes, having landed at 104:29:36 Ground Elapsed Time. In local time that's 8:23 p.m. [The] time of landing [was] not to far away from the planned landing point. After the crew has a chance to power down the Lunar Module, do some housekeeping they will have a sleep period which will begin at about 107 hours, about two hours and ten minutes from now. With EVA 1 starting tomorrow morning out about 10:30 a.m. Central Standard Time. This is Apollo Control at 104:51.

a16a1044126.speaker: Duke
a16a1044126.text: That suits us.

I haven't been able

I think we had so much adrenaline pumping we could have gone, probably two

a16a1052742.text: Okay. We copy that. [Very Long Comm Break]

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Okay, Houston. We're down to getting rid of the armrests (at the top of the right column on page 1-9 ). By the time we get this jettison bag full, I don't know if we're going to be able to open the door. 105:43:13 England: Right. I know what you mean. (Pause) [Jones - "Does Tony's statement imply that he went through some of these LM activities at some point in the training cycle?"] [Duke - "Yeah. He did that. Not with us; but he would practice so that he knew what it was like to doff and suit and to do all the activities, so that he could be familiar with it."] [Jones - "Let's see, the suppor

a16a1052742.speaker: Duke
a16a1052742.text: Okay, Tony. My personal dosimer (sic; means "dosimeter") reads 21109.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay; 21109. (Long Pause) When I went through that jettison business, I felt like I was throwing away half the cabin. [Contrary to the impression that Tony gives, the only items being stowed in the jettison bag at this point are three armrests: John's left-hand armrest and both of Charlie's. Additional items will be put in the jettison bag during the EVA Prep which, because of the landing delay, won't be done until after the first rest period. Nonetheless, removal of the armrests probably makes the cabin seem larger.]

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Mine is 22050, Houston.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay; 22050. (Long Pause) 105:44:24 Young: Okay, Houston. Before we do the ETB part of the cabin prep, we are going to take our suits off (as per page 3-4 ).

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: If we'd been smart, we'd have took them off at the first part of this thing.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: (Chuckles; Pause) Before you get your suits off there, you may want to bring that 500 millimeter forward from behind the engine cover there (as per the bottom of the left column on page 1-9 ). [Jones - "Was the 500-mm lens on a separate camera?"] [Duke - "It wasn't a separate camera. It was a separate lens. We'd just attach the lens to the Hasselblad."] [Jones - "Did you have three Hasselblads out on the surface, one for each of you and one for the 500?"] [Duke - "We might have. You're right; we had a separate...Gosh, now you've got me thinking."] [Jones - "I can't imagine trying to change tha

a16a1052742.speaker: Duke
a16a1052742.text: Tony, we're ahead of you. We already did that. And we got everything out from back here, and I'm putting up the ISS (Interim Stowage Shelf) now, and John's getting his stuff off (as per the right column on page 3-4 ).

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Good show. [Long Comm Break]

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1052742.text: Mm-mm!

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1052742.text: Okay, if you're listening, tape recorder, we're passing over King now. And - something I hadn't noticed before kind of unusual out here. There's a lot of clumpy material all around King. The central peaks definitely have big blocks sticking up in them. The things that we've called dark material are not dark, but rather they are big blocks that cast some pretty long shadows. They look like they're piled on top of some very soft and unconsolidated material. But they are indeed big blocks on the central peaks. And - I'll also say that they're on - surprisingly, they're mostly on the eastern side,

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1052742.text: Where'd you go, you sucker? [Sigh.] What'd that color wheel say I should have here? Let's see, 1/250, f/8.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Hello, Houston. Casper.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Casper, Houston. How do you read?

a16a1052742.speaker: Duke
a16a1052742.text: Okay, Tony. We've got three of us in here now; John's out of his suit.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Loud and clear.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: And, I assume, all three are walking around. (Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Casper, Houston. We need barber pole plus three on the camera.

a16a1052742.speaker: Duke
a16a1052742.text: Well, not exactly. One of them is sort of lying there (on the engine cover, face down as per page 3-4 ). [Comm Break] [Duke, from the 1972 Technical Debrief - "It's a piece of cake getting out of those suits. It sure fills up the cockpit; they seem to be fatter than all those old training suits. We stowed them back on the engine cover, but we still had enough room to do everything."] [A composite image ( 2.5 Mb ) made by Ed Hengeveld from Apollo 17 post-EVA photos AS17-134-20522 and 25, giving a wide view from the LMP's station.]

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Henry, I'm gonna - Okay, barber pole plus three.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: You have it. And would you remind me when you get about 30 seconds from Pan Camera to Stop.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Will do.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: I want to mark something on my chart, and then I'll talk to you for just a minute.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Roger.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay. And I put Battery A on Charge at 105:35.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Roger. Copy.

a16a1052742.speaker: Duke
a16a1052742.text: Tony, are y'all getting the high-bit-rate data here now? (Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Yes, we do, Charlie.

a16a1052742.speaker: Duke
a16a1052742.text: Okay. John should be back up here (on comm as per the second paragraph on page 3-5 ).

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Okay. I read you, Tony.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: I've got you out the window now; but it looks like half of you have gone away. It's all black.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Very good, John. (Pause) [They had planned to spend 30 minutes doffing the suits. John got out of his in only 10 minutes, in part because the suit is clean and the urine bags were only partly full.]

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: I hope we're in the sunny half.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: I guess our opinion of this operation right about here is that the cooling is really marginal in the suits, and we'd like to get permission to get a shot of cold (LCG) water through the suit loop, even with the power down situation, to keep us from sweating so much. Would that be okay? Whenever we're doing something in the suit, working in the cabin?

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Oh, I bet you're in the dark half. Aren't you? That shows how long it's been since you've been outside.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: It has been a while.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: As I came over, I finally got squared away; and as came across King, I had the binoculars out. And, sure enough, on the central peaks down there - the things we've been debating for so long about whether they were streaks or outcrops or what they were - are large blocks, which are on the - the central peaks. Most of the blocks seem to lie on the eastern side of the peaks; however, there are a few blocks on the western side - enough that you can tell that the reason they look dark is they cast pretty long shadows because they're pretty huge blocks. The floor looks like it's - looks like an old

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. We have to talk about that here. (Long Pause) Yeah. There's no problem with that, John.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Well, thank you. Just a shot, you know, like maybe 30 seconds worth, at a clip. (Long Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Orion, Houston. (Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Go ahead, Tony.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. On your Cabin Gas Return (Valve) , we'd like to go to Auto. [This step is at the bottom of the right column on page 3-4 .]

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Roger. Auto on the Cabin Gas Return.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. And on the Suit Gas Diverter (Valve) , to Cabin. (Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Okay, it's Push/Cabin.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. (Long Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: We got that, Ken. And, Casper, could we get High Gain, Auto?

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: You've got Auto, now.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Okay, Houston. We've got an ECS (Environmental Control System) H2O Sep light (on) . Isn't that because we got to go to Sep 2 or something while we're in this mode? (Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: And it's oscillating. Suppose I go back to - there it is. Okay. I had a little tone in my headset that was beeping very softly, and the signal strength was doing the same thing.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Copy, John. We're working it. (Pause) [The ECS contains two centrifugal water separators which remove excess water from the oxygen stream. As per the instruction near the middle of the left column on page 1-8 , they are currently using Separator number 1.]

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Yeah. The Suit Gas Diverter Valve is chattering; it's making a sort of a purr. (Long Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Roger. You want to go Block on the computer, Ken. And we show your Optics still in Manual. And, Ken, you're about ten seconds from Pan Camera, Off.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay. The computer's in Block. Okay.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: I was a little late with that one.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: [Laughter.] Okay. No sweat. We got it done. I'll check the Optics. And when you're ready, I'll start configuring the SIM bay.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: And, Hank, would you verify that it's okay to take the Optics and put them to CMC - or to zero them. I sure don't want to take any chances with it.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay, John. We'd like you to switch water separators. (Long Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Okay. It's okay. They say nothing will happen.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: And, Ken, we've got a little trouble with the High Gain. We need to go back to Reacq.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Okay. We're in Pull to Sep 2.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. [Comm Break. The control used to select between the two separators is a push/pull control.]

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay. I'm in Reacq. Want to go back to Auto now?

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Stand by. Okay. Cleared to go to Auto.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay. Auto it is. You got a good one that time. And if you're ready, I'm ready to start deploying things here.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Okay, Ken. Would you stand by? We're waiting for OSO to get his data.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Oh, very well.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Dum-de-dum (singing).

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Ken, while we're waiting here, how did your extend time go on the mapping camera?

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: I didn't time it that time, Hank. I - sorry.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Okay.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Casper. Pan Camera Power, Off.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Okay. We've still got a Water Separator light in here.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay. Pan Camera Power is Off.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Mark it.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. We copy that. (Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: OSO has his data now. We can proceed with boom deployment.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Let me tell you what our configuration is here. We're in Pull/Sep 2. The Cabin Gas Return (Valve) is in Auto. We're on primary (ECS) LiOH cartridge. The Suit Circuit Relief (Valve) is in Auto. We're in Push to Cabin, and our hoses are stowed against the bulkhead.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay. We button this up. Okay, the first one you'd like is a - how about a mass spec for 61 seconds?

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. We copy that. (Long Pause) Okay, John. Separator speed is slowly climbing up there. It looks like it will make it up all right. It's just a bit slow.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: That's affirmative.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay. Going to Deploy...

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Mark.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Okay, fine. (Long Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Deploy is Off this time.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Roger. You're clear to start the gamma ray out.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Orion, Houston.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Speak, Tony.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. They're thinking you may have the water-in-the-hose problem. They'd like you to drain the hoses down towards the floor. Maybe we can get some of that out of there. They'd also like you to hold your hand over the blue hose, to make sure you're getting good flow. (Long Pause) [After John took his suit off, he stowed the LM hoses in attachments on the wall. Note that, on checklist page 3-4 , near the bottom of the right column, they had the option of drying the suit out or stowing the hoses as per "Configure ECS for Sleep" on page 3-4 . Because they have not done an EVA yet and the suits ar

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Gamma ray is going out.

a16a1052742.speaker: Duke
a16a1052742.text: Okay, Tony. I'm back up (on comm). How do you read?

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Five by, Charlie. [It has also taken Charlie about ten minutes to get out of his suit.]

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Gamma ray is stopped.

a16a1052742.speaker: Duke
a16a1052742.text: Okay. (Concerning) this ECS , on the Push to Cabin, it sounds like to me that there's a flapper valve or something chattering back in there that is, sort of, perhaps stagnating the flow in the loop.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Okay, Ken. And could you give us barber pole plus 4 on the Map Camera.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay. That should be one more step. Right?

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: That's affirmative.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: All right. You've got it. Okay, now the Mass Spec experiment is going to On. The Ion Source is going to Standby.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Yeah, that's what it sounds like to me, too. (Long Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. Are you getting flow out of the blue hose?

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Alpha Particle and X-Ray Door is coming Open...

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Mark. And it's good.

a16a1052742.speaker: Duke
a16a1052742.text: That's affirmative.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: We're getting it out of there, but I feel the same way that Charlie does. It's got something trapped in there.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Yeah. Okay.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: And it (meaning the oxygen)'s coming out in pulses. Matter of fact, I can make it play what it sounds like for you. (Fluttering valve noise) Now what you hear there is the mike, right up against the hose and the hose blowing against the microphone. It's not a constant thing. It just sort of chattering like some valve in there is not doing its thing.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: And the X-Ray is coming to On...

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Mark.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: All right. We heard that, John. (Long Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: [Garble] somebody looks real good right now a - like to read you up a TEI-26 PAD block data.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay. Would you stand by just a second while I get some food going here?

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Charlie's is the same way.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Okay.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay, John. We'd like to go back to Egress on the Suit Gas Diverter (Valve) , and give us a mark when you do it. (Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Okay. 3, 2, 1, Mark. Okay. That's Egress on the Suit Gas Diverter.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. (Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Flow's good in Suit Gas Diverter.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. We copy. (Pause) Okay. We understand. All your noise went away?

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Yeah. It doesn't chatter any more in the Push to Cabin valve.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. [Comm Break]

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Ken, for your information we're planning on your retirement - to rest that is, at 109:30, the nominal time.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: I'm glad you clarified that.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: I hope you realize I'm too young to retire.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Roger.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Can you tell me anything about the status of the surface guys? Are they gonna get at least two EVAs out of this?

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: I think the plan is now, Ken, for two EVA's. They are busy buttoning up the LM now and getting ready to get some sleep. They're gonna move the EVA times - at least the first one's gonna be tomorrow morning about 10:30 Central, I think.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: And we're gonna change our shifts around too, so I'll be on again in the morning, and then Stu'll get it in the afternoon.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay. All right, now I got something soaking here. I'll be ready to copy. Okay. Go ahead.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Okay. The Suit Separator light is off now, of course.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. (Pause) [According to the Mission Report, the problem was ultimately traced to the Cabin Gas Return Valve , which allows gas to flow from the cabin back into the ECS . Apparently, the valve was not functioning properly in the Auto position, probably because of contamination in the valve mechanism. Figure 14-38 from the Mission Report shows the flow paths and subsystem locations in the ECS/Cabin/Suit system. Figure 14-39 shows details of the Cabin Gas Return Valve operation. They will return to the problem at 106:48:11 .]

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: Charlie's got the 500 all configured (as per page 3-4 ) and it works, which I'm not surprised (about) since it was stowed like it was expected to hit a lot harder than we could.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: (Chuckles) Okay.

a16a1052742.speaker: Young
a16a1052742.text: One of those 30g bags.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Well, it's nice to have a camera work. (Long Pause) [Jones - "I take it that 500 was well padded?"] [Duke - "Yeah. If I remember, the stowage configuration for this thing was like the Rock of Gibraltar. They were concerned that, if we hit hard and it rattled, it would break it."]

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay. That's a TEI-26, SPS/G&N; 38726; plus 0.72 plus 1.33; 125:14:27.47; plus 3170.3, plus 1101.6, minus 0310.1; 181, 089, and 021; Sirius and Rigel were the angles off the circ pad; two jets, 17 seconds; Lambda 179.02, and that's a minus.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay, John. At your convenience, we'd like to go back to Sep(arator) 1. (Pause)

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Good readback, Ken.

a16a1052742.speaker: Duke
a16a1052742.text: You got it.

a16a1052742.speaker: England
a16a1052742.text: Okay. [Comm Break] MP3 Audio Clip (13 min 17 sec)

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Okay, Ken; we're gonna leave you alone and let you eat now. We've still got about 49 minutes to LOS. And at your convenience, sometime a little later, we'd like to get the crew status report from this morning, which was omitted.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: [Laughter.] Okay. That's gonna take some bookkeeping; I'll work on that. Sure would rather look out the window, Hank.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Did anybody ever give you some words on the undervolt last night?

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Yes. The words we got were that I inadvertently attempted to get the pan camera on the same time the heaters all came on and - I guess the transient was just - just too much.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Roger. That's - that's the story as I get it.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Is that the way you understand it?

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: Right. That's affirmative.

a16a1052742.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1052742.text: Okay, well - I'm sorry we missed those photos, but it - it sure seamed like the prudent thing to do at the time.

a16a1052742.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1052742.text: We concur.

a16a1061545.speaker: Young
a16a1061545.text: Okay, Houston. I'm up to frame number 30 on mag A, Charlie's camera, and I just finished shooting sort of a partial pan out the front window. Man, this place is...It's not, anywhere, flat around here. 106:16:06 England: Very good, John. A-30. [After undocking from the Command Module, John and Charlie took photos AS16-113-18279 to 18295 on Hasselblad magazine A, also listed in the catalogs as AS16-113. Here, they have taken photographs out the LM windows. John took 18296 to 18303 out the left window and Charlie took 18304 to 18310 out the right window. Dave Byrne has assembled a composite .]

a16a1061545.speaker: Young
a16a1061545.text: It's rolling terrain. And I really don't believe we're going to have any trouble at all getting up on the side of that hill (meaning Stone Mountain), although the slope...I don't know, the slopes up toward Crown look like maybe 20 degrees. We'll have to take that very carefully. [The Rover was designed to handle slopes of up to 26 degrees. They will drive to the vicinity of five small craters named the Cincos (Spanish for "Fives"), for their first stop on EVA-2.]

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Roger. What about...

a16a1061545.speaker: Young
a16a1061545.text: That first bench is like about 10 degrees, but from there up to Cinco and Echo, it gets rather steep there.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: How about boulders?

a16a1061545.speaker: Young
a16a1061545.text: It is like we described, as very benchy on Stone Mountain. Boulders: well, we landed in a block field, you know.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Right. (Pause) Can you see any up on Stone?

a16a1061545.speaker: Young
a16a1061545.text: No. Sure don't. Yeah. Maybe there is. When we get closer to it, we'll be able to tell better. I see some funny shadows up on top of it.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Any problems in trafficability out on the EVA-1 direction (west)?

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Tony, I...(Stops to listen)

a16a1061545.speaker: Young
a16a1061545.text: It's gonna be a piece of cake, I think.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Beautiful.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Tony, the problem looks like finding a flat spot to deploy the ALSEP. It's just hummocky, rolling terrain with 4- or 5-meter ridges.

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: Henry, another thing that turns out to be a - a pretty nice little gadget is these nets that are in the stowage compartments. Particularly when you get in the food locker when it's about half full. Things are able to stay under some semblance of control. And that's a mighty nice thing.

a16a1061545.speaker: Young
a16a1061545.text: Yeah, 100 meters from here, it (meaning the ALSEP)'s going to be on the side of a hill.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: We can probably put it over to the left there, John. (To Houston) Tony, I looked out, down to about 4000 feet (during the landing at 104:27:03 ), assessing North Ray area. There were some large blocks, maybe 5 percent of the surface up around the rim. But, as you look back (south) towards Palmetto, they really petered out in a hurry, and I think we're going to be in good shape going that way (on EVA-3).

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: So those are working out real good, huh?

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: Yes, it sure is. That's been a very - help.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Good show.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: One final comment here so I get back to work. About in my 1 o'clock position, about 30 meters out, just beyond the LM shadow - about twice as far as the LM shadow - there is a secondary crater with a large meter-sized block still in it. It looks like it formed the secondary, and it's got black and white...The top 3 percent or 5 percent of the block is black and white. Apparently, below that is solid white. Over.

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: And, Ken you don't have to acknowledge. Look our plans are in the morning first thing to give you a clock sync and get back into the Flight Plan.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Very good. 106:19:07 Duke: And those black-and-white blocks, you can see them all over the place. [They will find these black-and-white breccias at many of their geology stops. These blocks were probably ejecta from South Ray Crater. Charlie comments on them again at 107:05:28 .]

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Is the (secondary) crater round, or is it oblong? Can you get a direction? [Secondary craters are formed in the low-velocity impacts of ejecta from high-velocity, primary impacts. If the secondary impact is relatively oblique, it will gouge an elongated crater which will show the direction of flight of the ejecta fragment.] 106:19:22 Duke: Yeah. It looks like to me it came from South Ray. It's oblong, stoved in (that is, deeper) towards Palmetto, just like those ones down at the Cape that they dug out with a bulldozer. [Jones - "I take it that you're talking about some practice craters..."] [D

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: That sounds like a good plan.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Oh, come on. You always got it.

a16a1061545.speaker: Young
a16a1061545.text: After about 2 or 3 hours, we always got it. (Pause) [Jones - "John's comment here suggests that, on some of your geology exercises, they'd dump you out with a map but didn't tell you exactly where you were."] [Duke - "That's right. Just to help us with map reading and figuring out how to adjust traverses. And that would give us training, and it would give the Backroom training. They'd put us out close, but they'd make it so we had to figure out where we were. And that was good training."]

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Are you through with your cabin prep there?

a16a1061545.speaker: Young
a16a1061545.text: Charlie's loading the ETB (as per the right column of page 2-1 ). Can't but one guy do that at a time because it's too crowded over there.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Rog. Okay. The one thing we would like you to see if you could decide before you get out is where you would put ALSEP. (Long Pause)

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: Oh, one thing you've got to be careful of up here is - when you go to look outside, you kind of have to watch it because you get your - you get too greedy and you get your nose up against the window. About one breath is all it takes, and it's all fogged over.

a16a1061545.speaker: Young
a16a1061545.text: Well, we'll keep looking at it; but the trouble is, right in front of us, about 50 meters, there's a ridge, and I don't know what's on the other side of that ridge. Out about 100 meters, I can see a lot of blocks, but I can't tell whether there are craters out there or not, because we're at zero phase. I just don't think we could make a prediction at this point.

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: Roger. I understand.

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: I think our humidity must be running fairly high.

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: I'm passing over a nice little guy right now and would guess - on, I haven't been paying any attention to where I am - looks like I must be - probably looking the the north at - somewhere around the - Guts - Gutenberg uplands. And I'm passing over a little crater that's got another large fill in the center and nice big crater in top of him, a little crater chain around it. And as I said earliest, everything out here has this linear pattern or these lineaments and it doesn't matter whether it's a flat surface, a horizontal, vertical, inside of a wall of a crater - they all seem to have it in on

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Okay. We copy that. (Long Pause)

a16a1061545.speaker: Young
a16a1061545.text: Those blocks around South Ray are about the whitest blocks I've ever seen, around the rim of that one. (Pause) 106:22:33 England: Okay. And, John, about the time we saw that separator spinning down, we saw a rise in the suit loop pressure. We'd like you to confirm that you connected the suit hoses, blue-to-blue and red-to-red. (Pause) The stowage on the wall. [Here, Tony is asking if the blue suit hose was attached to the blue wall mount and similar for the red hose.]

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: Okay, Ken. if - if our plot board up here is right, you ought to be in - coming up on landing site.

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: Okay. Let's see.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Tony, that's affirmative. Blue-to-blue and red-to-red.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Okay.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: That was on the wall. Now they are disconnected. The blues are disconnected at this point.

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: Oh, maybe I'm out the wrong window here.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Okay. We copy. [Comm Break]

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: You're right, Henry.

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: And, if you'll remember that little black dot that we drew on our map and talked about. There's a little black spot about in the right area, and I don't have my map so I just looked out at it. But I'll come back next time and take a look and - sure like it is something - entirely different texture.

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: Are you talking about right in the area of the landing site?

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: In the - in the landing site area, but not in the landing site - traverse regions. But that little dark thing looked like a - a possible cone that was out to the - north and to the west. There's a little black dot out there that looks like there may be something that's - that is distinctive. And next time I come over, I'll be better prepared to look for it.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Just to put your minds at rest a little bit about EVA-1, we're looking at a pretty nominal EVA-1. We'll probably give you some new targets for the UV camera, and we can do that real time. And we won't have the TV when you get out. We'll get it when you get the LCRU (Lunar Communications Relay Unit) up. But otherwise, it looks pretty nominal right now. (Pause)

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: Okay. I remember that one, that was in the edge of the plotter, wasn't it?

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: Yes, sir.

a16a1061545.speaker: Young
a16a1061545.text: Roger, Tony. [Comm Break. As was the case on the prior missions, the TV camera is mounted in the MESA so that Houston could watch the astronauts descend the ladder.] [Duke - "Since we were powered down (to conserve LM battery power in the aftermath of the late landing), we weren't going to do that (meaning watch John's initial descent to the surface, the Rover deployment, etc.). We were going to wait until we got it (meaning the TV and the LCRU) on to the Rover before we would have the TV."] [See Tony England's transmission at 116:15:01 for a full explanation of Houston's reasons for deleting

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: I tell you, it sure is impressive how much - how much the scenery changes as the Sun angle changes and how rapidly that goes down.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Okay, Tony. I've got the EVA maps out (as per the last typed item in the "Stow in ETB" paragraph on page 2-1 ) and as I can gather here, we got two maps and one return chart. Is that what you agree with? (Pause)

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Okay; we'll work that a second. (Long Pause) Okay, Charlie. That looks good here.

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: Your plot boards show me over Albategnius, you say?

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: Say again.

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: Does the plot board show me over Albategnius?

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: That's affirmative.

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: Okay. Now let me tell you a little something here. Just to the north and mostly to the west of Albategnius, the ground - and I think in the higher Sun it's going to look like - look a lot like Imbrium sculpture but not here. It has the mottled effect and the same appearance that the Descartes area had at the same Sun angle yesterday. And that's almost directly south of - it's a little south and a little bit to - of Ptolemaeus, and it's a little bit to the east of Alphonsus.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Okay. I'm going to optimistically leave the walking traverse map in the cabin.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: All right. [Jones - "Did you do much training for walking traverses?"] [Duke - "No."] [Jones - "Just talked about it?"] [Duke - "Yeah."] [Comm Break]

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: Roger. You ought to be coming up on a terminator now. Is that right? Pretty close to it?

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: Yes, sir. My view is disappearing rapidly.

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: You should be over Ptolemaeus now.

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: Casper, for your information, everything in the SIM bay is looking good now.

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: Okay. I just saw something that - I really don't know what to make - I'm in the - I think the spacecraft is just about in the dark, but not quite. We've passed the ground terminator, and I'm looking out of window number 3 down towards the ground. I'm trying to get a preview of what's coming in earthshine. And there's a bright flash that's going along out there. At first, I thought there was something that was on the deck, but it's apparently a piece of debris that's in orbit with us. It's sitting there, tumbling over and flashing.

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: It's traveling along with you.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Okay, Tony. The ETB is stowed over in my corner.

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: It moves across the ground, so it must be a piece of debris. Yeah.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Okay, very good. (Long Pause)

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: And you know, in training, I could barely lift this thing, and, in one-sixth(-g), it's one finger. (Pause)

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: As a matter of fact, I look around now and there's quite a few of those.

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: Can you get any idea how far away they are...

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Just tells me we should do more work on the Moon.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Boy, I'll say. [Comm Break]

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: ... Depends on what effect that has on - no I can't, Hank. It's just a piece of something that's out there, and it's tumbling so that it gives you an occulting reflection. No field [feel?] at all for it, but it's moving in approximately the same velocity that we are.

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: Ken, in reference to your observations of Crater King, we got some ideas about those swirls that are northwest of King. And we'd like for you to get a comparison of those with the swirls of Ibn Yunus. And I wonder if those also have topographic expression?

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: Okay. I'm too - I'll have to do that some other time, because today I'm too far south to see those things up by Ibn Yunus. I can just barely see up to Neper.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: How's the ECS looking to you now, Tony?

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Right now, it's looking pretty good. [Comm Break]

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: Roger.

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: But we sure need to keep that in mind.

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: And another thing you might be thinking about if you get an opportunity on some round is to get us a description of the area north of Crater King, including the Soviet Mountains.

a16a1061545.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1061545.text: Yeah. I was thinking of looking at that. I really hadn't planned to spend much time on King this time. I was going to just kind of look at the - look at the ole crater there. But, got so interested in it that - it looked like there's another crater that's just to the east of King that has, say, a little bisected, central feature just like King. You know the thing that makes that - that little Y-shape. And it looks the same way. That's kind of - kind of interesting, I thought.

a16a1061545.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1061545.text: Yeah. I guess we hadn't seen that in the photos.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Okay, Tony. We've done all of your sequence here. We got the suits off and stowed, the cabin configured, and I guess we're ready to go to an eat period and bed down. Okay? 106:35:33 England: Okay. I've got a little bit of a checklist change I'd like to read up to you here when you're ready. It's in the Surface Checklist.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Go ahead. 106:35:45 England: Okay. This debriefing with Houston (on checklist page 3-5 in the middle of the left column) will be at 106:28. The time now is 106:35, so we're real close on that. Your eat period is to start 106:43. And then the PLSS and O2 and H2O recharge we'll skip. The feedwater recharge we'll skip. On to the next page ( 3-6 ). The Pre-sleep at 107:28, and we'll skip the computer work there, that first line under Pre-sleep. And the rest period will begin at 107:53. And number 8, the next step (at the start of page 3-7 ) will be at 115:53. That will be post-sleep. Again, in tha

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Stand by. Hey, you lost me, Tony. Okay. Here we go on page 3-7, Post-sleep. Go ahead. 106:37:03 England: Roger. Post-sleep on page 3-7 . Step 8 there - or my number 8 - is at 115:53, that's post-sleep. And then three-quarters of the way down that page under post-sleep, there is some computer work, "Pro, Verb 37 Enter". We'll drop all of that. Eat period will begin at 116:18. And the last line on that column is "top-off PLSS O2" (which) we'll delete. Okay. On the EVA-2 Planning with Houston, we'll skip all that, and then we'll don suits on the next page 3-5 . We'll don suits at 117:03. (Pause)

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: We copy.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: ...Okay, and at the end of that page we'll go to page 2-5 (to start the pre-EVA-1 tasks). (Pause)

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Okay. 106:38:08 England: Okay, and (on 2-5) we'll prep for EVA-1 at 117:53, and then, from then on, we're nominal. (Pause)

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Okay. At 2-5, what was the time?

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Okay, copy. Let me go through this now. (Pause) Okay. We've doffed the PGAs. EVA debriefing with Houston comes next as step 2. Step 3 is the eat period.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Okay, Charlie.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Turn the page. Step 4...(Stops to listen) Go ahead.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Okay. Just to get our steps numbered straight here, I guess, assigning numbers to these things. Debriefing with Houston is step 4, eat period is step 5. And the times you read were right, and then the Pre-sleep is step 6 and each number goes on from there.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Okay. Pre-sleep is 6, (animated) then we wake up for post-sleep! And that's number 7.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Roger. Rest period is number 7.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: And we got a...(Stops to listen) Oh, okay; rest period is 7. I see. Okay. And then 8 is post-sleep?

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: That's affirmative.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: And skipping the computer activity stuff, number 9 is the eat period; and we delete the "top-off the PLSS"; we turn the page, we skip...Well, we skip EVA-2 planning; we turn the page and that step, don suits, is next.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Right; that's number 10.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: And that's step 10. (Pause) Okay. Then we go to 2-5, and we're just about back to nominal, then.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Rog. And that's step 11 on 2-5.

a16a1061545.speaker: Duke
a16a1061545.text: Copy.

a16a1061545.speaker: England
a16a1061545.text: Okay, have a good meal. [Duke, from the 1972 Technical Debrief - "We had a few changes because of landing six hours late. They had us power down the AC bus and also the LGC DSKY breaker to save power, and all that worked just great. I thought those procedures came up in good shape. We just floated right through the checklist for those changes and then we were right on."] Landing at Descartes Apollo 16 Journal Window Geology

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: Okay, Tony. Let's do the debriefing. We don't really...I'd like to describe for a LM window description. We had so much practice at that, I'd like to see how I could do. [Charlie wants to try his hand at a description of the scene out his window.] [Jones - "Would you do this sort of thing when you went out on field trips to Hawaii or wherever?"] [Duke - "Yeah. They'd start us out (as if we were) in the Lunar Module; and we'd sit there and just describe what we could see from about 12 o'clock around to 3 o'clock. And we'd describe everything: the size of the rocks, the terrain, if we could see

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Have at it. We'll take (meaning "listen to") any words you've got. We expended all our questions a few minutes ago with John, and in fact I didn't even have to ask any; he just answered them all. But press on.

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: Okay. Looking out at 12 o'clock on the horizon, there is a very hilly, subdued region - well, let's say hilly terrain - at 12 o'clock that goes on out of view around to 11. It's rolling with white pockmarked craters there, and I'd say that's maybe 50 to 100 meters above the surrounding terrain where we are. As you move around from 1 to 3 o'clock, approaching the...At about 1 o'clock I would say we can see maybe a kilometer or so, but it might be very deceiving on that distance. And we see more rolling terrain, similar in albedo. It's a light gray, with fresh craters being white. As we come on

a16a1064036.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1064036.text: I guess, Hank, I ought to be passing Flamsteed now.

a16a1064036.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1064036.text: Roger. That looks right.

a16a1064036.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1064036.text: It's really impressive how much you can see in the dark.

a16a1064036.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1064036.text: I don't believe you can see as much now as you could last night. Of course, partly we're - I'm higher now than I was when I looked at it last night. And the Earth is noticeably smaller, so I guess it's getting - it's losing it's reflective ability rather rapidly.

a16a1064036.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1064036.text: Roger.

a16a1064036.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1064036.text: I was also very impressed with the way you could see the - the LM outline in earthshine. That was something I had not anticipated. Last night as we came across - well let me see what it was - it starts with an H - over on the western rim. Hevetius. Yeah. We drove across that last night, and you could really see the floor patterns in that beautifully.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Very good, Charlie. Where again was this boulder with the fillet?

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: It's at about 2:30, maybe a couple of hundred meters out, and it's on this side of the ridge that trends east-west here, that blocks out Smoky.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Okay. Could it be sliding down the ridge, and that's why the fillet's on the south?

a16a1064036.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1064036.text: Okay, Hank. Let's see. I owe you a crew status report from this morning. Right?

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: That might be the reason. I was just going to say, it's downslope so that might have been what happened.

a16a1064036.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1064036.text: Roger.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Very good.

a16a1064036.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1064036.text: Okay. Let's see if I can give you that thing now.

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: Though the slope doesn't appear that steep, Tony.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Okay. How about the Buster area? Can you identify that? [As indicated on the "Descartes EVA-I, III 1 of 3" traverse map ( 3.0 Mb or 0.6 Mb ), Buster is a 90-m crater centered at CB.2/76.5. See also, a detail from the Pan Camera frame . The LM can be seen near the right edge of the picture area just above center. North is up and the LM is in the bright area created by the engine exhaust on the west side of a small crater. The large crater at bottom center of the picture area is Spook and the large crater at the upper left is Flag. The diameter of Spook is about 350 meters. Buster is the 100-m c

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: Boy, that's really...(Stops to listen) We sure saw it on descent. I don't see it right now. There's a bright crater to the right, maybe 50 meters of what I think is Spook, which is probably Buster, but I really wouldn't swear to it. [Spook is centered at about CA.0/77.0 and is about 400 meters across.]

a16a1064036.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1064036.text: Okay. Alpha 1, 22047; Alpha 3, 6; Alpha 4, negative. Bravo 1, 15044; Bravo 3, 6; Bravo 4, negative. Charlie 1, 21095; Charlie 3, 7; Charlie 4, 1 Seconal.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Okay. Can you tell (meaning "see") boulders over there?

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: There's not a one, as far as I can see.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Okay. (Pause) Very good, Charlie. You're right up to your old peak. 106:45:49 Duke: Coming down on...(Listens) Okay, coming down, Tony, on descent it looks...As John has described...There's a distinct ray pattern across our landing site from South Ray. And the boulders get...effectively (thin out and) disappear by (the time) we get to Palmetto. And then they don't reappear again until almost the flank of North Ray. (On the "Descartes EVA-I, III 2 of 2" map and the corresponding contour map, which is Figure 3.6.2-4 in the Lunar Surface Procedures volume) you can see that depression that trends

a16a1064036.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1064036.text: We copy, Ken.

a16a1064036.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1064036.text: Okay. Now I'm going to try to go down the menus here. We're looking for Day 4. Is that correct?

a16a1064036.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1064036.text: Affirmative.

a16a1064036.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1064036.text: Okay. On commander, Meal A, you can delete the mixed fruit, and meal B, you can delete pea soup; Meal C, delete chicken stew and add a chocolate pudding. For me, you can take Meal A and delete the mixed-fruit. You can delete the bread and Jelly. On Bravo, you can delete the pea soup, meatballs. On Charlie, you can delete the chicken stew, and I guess that takes care of those things. The reason for so many of these - we all deleted these canned things, because we got them all over the spacecraft last time, and we decided that we really couldn't afford to do that again.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Very good. You were mentioning the boulders and the rays from South Ray. The ray itself, could you map out what extent it was, or was it just the whole general area? [Here, Tony is asking about a bright ray from South Ray Crater that crosses the landing site and shows up on the "Descartes EVA-I, III 2 of 2" map as the whitish streaks running SW to NE around Spook and the Turtle Mountain area. See, also, the larger scaled maps shown in Figures 3.6.1-1 and 3.6.2-3 in the Apollo 16 Lunar Surface Procedures volume.] [Readers should note that, although John was looking out the window from before pi

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: It was a pretty wide ray coming across here. I would say it goes from our position perhaps to Spook. And maybe behind us maybe another 100 meters or so.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Very good. How about left-right extent, did it go all the way back to South Ray?

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: Well, you'll have to ask John that. I couldn't see out that way. As we...The biggest block that I saw was one we flew over which is maybe 100 meters to 200 meters behind us, and it looked like Volkswagen size.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Very good. (Pause) [The Volkswagen "Beetle" is about 1.5 meters high, 1.5 meters wide and 4.5 meters long.]

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: John is off comm momentarily. He'll be back up in a little bit, and I'm going to start the chow. (Long Pause)

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: And, Tony, I wouldn't give you 2 cents for that orange juice as a hair tonic; it mats it down completely. 106:48:11 England: Well, that might be the point. [Young, from the 1972 Technical Debrief - "The night before (the landing), we filled the drink bags full of orange juice in the CSM; and the next morning, prior to suit donning, we put them in the suit. Charlie really got covered with it. It really was an annoying proble

a16a1064036.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1064036.text: Roger. We copy.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: We'd like to go your Suit Gas Return (valve) back to Cabin. Give it a try. (Pause)

a16a1064036.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1064036.text: Okay. And let me find Charlie's here.

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: Okay. We'll try it in Cabin. We also tried this in orbit and we got the same sound, Tony. We're going to Cabin now. Mark. (Pause) Okay, it gives us the same sound.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Okay, we'd like to go back to Egress.

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: Hey, Tony. I tell you what it is. I just (manually) opened the Cabin Gas Return (Valve) and it stopped it (meaning the noise). What it was is that the Cabin Gas Return check valve is not working right. The flow is great now. (Long Pause) Our configuration is Suit Gas Diverter (Valve) , Push-Cabin, and Cabin Gas Return to Open, and everything sounds normal.

a16a1064036.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1064036.text: Okay. Here's Charlie's. And on Meal A, you can delete mixed fruit and jelly. Meal B, you can delete sugar cookies. Meal C, you can delete the pudding and the chocolate bar.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Okay. We'd like to leave you that way. (Pause) 106:49:33 Duke: Okay. Have you guys got a suggestion of what meal you want us to eat? (Pause)

a16a1064036.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1064036.text: Roger. Copy.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: We're working that one. (Long Pause) [The meals were listed in the Medical Log and, because of the landing delay, Charlie wants to know if Houston wants to change the order. Details for the meals can be found in the LM Menu given in the Apollo 16 Press Kit ( 5.6 Mb PDF ).] [Jones - "Can you describe how the meals were packaged?"] [Duke - "Yeah. Let's see."] [Jones - "Were all the packages for one meal taped together?"] [Duke - "Yeah. Each day we had packets for each meal. Like Day 1, Meal A. A, B, C was for breakfast lunch and dinner - (although), on the lunar surface, we only got to eat two m

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: (Ready to answer Charlie's meal question) Okay.

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: I got day 5, meal B.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: I guess we'd like you to just go ahead with your first lunar meal. I guess that deserves some champagne, I don't know.

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: Well, like John said earlier, we're definitely not going to get scurvy; we've got so much orange drink here.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Rog. (Long Pause)

a16a1064036.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1064036.text: Now we're coming across Hevelius again, and I can see Grimaldi and a couple of fractures that go across its rim. You can really see a lot of detail here. You can see the rilles, you can see - as everybody pointed out, the - they look like ribbons that are just dropped down, and they go all the way across the crater like Hevelius. And it looks like they go out from [garble], and they come down - in fact, they go all the way down to Grimaldi. And just before they get to Grimaldi, they run into a crater. And it looks like they might have been filled a little bit. In fact, it looks the same way th

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: Okay, Tony. We're going to eat day 5, meal B. (Pause) [Charlie's "B" sounds more like "D".]

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Okay. Was that Dog?

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: Bravo, as in "boy."

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Rog. (Long Pause)

a16a1064036.speaker: Duke
a16a1064036.text: Houston, John finally found his spoon.

a16a1064036.speaker: England
a16a1064036.text: Very good! (Long Pause) [Jones - "John lost his spoon?"] [Duke - "Yeah. I don't know where or when; I don't remember the details, now; but we looked high and low for that spoon. And he finally found it. (Chuckling) And I don't even remember where he found it!"] MP3 Audio Clip (3 min 06 sec) . a16a1065300.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1065300.text: Roger. That sounds real interesting.

a16a1065300.speaker: Young
a16a1065300.text: Hello, Tony. (I'm) back on comm. (No answer; Pause) Tony?

a16a1065300.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1065300.text: Riccioli has quite a few elongate little craters around it. Several of them that are - elongate - and one of them is quite long. I'd say it's maybe - it's curved and looks like it's maybe ten kilometers long. And it has just a slight arc to it. But, it is a very elongate feature. Now, we are moving into material that's very hilly and I don't see a lot of small craters. I don't see a lot of bright ones. You can see bright rims in here quite well. The things that do stand out to the west of Riccoli are the very dramatic cross cutting graben-type rilles. They cross, in one place here, almost 90 d

a16a1065300.speaker: England
a16a1065300.text: Go ahead. [In reading the following ray discussion, readers may want to refer to Figures 3.6.1-1 and 3.6.2-3 from the Apollo 16 Lunar Surface Procedures volume and Figure 6-4 ( 648k ) in the Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report .]

a16a1065300.speaker: Young
a16a1065300.text: I can't see how far the rays...I just assumed that this is a block field we're in from South Ray. It goes about 100 meters out at 10 o'clock and goes over a ridge and disappears. The next time I see it, is at South Ray, which is, you know, pretty far away from here (about 6 km). South Ray is a doggone interesting crater. I wish we could get to it. [See AS16-112- 18246 , 18247 , and 18256 , which are 500-mm frames taken from Station 4. David Harland has assembled the mini-pan . See, also, a portion of the Apollo 16 Pan Camera frame, taken from the Service Module, which shows the area south of t

a16a1065300.speaker: Young
a16a1065300.text: The boulders on the west rim of it (meaning South Ray Crater) are just thick and white as they can be, and in the middle of it - you know, on your map where it looks like it's a depression - there appears to be a brown...(Having some trouble expressing himself) A sort of a gray, patch of dirt or something that was thrown out of that side of it. And then on the north, there's another ray of very white boulders coming out of it. Of course, we could see the ray pattern long before pitchover. At 22,000, I was able to get my nose up against the window and see...The clue to where we were was South R

a16a1065300.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1065300.text: Roger. Copy.

a16a1065300.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1065300.text: Ken, we have...

a16a1065300.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1065300.text: Okay, Houston, we are getting ready to...

a16a1065300.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1065300.text: Ken, we've got your Flight Plan here...

a16a1065300.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1065300.text: Go ahead, we're ready for LOS, so...

a16a1065300.speaker: England
a16a1065300.text: Very good. How about the albedo?

a16a1065300.speaker: Young
a16a1065300.text: I can't...(Listens)

a16a1065300.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1065300.text: Okay. Do you have time to read it to me?

a16a1065300.speaker: England
a16a1065300.text: How about the albedo?

a16a1065300.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1065300.text: I think so; if you are ready to copy.

a16a1065300.speaker: Young
a16a1065300.text: Tremendous difference in albedo. On the...North Ray is pure white; South Ray is pure white; and it blends into a gray (as you move away from either crater); and then over here by us, it's almost totally gray. I guess you just get the feeling that these rocks (around the LM) may have come from somewhere else (rather than from the immediate landing area). There's a big subangular rock that I see at 10 o'clock - no, at 11 o'clock at about 100 meters (out from the LM) - that I would sure like to go over and look, because it looks like it's just one big piece of whatever rock it is.

a16a1065300.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1065300.text: All right. Can you tell me where I should start?

a16a1065300.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1065300.text: Okay. LOS will be at 107:02. Approx...

a16a1065300.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1065300.text: Okay. Should I be in the Flight Plan or should I be writing in something separate?

a16a1065300.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1065300.text: I think you better write in something separate.

a16a1065300.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1065300.text: Okay, stand by. Okay, shoot.

a16a1065300.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1065300.text: Okay. 107:02 LOS. And approximately 107:10 - approximately eight minutes after LOS, configure DSE - stop High Bit Rate, Command Reset, Forward. 107:21, sunrise. 107:25, O 2 Heaters 1 and 2, Auto. O 2 Heaters, three, Off. 107:38, Image Motion, Increase. Barber pole, plus 3. 107:48, AOS. 107:57, Pan Camera, Standby - Stereo, Power. 107:58, 13 - This is your T-start. Pan Camera, Operate. Mass Spectrometer, Ion Source, On. At the same time - right after you get the Pan Camera. 108:04, Motion, Increase, barber pole, plus 4. T-stop. 108:28:13 - that's also T-stop for the mapping camera, which read u

a16a1065300.speaker: England
a16a1065300.text: Right; I was wondering about...

a16a1065300.speaker: Young
a16a1065300.text: Oh, and I do happen to see a white clast in the bottom of it.

a16a1065300.speaker: England
a16a1065300.text: I was wondering about the albedo on your surface chart, on the strips and things, whether the rays are as obvious as they are on the high-Sun-angle chart that you're carrying, or whether they look very much different at your low Sun angle.

a16a1065300.speaker: Young
a16a1065300.text: No, they're not, I don't think. I can see from here down to Survey Ridge (BT/83) and the albedo on there is a lot lighter. It's a general...(correcting himself) gradual downslope from our landing point to Survey Ridge, and it looks like it drops maybe a hundred meters and then starts to go right back up Smoky Mountain (means Stone Mountain). I guess you could see on a contour map where the low spot is.

a16a1065300.speaker: England
a16a1065300.text: Okay...

a16a1065300.speaker: Young
a16a1065300.text: But there are some strange looking craters over there on Stone Mountain (see, for example AS16-113- 18325 ), and the albedo contrast is really pronounced in those craters. There's some...(Pause) It may be a function of shadow, we better wait until we get over there. I hesitate to say, they almost look like big...(Pause) Well, they must be impact craters, I guess. [Jones - "I know that some of the geologists were hoping to find evidence of volcanics on Stone Mountain. Is John speculating about that here?"] [Duke - "He doesn't want to commit to what it is, yet."] [Jones - "But is he entertaining

a16a1065806.speaker: England
a16a1065806.text: Okay. I was just wondering about whether you could recognize whether you're on a ray by albedo as well as the boulder content.

a16a1065806.speaker: Young
a16a1065806.text: I think you're going to be able to; but, boy, you're not going to pick up a contact; it just tails out into something.

a16a1065806.speaker: England
a16a1065806.text: Outstanding, that's better than I thought.

a16a1065806.speaker: Young
a16a1065806.text: You ought to be able to work across the contact. [The nature of the ray edges, the lines of contact with non-ray material, was a point of practical interest. If the contacts were sharp, then John and Charlie could sample material on both sides at one geology stop. Here, John is saying that, while there are no sharply defined contacts, he thinks they will be able to find places that are definitely on a ray or off a ray.]

a16a1065806.speaker: Young
a16a1065806.text: But you mainly would do it (that is, tell if you were on a ray) by the white boulders in the ray, I think. I can see, on ridge lines, from here, I can see three different rays out of South Ray, I believe. (We'll) have to go down there and look at them to make sure. They seem to be riding on the ridge lines, although that's probably deceptive because I can't see down in the holes.

a16a1065806.speaker: Duke
a16a1065806.text: Tony, one other comment from my side. Distances are pretty deceiving here for me. I'm looking out over John's shoulder, and it looks like to me you could throw a rock into South Ray from our present position - which is, I know, impossible. [Young, from the 1972 Technical Debrief - "I think, because we practiced so much with the L&A, we had a pretty good hack on how far away we were from things."] [Training photo 72-H-430 shows John and Charlie doing a traverse simulation in which the TV image from the Landing and Ascent (L&A) facility - consisting of a site model suspended over a moveable TV c

a16a1065806.speaker: Duke
a16a1065806.text: A second comment has to do with the orbital, since we got so much (of a) look at the ground sailing around (for three extra orbits) waiting to come down. Everywhere we saw the ground - which is just about the whole sunlit side - in the crater walls and on the ridges, we had the same lineation that the Apollo 15 photography showed on Hadley Delta and Hadley Mountain (see, for example, AS15-90- 12208 ). It was really remarkable how, in the crater walls, primarily, and in the ridges....And it gave you the impression that it was a fracture pattern that was all trending parallel to the...(finding t

a16a1065806.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1065806.text: Outstanding. You guys really do good work. Okay, I think I've got everything here. I didn't have any questions about it. You want me - How much time do we have? I don't know whether it's worth trying to read back or not?

a16a1065806.speaker: England
a16a1065806.text: Okay, very good.

a16a1065806.speaker: Young
a16a1065806.text: And I'm looking out here at Stone Mountain, and I got a picture of it (earlier). And it looks like it's got...Looks like somebody has been out there plowing across the side of it. The benches just look like one sort of terrace right after another, right up the side. And they sort of follow the contour of it right around. [John is referring to the pictures he took at 106:16:06 , particularly AS16-113- 18296 . See, also, 500-mm frame AS16-112- 18217 which shows the summit of Stone Mountain as it appeared from near Spook Crater at 124:24:53 . In the 18 hours between the times at which these pictu

a16a1065806.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1065806.text: Okay, we've got 2 minutes to LOS. You don't have to read back. I think...

a16a1065806.text: Okay, here goes. 107:02, LOS. 107:10, configure DSE - stop High Bit Rate, Command Reset, Forward. 21 is sunrise; 25, O 2 heaters, 1 and 2 to Auto. O 2 Heaters Tank 3, Off. 38, IMC, Increase; barber pole, plus 3. 48, AOS; 57, Pan, Standby - Stereo and Power. 58, 13 - Pan Camera to Operate; Mass Spec Ion Source, On. 04, that's 108:04, IMC to barberpole, plus 4. 28, 13, T-stop for Pan Camera to Standby and Mapping Camera to Off.
