a16a1211132.speaker: Duke
a16a1211132.text: That works like a champ.

a16a1211132.speaker: England
a16a1211132.text: Right. That new wrench is pretty slick.

a16a1211132.speaker: Duke
a16a1211132.text: Yeah, it is. (Pause) [Charlie gets the drill off, grabs it by the wire loop and puts it down, well out of the way.]

a16a1211132.text: (Talking to a piece of equipment) Why don't you open? (Laughs) Video Clip ( 1 min 12 sec 0.3 Mb RealVideo or 11 Mb MPEG )

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: (Moving forward) Okay. The next one we skip because it has got a black wire on it. (Long Pause) [As Fendell follows John, Charlie comes into view. He is on the northeast corner of the magnetometer, trying to release the sunshade as per the instruction printed on LMP-18 under the symbol for the 3-foot close-up of the magnetometer.] [Because of the skipped location, the distance between shots 11 and 12 is 30 feet (9 meters).]

a16a1221101.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1221101.text: I tell you, Hank, I think that the terminator got hung up here on a high mountain or something. It doesn't look like it's moving as much as it is everywhere else on the Moon.

a16a1221101.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1221101.text: Roger. Is Davy still in the dark?

a16a1221101.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1221101.text: Well. I'm not to it yet, but it sure - I don't see anything beyond it. That's a - Hey, old Alphonsus and Arzachel show up nicely. And here comes the crater chain, by golly. Yes, but much to my amazement, but the peak in Albategnius is still - is in daylight.

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Okay, number 12, Houston. (Pause) 4, 3, 2, 1, Fire. (Long Pause) [Charlie appears to be pulling a lanyard to deploy the sunshade and the southwest arm moves inward in response. AS16-113- 18372 is Charlie's close-up, which has probably been taken by now. The sunshade is the roll of gold-foil material on a string suspended between the SW and NW arms.] [John walks forward to the top of the ridge and positions himself for the next shot.]

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Number 13, Houston. (Long Pause) 4, 3, 2, 1, Fire. (Pause) [Now that John is out of the depression, we see the spray of dust kicked up by the thumper.]

a16a1221101.speaker: Duke
a16a1221101.text: It's firing, babe, I'll tell ya.

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: It's getting me all dirty. Video Clip ( 2 min 44 sec 0.7 Mb RealVideo or 24 Mb MPEG )

a16a1221101.speaker: England
a16a1221101.text: Great. Not great it's getting you all dirty; great it's working. (Pause) [After standing motionless for ten seconds, John moves forward for the next shot and Charlie goes around to the southwest arm and pushes it down.]

a16a1221101.speaker: Duke
a16a1221101.text: Okay, Tony, one of the arms of the LSM, when I pull the sunshade, the arm to the northwest (means southwest) (pause) does not lock.

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Well, lock it, Charlie.

a16a1221101.speaker: Duke
a16a1221101.text: How do you do that? By pushing down?

a16a1221101.speaker: England
a16a1221101.text: Charlie, they don't lock.

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: No, it doesn't arm (means 'lock'). They don't lock. 122:17:51 Duke: But I can't unravel this sunshade; it pulls up the arms. (Pause) Go ahead (with the next shot).

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Okay. (Pause)

a16a1221101.speaker: England
a16a1221101.text: Okay, if you can't get that out there...

a16a1221101.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1221101.text: Oh, I see what's happened now. There's a - there's a little hill that's shielding - I - I see where Davy Crater Chain is now. And it's right in the middle of a big long shadow that's being cast out there. And it's shielding that whole area because Davy and Davy Y show up nicely. And Davy G is easy to see. But the chain itself, I can just make out, and I'll take a picture - well, this is a skewed angle. I don't know if I can get it to show you, buy - they sure must not have much of a lip on them if they don't show. But, by the time we see them, they may be in a fairly high Sun.

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Houston; number 14.

a16a1221101.speaker: England
a16a1221101.text: ...just leave the sunshade down.

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Okay, 4, 3, 2, 1, (Fire)...(Long Pause) [After the thumper fires, John forgets to remain motionless and starts forward after only a couple of seconds.] [Charlie steps between the SW and NW arms and reaches in carefully to take hold of the sunshield.]

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Okay; Number 15, Houston.

a16a1221101.speaker: England
a16a1221101.text: Okay.

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: 4, 3, 2, 1...(Long Pause) [This time, John remembers to stand still. Just before Tony's next transmission, Charlie frees the sunshade.] [John runs forward to the next location. He covers the 4.5 m distance in 8 strides.]

a16a1221101.speaker: England
a16a1221101.text: Charlie, I guess we'd just like you to leave the sunshade alone; just let it hang there.

a16a1221101.speaker: Duke
a16a1221101.text: I got it. It was wrapped around a couple of times. I didn't touch (it more than a) little bit, or disturb (the) level. It's okay.

a16a1221101.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1221101.text: I'm taking a strip this time, anyhow, because it'll show all the area around Davy. And there are some craters in there - an awful lot of them that have absolutely no rims, which seems to me - it looks entirely different than what you see and what you think of. These things are all very subdued. They just drop in. And you see glows - in the low Sun, you see the - you see the far lip before you see the near lip of the crater. Although there are a few that have raised rims and they - they kind of are the exception here instead of the rule. Whereas most low-Sun-angle places we see are - I'll take

a16a1221101.speaker: England
a16a1221101.text: Okay.

a16a1221101.speaker: Duke
a16a1221101.text: Wait a minute, John. Okay. [Charlie moves away from the LSM and gets settled for the next shot.]

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Okay, number 16, Houston.

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: 4, 3, 2, 1, Fire. (Pause) Okay. (Long Pause) [John moves forward and Fendell follows him.]

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Okay, number 17, Houston. Video Clip ( 2 min 55 sec 0.8 Mb RealVideo or 26 Mb MPEG )

a16a1221101.speaker: Duke
a16a1221101.text: Just a minute, John. (Pause)

a16a1221101.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1221101.text: Roger, Ken. And you're about 20 seconds from T-stop on the mapping camera.

a16a1221101.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1221101.text: Okay. Going to it. Thank you.

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Ready, Charlie?

a16a1221101.speaker: Duke
a16a1221101.text: Yeah, go ahead.

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Okay, number 17 again, Houston.

a16a1221101.speaker: England
a16a1221101.text: Okay.

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: 4, 3, 2, 1, Fire. (Pause) Okay. [John moves forward.]

a16a1221101.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1221101.text: And, Hank, this system is really good. I don't have to give a second thought to - to what's going on. And just by not having to watch that clock, it just frees your hands to go do everything else that you want to do. It really - on the back side, I get all bent out of shape with myself because I get - I get behind. I start - You just don't have a chance to do anything except those items which are timelined A, B, C and do them in exactly the sequence that they give you.

a16a1221101.speaker: England
a16a1221101.text: And, Charlie, while you're taking the pictures and all, verify the area around the Central Station is policed up.

a16a1221101.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1221101.text: Okay; the Mapping Camera is Off. I'll wait 30 seconds.

a16a1221101.speaker: Duke
a16a1221101.text: Okay, I will. [The concern may be that reflections off the trash might create thermal problems for the experiments.]

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Number 18, Houston. (Pause)

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: 4, 3, 2, 1, Fire. (Pause)

a16a1221101.speaker: England
a16a1221101.text: And we're still getting good signals. [John now moves forward 9 meters to do the last shot next to the geophone they deployed near the Central Station.]

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Okay. Coming up on the last one. (Pause) And I see the black thing (halfway between locations 18 and 19); skipping that one. Going up here by the Central Station. (Pause) Going to fire it at the white line next to the first geophone. [John reaches the final thumper location. He is about 3 meters west of the anchor.]

a16a1221101.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1221101.text: Roger. The only hitch to this is I get interested in what you're saying and I might forget.

a16a1221101.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1221101.text: (Laughter) Well (laughter), just remember, they go on your card, the back side goes on mine.

a16a1221101.speaker: England
a16a1221101.text: Okay, and, after you fire this one, we'd like you to stand still until we give you the Go.

a16a1221101.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1221101.text: Actually, though, I got a bunch of guys backing me up.

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: All right.

a16a1221101.speaker: Duke
a16a1221101.text: Wait a minute, John. (Pause) Okay. Go ahead.

a16a1221101.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1221101.text: Well, I tell you, this place is so fascinating that you just - you just don't dare let anything go by. It's - You know, I think you could stay here a lifetime, and never see it all. I guess that's - that's kind of a silly statement because it's true in almost anywhere you go. It sure is dramatic. At first glance, particularly the back side looks like an old gypsum plant. It just looks like someone's poured stuff all over it, and just made it - and just tried to hide it, camouflage things. The more you look at it, then you start to pick out subtle differences. Unfortunately, I'm not smart enoug

a16a1221101.speaker: Young
a16a1221101.text: Okay, Houston. Last one. 4, 3, 2, 1, Fire. (Long Pause) [At about this time, Charlie takes two up-Suns of the magnetometer, AS16-113- 18373 and 18374 . Both show the deployed the magnetometer sunshade. The RTG and the Central Station are in the background. John is near the Central Station firing shot 19.] MP3 Audio Clip ( 14 min 09 sec )

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Okay. You can go.

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: (Amazed at how long they are having to stand still) Houston, you got to be kidding. (Hearing Tony and chuckling) Okay. Was the signal reverberating that long?

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Right. It really rings down. (Pause) [Figure 10-7 from the Preliminary Science Report shows the signals recorded at the three geophones for shot 17. The pre-arrival noise at the left side of the figure is not indicative of the true noise level because it includes residuals from prior shots and the crew's movements between shots. By having John and Charlie stay motionless for about 25 seconds after the last shot, the experimenters get a better idea of the true noise level.] [John moves a few steps to the northwest and uses a sidearm motion to toss the thumper off to the north. Charlie comes int

a16a1222218.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1222218.text: Are you in Standby now with that Mapping Camera, Ken?

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: All finished (with the thumper). Good show. Tony, ain't there some way we can fix that heat flow?

a16a1222218.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1222218.text: Yes, sir. I went to Standby and took the Image Motion, Off.

a16a1222218.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1222218.text: Okay, thank you.

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Looks pretty bad there, Charlie. We suggest you just not worry about it there. You've got a good ALSEP, and the other experiments are working fine. [John has moved northeast of the Central Station and throws a piece of trash off to the north. Charlie takes a picture across the top of the Central Station from the north. This is AS16-113- 18375 . Stone Mountain is in the background.]

a16a1222218.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1222218.text: Thank you. I forgot to tell you about it.

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: Well...All those hours (of work devoted to the re-design of the drill stems and to training). [Charlie takes a moment to go through his checklist. John waits for him to get out of the way.]

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: Okay. We got all the pictures except for the ones John's supposed to take of the mortar package (as per LMP-19 and CDR-28 ). And I'm skipping the heat flow ones. And we're up to magazine...We're 102 on...(Correcting himself) 101 on magazine Alfa.

a16a1222218.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1222218.text: Paul, let me give you the reading on magazine SS before I forget it. I'm now at 35.

a16a1222218.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1222218.text: Roger; 35.

a16a1222218.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1222218.text: And I guess we could - I guess we could sort of say we have filled the - the Davy square. I don't think we ought to keep trying that. Get a chance, why, we will, but I'm not going to keep trying after it.

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Okay. (Pause) [Charlie has taken the camera off his RCU bracket and sets it down on top of the Central Station for John's use. John moves in and gets a UHT. He moves away from the Central Station, looks at his checklist, and turns pages until he gets to CDR-28 .]

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: (Heading for the Rover) Okay. I'm going to get the hockey stick, John. [The 'hockey stick' is the locking pin that fell out of John's purge valve. Charlie stowed it under John's seat after he found it on the ground next to the Rover.]

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: Okay. I'm going to... Gotta switch 5 clockwise here to safe the beast. [John goes around to the south side of the Central Station, stepping carefully over cables as he goes. He is making sure that the mortar package can't get a signal from the Central Station and fire a mortar while he is working around it.]

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Okay, Charlie. Do you have that pin in John's suit yet?

a16a1222218.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1222218.text: And the zodiacal light I'll keep on - keep on XX.

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: I'm going to get it right now.

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Okay. [Charlie uses the foot-to-foot, loping stride until he gets to the soft-rimmed crater and then switches to his skipping stride.]

a16a1222218.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1222218.text: Roger; XX.

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: Coming your way.

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Rog. Seeing you coming. [John turns the mortar package switch and then uses the UHT to clear some debris from around the Central Station.]

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: What's the heart rate when I'm going like this, Tony?

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: About 10.

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Okay, you're going about 110 right now.

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: Am I? Thank you. [It takes Charlie about 42 seconds to cover the 35 meters between the Central Station and the Rover.]

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: (With a touch of little-boy petulance in his voice) Well, what's mine? (Pause)

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: John, you're about 80.

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: That figures. (Pause) [Figures 10-3a from the Mission Report shows John's heart rate and 10-3b shows Charlie's. John's is the lowest it has been since he got off the Rover at the ALSEP site. Charlie has also just come through a minimum, and in both cases they have both gotten quite a bit of rest, standing still while John did the series of thumper shots. If Charlie had a brief period of 110 beats per minute due to the run back to the Rover, it doesn't show up in the plot, probably because the plotted points represent averages over intervals of a few minutes.] [John is north of the Central Stat

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: See that right there, Tony?

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Yep, sure do. [As Tony indicates at 122:25:23 , he sees what he thinks is the so-called 'red apple' which the astronauts would use to open the purge valve. I was expecting to see the locking pin.]

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: Okay, the old Central Station is all cleaned up.

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Good job.

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: All the junk is gone somewheres. [John heads for the mortar package carrying the UHT.]

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: Did you see what I held just in front of the camera, Tony?

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Yeah, we sure did.

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: It was a solid piece of glass - spherical - and part of it's broken away, but it really (is the) most unique piece of glass I've ever seen in all the samples. I think. [Fendell pulls back on the zoom and we see John going past the Central Station to get a piece of equipment.] 122:25:23 England: Outstanding, Charlie. I thought you had the ball on that OPS (the 'red apple')...(correcting himself) or that purge key.

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: No, it's a solid piece of glass!

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Fantastic. (Pause) [We get a glimpse of Charlie's shadow as he heads for the Central Station.] Video Clip ( 2 min 47 sec 0.7 Mb RealVideo or 25 Mb MPEG )

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: And it was right out here by the drill. (Pause) [In looking at the video again, I finally picked out the glass sphere. It is about two to three centimeters across. Charlie held it between his thumb and forefinger and it is very difficult to see against the dark background of his very dirty fingers. Charlie collected the glass sphere at 121:53:10 just after he dropped the rammer-jammer down the core hole. According to the Apollo 16 Voice Transcript Pertaining to the geology of the landing site by N.G. Bailey and G.E. Ulrich, this is sample 60095, which weighs 46.6 grams. The glass sphere is sho

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: Okay, Charlie. I'm going to deploy this...

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: Okay, wait a minute. Let me get this thing (meaning the purge valve pin) in, and I'll go back and start on that heat flow. (Correcting himself) I mean the (core)...Can you step away so I don't get these (mortar package) cables?

a16a1222218.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1222218.text: [Garble] for 20 seconds [garble] zodiacal light.

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: What is it you want to do?

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: I got to get this in.

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: Oh. Gosh, it is it, isn't it? Can you see it?

a16a1222218.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1222218.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I was playing my tape recorder back to myself.

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: Yeah. [John has backed away from the mortar cable. Charlie bends his right knee and leans to his right to get at John's purge valve. He then puts his left foot back and sinks down onto his right knee to get a little lower. John bends his knees and pulls his head and shoulders back to raise the purge valve.]

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: How did I do it is what I'd like to know. [Charlie is now down on both knees.]

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: Manual dexterity test of the year. I'll bet...

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: Okay, it's in. [Charlie rises without difficulty, possibly keeping himself steady by taking John's hidden right hand or by grabbing part of his suit.] 122:26:34 Young: I'll bet when I undid my seatbelt , I pulled it off.

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: Probably.

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: I'll bet you 100 dollars. [Charlie turns to head back to the Rover. Once he has a little forward momentum, he springs up off both feet and does an elegant kangaroo-hop over the cables, clearing them easily.] [John's 'red-apple', which is on the end of the lanyard for his purge valve pin, can be seen in a frame capture ( 162k ) from 16-mm film of the LM/LRV checkout on 4 April l972.]

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: Okay, Tony. That is back in on the Commander.

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Good show. (Pause)

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: These Rover tracks are amazing. They're just barely (sinking in)...(Pause) [Post-mission analysis of photographs indicates that the maximum depth of the Rover tracks is about 5 cm. The deepest penetration, of course, was seen in the rims of small, relatively fresh craters. The average track depth was 1.25 cm. Based on lab tests done with crushed-basalt lunar-soil simulants, the track depths indicate a typical porosity of 41 percent.] 122:27:01 Duke: Oh, heck. (Long Pause)

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: Gah. (Long Pause) [John has attached the mortar base to his UHT and carries it over to the geophone anchor. As per CDR-28 , he will align it with the geophone line and read off a sun angle which he will then use to properly align the base under the mortar package. Photo AS16-113- 18380 is a close-up of the deployed mortar package and base. At the present moment, John has the UHT fitted into the hole at the center of the compass pattern on the base and the UHT shadow gives him the proper alignment. The UHT will, of course, serve as a gnomon during the deployment as well.] 122:27:48 Young: My go

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Outstanding, John. [The western half of the geophone line was on the other side of the ridge and John is proud of the straight-line deployment he achieved. He mentions the fact again during the post-mission Technical Debrief.]

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: And for the geophones to be in the same line (as the line-of-fire of the mortars), it'll have to go with a Sun angle of 333.

a16a1222218.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1222218.text: Ken, are you free right now?

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Okay. (Long Pause) Video Clip ( 2 min 55 sec 0.7 Mb RealVideo or 26 Mb MPEG )

a16a1222218.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1222218.text: Say again, Hank.

a16a1222218.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1222218.text: Roger. Are you free right now? Are you doing something?

a16a1222218.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1222218.text: I'm setting up the camera for the zodiacal light. What do you need?

a16a1222218.speaker: Young
a16a1222218.text: I mean the thumper (actually means mortar) package. Excuse me. (Pause) [John's difficulties in picking the right word are legendary. Readers may want to consult the discussion he had with the Apollo 17 crew during their EVA-2 Preps. During the rest period between EVA-1 and EVA-2, John had tested a design for a makeshift replacement fender for their Rover and had some difficulty describing the procedures. This is all part of the John Young 'Country Boy' demeanor which masks a superb intellect.] [John turns and walks toward the mortar package. In the foreground, we see the core stem move as Char

a16a1222218.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1222218.text: Okay. I was just thinking. In case we lose comm, there is one little change. After we get LOS, where you have to configure the DSE, since we've added then this mapping camera pass - oblique, we want to get High Bit Rate instead of Low Bit Rate.

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: Boy, that beauty (meaning the joint at the middle of the core string) almost didn't want to come loose, Tony. But we got it. (Long Pause)

a16a1222218.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1222218.text: Okay. Let me write that down. Figuring it says Low, and you want me to go High. Okay; and if you'd remind me of that just before LOS.

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Charlie, what was the cap on the bottom end? We missed that.

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: Baker.

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Okay. [John has backed off-camera to the right, fully deploying the mortar cable. Fendell follows and, in the foreground, we see Charlie rotate the bottom two core sections so he can look at the top of the second one.] 122:29:06 Duke: (Delighted) It's all full, Tony!

a16a1222218.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1222218.text: Roger; intend to - and - in regard to your comments about King, was there any other thing back - on the back side that you had of interest?

a16a1222218.speaker: England
a16a1222218.text: Outstanding. (Long Pause) [John gets to the end of the mortar cable and then moves back in a meter or two and somewhat to the west, possibly to find a level spot. He puts the base down and then sinks to his knees. He puts the mortar package down and then stands, picks up the base and knocks some dust off with his free left hand.]

a16a1222218.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1222218.text: I - I found a couple of items back - mostly to the - I think almost all of the things that I had a chance to look at this time were to the - to the west of King. Between there and about AOS, I had a chance to look at the swirls, and to look at King - and a - and a crater - I first felt like I'd found - my first comment was that if there's ever a crater on the Moon that's got stratigraphy exposed, that's got to be it. And I hope that's wrong because there wasn't anywhere I was looking. And I took a picture of that one, and there was another little bright-rayed guy - a little splashed-out crater

a16a1222218.speaker: Duke
a16a1222218.text: Okay...(Pause) Delta and Baker on the bottom (two sections). (Pause) [Baker is the cap on the bit end of the first (deepest) core section; and Delta is the cap on the top of the second section.]

a16a1240448.speaker: England
a16a1240448.text: That's it. (As Charlie touches the top of Big Muley with the scoop) You got it, right there.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Okay, that's a...

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: That's a football-size rock.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: It's a "Great Scott" size. [Great Scott is a 9.6 kg basalt that Dave Scott collected at the edge of Hadley Rille. At the time, it was the largest Apollo sample, having surpassed a 9.0 kg Apollo 14 breccia known as Big Bertha. Big Muley, sample 61016 ( 172k ), is an 11.7 kg breccia with a dark matrix and light-colored clasts. The largest Apollo 17 sample was 70215, an 8.1 kg basalt, so Big Muley retained the record. NASA photos S72-41841 and S72-41550 are post-mission portraits of Big Muley.]

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Are you sure you want a rock that big, Houston? (Pause) [Charlie stands at rest, leaning slightly forward on the scoop while he waits for an answer.] 124:08:01 England: Yeah, let's go ahead and get it.

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: That's 20 (9.1 kg) pounds of rock right there.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Okay. (Pause) [With his left hand on the top of the scoop, Charlie drops to his knees and rolls Big Muley over against the front of his right leg.]

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: It's got some big clasts in it, John.

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: It sure has. (Pause) [Charlie can't get his hand low enough to get under the rock, so he uses the tips of his fingers to try to roll it up onto his thigh. It falls off. He then strains forward until he can get his hand curved around the rock far enough that he can, at least, press it against his leg and, finally, he stands (video still by Ken Glover). Dave Scott used a similar technique when he collected Great Scott ]

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Agh! (Pause) [Charlie plants the scoop, gets his left hand under the camera and does a little jump so that the rock floats upward far enough that he can get a solid grip with both hands. The Hasselblad is clearly getting in the way.] 124:08:29 Duke: If I fall into Plum Crater getting this rock, Muehlberger has had it.

a16a1240448.speaker: England
a16a1240448.text: We agree. [Bill Muehlberger is the Principal Investigator for Apollo 16 geology. As is discussed at 127:16:10 , Big Muley is named for him.] [Muehlberger, from a 1996 letter and a 1997 e-mail message - "Big Muley was a problem from the moment we saw it on TV. The crew had been told to pick up nothing larger than their fist - the lab types could analyze remarkably small pieces and get reproducible results. So, when we spotted Big Muley with the television camera and saw what looked like a large rectangle flashing at us, we jumped to the conclusion that it was a crystal - or cleavage - face of p

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Okay; I've got it! That's 20 pounds of rock! (Pause) [Jones - "That's a nice sequence there of you picking up Big Muley. It didn't look like you had stability problems at all."] [Duke - "No, I was a little over the rim, down inside and so I was a little bit below the rock, which really helped. When you could get below something, it really helped. And then, of course, I was leaning on the shovel with my left hand. And I was trying to roll it up my leg; but I never could get it up past the stuff down in here, which I think was part of the camera and stuff. But I was able to hold it against mysel

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: You want to put it in here, Charlie? I'd just as soon you didn't. Look at the size of that moose!

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: I know it. (Pause) Oh, Tony! It's got some beautiful crystals in it though. That was a good guess.

a16a1240448.speaker: England
a16a1240448.text: Good show.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Okay, put it in there, John.

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Put it in where?

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: In your SCB.

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: I don't think it'll fit. (Pause) Don't think it will fit. (Pause) [The TV jiggles slightly as they work around the Rover.] Video Clip ( 2 min 32 sec 0.6 Mb RealVideo or 22 Mb MPEG )

a16a1240448.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1240448.text: Ken, for your information, John and Charlie are at Flag now.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: It ain't gonna fit.

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Put it under your seat.

a16a1240448.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1240448.text: Okay, I'll wave to them. I'll tell you, NASA needs to recruit some octopuses. I could really use a couple of more hands.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Yeah. Kind of dusty. Whew! Hey, do you want some more (individual sample) bags here?

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Yeah.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Okay, here's your a good one. [Fendell finds John at the CDR seat, collapsing the gnomon legs into a slender bundle so he can stow it in the sleeve behind his seat. We get a good close-up of John's sample bags.]

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Okay, Tony, I'm gonna put that little glass ball that I haven't sacked yet...Look at that, John.

a16a1240448.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1240448.text: (Laughter) Roger.

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Yeah, it is a good piece of glass.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Solid glass.

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Black glass.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Going into bag 4. (Long Pause) [This sample is 60095, a 47-gram piece of glass that Charlie collected at the drill site at 121:53:10 and showed to Houston at 122:25:42 .] [John stows the gnomon.]

a16a1240448.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1240448.text: Okay, I'm going to concentrate on North Ray as I distinctly believe that the - area that the traverse drawn on that goes up on the North Ray comes up on a - material that looks like it has flowed around and is part of the basic furrowed Descartes unit that's mapped back further to the east. And it looks to me like it runs down around the crater and - and straight into it.

a16a1240448.speaker: England
a16a1240448.text: Okay; and we'll need an EMU check before you drive off. (Pause)

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Stand by. [John puts his left hand on the RCU and tilts it so he can get a clear look at the oxygen gauge on the top. As is shown in the accompanying figure, the gauge is recessed and is difficult to see.]

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Okay, I'm running at 48 percent (oxygen remaining); (looking at his cuff gauge) 3.87 (psi suit pressure). I'm on halfway between Intermediate and Minimum (cooling) and I didn't have any (warning) flags. (To Charlie) We got to do something with this bag (meaning his SCB) before we can leave, Charlie.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Put it under your seat. Or under my seat.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Okay, Tony, I'm clear on the flags. My frame count (pause) is 65. I've got...Hmm. (Pause) [John puts his SCB under the CDR seat. He then stands, flexes his shoulder back, possibly to change the position of the cables in the suit, and then rests for a moment and watches Charlie, who is off-camera at the LMP seat.]

a16a1240448.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1240448.text: I can see evidence of stratigraphy in North Ray, and lots of it in South Ray. And as we come across at - boy, I'll tell you, the - the general topography down there looks about the same all the way across the board.

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: What you got, Charlie?

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Looks like I'm at about 35 percent, and I'm between Intermediate and Min; and I'm at 3.85.

a16a1240448.speaker: England
a16a1240448.text: Okay. [John moves his right hand back, then forward, and then back again to reach his cooling control . This "double wave" is necessary to overcome the resistance of the suit cables.]

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Yeah, make sure you're in Min I guess, before we get in and start driving.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Yeah. Going to Min. That's a good point. Thanks.

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Okay.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: (Getting on the Rover) Leaps. Single bound. [John goes to the front of the Rover to turn the TV off.]

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: MODE switch is going to 1, Houston.

a16a1240448.speaker: England
a16a1240448.text: Okay. [TV off.]

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: I'm going to position your TV horizontal and CCW (counter-clockwise), which it almost is. (Pause) It is. You (meaning Ed Fendell ) saved me a lot of work there. (Pause)

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Uh-oh.

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: What's the matter, Charlie?

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Oh, my seatbelt came off my ring. Can you get it for me, John?

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Yeah.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Will you get in...

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: I couldn't see it...Oh, there it is. Let me get it for you.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: I'll do it. I think.

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Yeah, you got it.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Okay. (Pause) Boy, this is a nice belt. [Duke - "It really cinched you in there. It had a good over center position and it was easy to operate. And it had a big hook on it so you could just reach over and hook on the outside handle of your seat, which was real easy to do. You really couldn't see it; you were working blind. And, then, that big handle would give an over center lock and it really cinched you in there firm."]

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Okay, we're in Mode switch 1; and the TV off (and) stowed. (Pause) Can you see my (purge valve) pin over there, Charlie?

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Can I see what?

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Can you see whether I'm about to pull out my pin or not? (Pause)

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Pull up your (garbled)?

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Pull out my pin.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Oh, I can't see. No, it doesn't look like it. (Long Pause) Man, are we filthy! (Long Pause)

a16a1240448.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1240448.text: And just at a cursory glance, we're coming up on Albategnius now and that material that's over to the east of it - that kind of hummocky and undulating material and it's furrowed. And it looks very much like the material around Descartes. I said it did in a very low Sun, and it has the appearance of having many of those same characteristics.

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: Okay.

a16a1240448.speaker: Duke
a16a1240448.text: Okay.

a16a1240448.speaker: Young
a16a1240448.text: (Garbled) Traverse to Station 1 Apollo 16 Journal Traverse to Station 2

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: Okay, Tony, we're just about underway. (Pause)

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: Okay; we're going to follow our footsteps back.

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: Okay, that's a good idea. (Pause) Tony, did you read?

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Yeah, we sure did.

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: (Lost under Tony)

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Okay, and we're looking at... 124:14:32 Duke: Okay; we're underway. 124:14:38 England: And, we're looking at a few changes there at Spook. We're going to cut that station down to about 19 minutes. [Pre-mission planning assumed they would leave Flag Crater at an EVA elapsed time of about 4+57. The EVA started at 118:53:33 and, consequently, they are 5 hours 21 minutes into it and about 24 minutes behind schedule. They had planned to make a 5-minute drive back to Spook and then a 56-minute stop.]

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: And if you get there in time, (As per CDR-34 and CDR-35 ) we'll have John go ahead, as nominal, and do the LPM (Lunar Portable Magnetometer). And then we'll end (with) the LPM site measurement. And Charlie, you can do your 500-millimeter (photos) near the edge of Spook, and do a pan near the rim of Spook. And run over and do a couple of samples of Buster if you have time left. And that'll be our Station 2.

a16a1241410.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1241410.text: Have you got pretty good shadows in this area now, Ken?

a16a1241410.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1241410.text: The shadows are right here coming across Albategnius. They're pretty well cleared out. You just get the shadows from the very big peaks. At Ptolemaeus, it's almost completely clear of shadows. Alphonsus still has some. I can pick out the crater chain now. It's just now getting out of the shadow, and, sure enough, there is a great big little ridge that lays across the front of it that's been masking it all this time. The floor of Ptolemaeus looks to be like all the rest of the Cayley material. It's got a great deal of craters as you can see from the pictures. I would say the preponderance of th

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: Okay, why the cutback?

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Okay; it's your (cooling) water consumption there, Charlie.

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: Ah, rats! Okay. [Although Houston is concerned about Charlie's use rate of PLSS feedwater, the fact that they are about a half-hour behind schedule is also a consideration.]

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: That's all right. You're getting some really good geology there. Don't feel bad. (Pause)

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: Okay; we're making good time going back, and it's easier going up-Sun. You can see the craters a lot better. The characteristics of the regolith are the same.

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: Are you using the 16 (mm movie camera), Charlie?

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: No. (Pause) [Charlie does not take any photos during the drive back to Spook but does during the drive from Spook back to the LM.]

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: Well, it ain't easier (driving) for me. If I wasn't following these tracks, it would be bad. Up-Sun or down-Sun, it's bad for driving.

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Roger. We figured it probably would be.

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: You're making great time, John. We're doing 11 clicks.

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Outstanding!

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: Super!

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: The Grand Prix driver is at it again. 124:16:20 Duke: Barney Oldfield.

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: I can follow a road. [Jones - "I'm afraid I'm a little too young to be absolutely certain who Barney Oldfield was."] [Duke - "He was a great race car driver back in the 20s or so. As a kid, I can remember everybody talked about Barney Oldfield. I don't even think he was driving when I was a kid."] [Journal contributor Brian Lawrence supplied the following information. "Oldfield was born in 1878 and began driving for Henry Ford in 1902. Among other distinctions, he set a speed record of 131.275 mph over a measured mile at Daytona, Florida, in a German Blitzen Benz on March 16, 1910. He competed

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Back to the on-off switch mode.

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: (Lost under Tony) [This is probably an inside joke, possibly a reference to John's ability to change jobs - from Rover driver to geologist and back - without a moment's pause.]

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: John, did you dust that TV lens?

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: I dusted it somewhere.

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Okay, fine.

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: I don't remember if it was that station or not. (Pause)

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Okay, I guess we'll need it dusted again at this next stop.

a16a1241410.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1241410.text: And as we come upon Davy chain, it appears that they do have - they don't each have an individual rim. There is mottled material in this area, and I'm going to try and get that magazine. I think you need to see this. Can you give me the settings for the - so we can take a picture of this real fast.

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: All righty.

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: Okay, Tony. As I look up-Sun here, going back through (pause), you can see these lineations, mostly furrows, I'd call them, with random orientation. And they're definitely (due to) the Sun casting shadows on unconsolidated regolith.

a16a1241410.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1241410.text: Stand by.

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Right.

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: You can't believe how up and down this is, Tony.

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: How about when you're driving across rays? You noticed any difference in the Rover tracks?

a16a1241410.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1241410.text: Using VHBW.

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: (Chuckles) I notice an increase in block population. But the tracks you can't see; they're behind you.

a16a1241410.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1241410.text: Okay. I'll - we see if we can get them, Ken.

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Okay; I thought maybe you could see them behind the front wheel there.

a16a1241410.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1241410.text: Okay. I'm going to take one here now at - that was 5.6 and t/125 I'll take a 250th. Second one's a 250th. And that ought to bracket it, I hope. And that's of the crater chain itself. And it just - it appears that they're essentially rimless, but the whole area down there is kind of mottled.

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: (Laughs)

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: It's a cloud of dust, Tony.

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Okay; we copy. (Long Pause)

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: (To Charlie) That's Spook , isn't it? That big one right there?

a16a1241410.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1241410.text: Roger. Did you use the EL for that?

a16a1241410.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1241410.text: It's a very pretty scarp. No, I used VHBW.

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: Yeah; I think it is. (Probably indicating another crater) That's the one we called Buster. Okay. We got to go up north if you're gonna...(Pause) [If, indeed, they are approaching Spook, they need to turn northeast to park the Rover at a point on the rim of Spook nearest Buster. See the Descartes EVA-I, III 1 of 3 map .]

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: Okay, Tony. We're in a real blocky boulder field here. It's probably thrown out from Spook. What we originally called Spook was not Spook. I think this blocky one is Spook. And we're coming up from the south side of it. [As indicated below, they are probably northwest of Spook and south of Buster. Charlie seems to be mistaking Buster for Spook.]

a16a1241410.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1241410.text: Casper, Houston. You're coming up in about 20 seconds to a T-stop.

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: (Thinking about where he landed) Yeah, I'd say, Houston, that I was farther past...I guess that I was farther past Double Spot...(Pause)

a16a1241410.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1241410.text: I sure am. Okay. Thank you. Give me a call at T-stop.

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: But we got 0.8 mile (means 0.8 km), John, and Spook is supposed to be a mile (means 1 km) from the LM, as per the map. That's got to be it right down there. [If they are 0.8 km from the LM , which is near CB.1/80.6 , and have been following their outbound tracks, they are south of Buster near CA.7/76.6.]

a16a1241410.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1241410.text: Mark it; T-stop.

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: Buster?

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: No, that's Spook.

a16a1241410.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1241410.text: Okay. We're at T-stop. Thank you.

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Okay...

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: (Lost under Tony)

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: ...Spook should look about the same size as Flag. 124:19:23 Duke: Nope; that doesn't.

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: Does it look the same size?

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: No, this is the biggest crater right over here to the right.

a16a1241410.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1241410.text: Okay, that's - We're now in frame 36 on magazine SS.

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: Okay; well, this is Buster (on the left).

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: Okay, that's what I thought. It's a blocky crater. [Finally, they have it sorted out.]

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: Let's stop the Rover halfway between them?

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: Yeah.

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: No, near the edge of Spook.

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: Buster is a lot bigger than...(Responding to England) Yeah, okay, it (meaning Buster)'s about 50 meters or so. We're bearing 089 for 0.8.

a16a1241410.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1241410.text: Okay. You can go - Standby on a Mapping Camera and Image Motion, Off.

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Okay. [This readout puts them near CB.0/76.6 .]

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: We're supposed to park 180 about halfway, John, (as per LMP-24 ). Don't...We're in a big hole back over here, Could you...Go forward (lost under Tony)?

a16a1241410.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1241410.text: Okay. Standby and Image Motion, Off. Barber pole - gray.

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Little bit nearer to the end of Spook so we can see into Spook.

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: What you really want to see into is Buster. Buster is about the same size as what we called Spook here. In fact, it's a more impressive crater!

a16a1241410.speaker: England
a16a1241410.text: Okay, whatever turns you on, there.

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke
a16a1241410.text: John, that thing's...(Stops to listen) That, that's got to be...Tony, is there a big crater to the south of...

a16a1241410.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1241410.text: It's very interesting, Hank. I've got a little stranger back here that's trailing me. Must be one of Casper's friends.

a16a1241410.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1241410.text: All righty. We'll...

a16a1241410.speaker: Young
a16a1241410.text: Spook?

a16a1241410.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1241410.text: Got a little light's just sitting out there. I guess he's - I have no idea how far away it is, you know, though - I have the impression it's like ten feet, but it could be 100 feet or 1000 feet. But it's apparently some little particle that's in orbit with me, and it's - it's probably rotating, because it's winking. I first saw these last night, and I thought I'd seen something on the ground. Then I realized I'd - it was moving at the same rate I was and every now and then I look out and I see these particles that are reflecting around me.

a16a1241410.speaker: Duke

a16a1243958.speaker: England
a16a1243958.text: ...can you check and make sure your purge valve pin's still in?

a16a1243958.speaker: Young
a16a1243958.text: Is it in, Charlie?

a16a1243958.speaker: Duke
a16a1243958.text: Ain't no way I could tell, unless you...Yeah, it's there. Uh-huh, I saw it.

a16a1243958.speaker: England
a16a1243958.text: Outstanding.

a16a1243958.speaker: Duke
a16a1243958.text: Whew! (Pause) (Playing verbally) We are mounting upon the vehicle! As they say, Houston.

a16a1243958.speaker: Young
a16a1243958.text: Okay.

a16a1243958.speaker: England
a16a1243958.text: That skill is awesome.

a16a1243958.speaker: Young
a16a1243958.text: (Lost under Tony) Charlie.

a16a1243958.speaker: Duke
a16a1243958.text: Okay. (Pause) Traverse to Station 2 Apollo 16 Journal Grand Prix

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay; I'm going to take some pictures going (back to the LM)...Wow, is that Sun bright! Ooh! There's home. You see it?

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Yeah. [As is indicated in Figure 6-4 ( 648k ) in the Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report , they are about 800 meters west of the LM. Charlie's first traverse photo, AS16-109- 17849 , shows Spook crater. Charlie may have taken it before they started rolling and before John turned into the Sun.]

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: John, you're not going right. (Pause) That navigation (system) has us right on! You turn to 086, we'd be pointed right at that beauty (meaning the LM).

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Let's do that. [AS16-109- 17850 shows the up-Sun view. The remaining photos taken during the traverse are 17851 to 17862 . In frame 17852 , the outbound Rover tracks are at the left and Stone Mountain is at the right. In 17853 , Orion is just below the fiducial immediately right of center.] [The traverse photos - 17849 to 17862 - are presented as a strip.] [Jones - "(Frame) 17860 is on the way back. The Rover tracks really give a graphic illustration of the undulating terrain."] [Duke - "Yeah. And you can see how it changes the albedo."]

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Look at it, John. Four more degrees and you got it! Snockered (meaning that John has the Rover aimed at the LM). 087 now. You're about 084 and you'd have it.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: (Bracing himself) You're gonna have that big crater! [Charlie's tone of voice in this transmission is that of someone who has just reached the top of a roller coaster and, on "big crater", is about to plunge downward. You can almost hear him grabbing for the handholds.]

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Man, this is a fun ride. (Pause) Okay, Tony, we're doing 10 clicks.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Outstanding.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Occasionally, the back end breaks loose, but there's no problem. This is really some machine. (Pause)

a16a1244820.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1244820.text: Casper, Houston. We're about two minutes from LOS, and everything's looking good from this end.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Hey, looking back up-Sun, the rays are even more pronounced. Looking up-Sun rather than down-Sun, the blocks stand out like black spires.

a16a1244820.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1244820.text: Okay, Hank. You're cutting out; I understand.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: It's just like driving on snow, Houston. By golly!

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Gee, I know all about that.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: I know you do; but us Florida boys (chuckling) don't know much about it.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: It takes these small craters up to a meter (in diameter) just like a piece of cake. You occasionally get blinded by the (reflections of the Sun off the) LCRU mirrors and the TCU mirror.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: By gosh, this is really something.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Sure is. (Long Pause) [In the following, John maneuvers to avoid a rock or, more likely, a deep, fresh crater.]

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: And the Sun!

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Well, that's what I meant. Oh, you mean (the direct Sun)...I got my thing down.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: There's a good idea. (Pause) [Since they both probably have their gold-plated sun visors down, Charlie is probably referring to the hinged, opaque sun visor at the top of the face plate.]

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Lookit there, you can see your (geophone) flags out, John.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Yeah.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: And Charlie...

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: (Lost under Tony)

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: ...could you look at the amps during the higher speed part. We'd like a number.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay; well, let us get a higher speed part.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Well, the voltage is...The switch is on Volts right now, John, and I don't want to move to reach down there.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Yeah, if Charlie moves the switch while we're driving, I turn left every time.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Okay; understand. (Long Pause) [What John is saying is that, if Charlie were to reach for the switch, he would knock John's arm and displace the handcontroller to the left.]

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay; we've been making about 10 clicks, Tony, and going just super.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Outstanding.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Go, man.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Yahoo!!

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Ho, ho, ho, ho, ho.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Look at that thing dig in.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Boy, we just missed a baddie.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Are you steering all four wheels?

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Yup.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: No problem?

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Nah. I was really going slow at first. I think it would be a problem when you're navigating under unknown terrain. [Jones - "I take it that this was one of those occasions when you'd come up over a little rise and..."] [Duke - "Yeah. Uh-huh. And there would be a rock or a boulder there or a crater that was more than we thought we could handle. So John would have to steer around it. And what we're describing, I think, is we were really moving - I guess about ten clicks or so - and it really got to bouncing on us. That's what I was talking about on the 'yahoo!'."]

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: But you see, going down-Sun or into the Sun - which we're not gonna be doing much of any more - is really...You can't plan ahead far enough to do yourself any good.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Rog. [The EVA-2 and EVA-3 traverses will take them south and north of the LM, respectively, and they won't have to do much down-Sun or Up-Sun driving.]

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: That's why I was going so slow there at first (during the drive to Station 1). (Pause) [See the discussion following 123:02:43 .] 124:52:30 Duke: Okay, John. We need to stop out here for the Grand Prix.

a16a1244820.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1244820.text: (Singing) Bah-dura-bah - There we go. Doo-doodoo- doo-doo-bee-dee-dee-dah.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay. [Charlie will get off the Rover and use the 16-mm camera to photograph John while he drives the Rover through some pre-planned maneuvers. Details of the Grand Prix are given on CDR-36 . Dave Scott drove a Grand Prix on Apollo 15 but, unfortunately, the 16-mm camera malfunctioned and Jim Irwin did not get any usable film.]

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: And it's a...(Pause)

a16a1244820.speaker: Noise (CM onboard)
a16a1244820.text: (Music)

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Here's a flat place, sort of.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: We got to get over there where the...I'd like to get over there so I won't have to get back on, see, and pick up the core stems (as per LMP-27 ).

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay. I got you.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: You've got to arm the mortar package...

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Right.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: ...Central Station and Switch 5, CCW (Counter-Clockwise). (Pause) Okay, why don't we go over to the right, where the (core) stems are. About boresighted on (meaning "heading toward") the LSM now.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Yeah. (Pause)

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: That is a big one, John. [Charlie may be referring to the two-meter boulder at the ALSEP site.]

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Oh, man.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Hook a right. (Long Pause)

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Tony, again, we're just driving by the ALSEP and apologize for that heat flow. I wouldn't trade you...The drill seems to work just great, though. I think it's in good shape right now for the next flight.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Good show, Charlie. 124:54:07 Young: Here's a flat place right in here, Charlie.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Yeah, that's what I was thinking. See, you could go out up that way and then out over that way towards the LM. Okay?

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Right. Right.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay. Let me jump off.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: A day ago, it didn't look like we were even gonna land, and now we've sampled our first highlands. I feel pretty good about the science (even) without the heat flow.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Well, I know Mark's disappointed, and I sure am.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Me, too.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Frankly, that was just a real shame. That was my big moment, was to get that thing going. Put this (Hasselblad) camera in here, John. Okay?

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Yep. [Charlie has taken off his Hasselblad so it won't get in the way while he uses the 16-mm camera. The Data Acquisition Camera (DAC) has a bracket mounted on the back which would allow Charlie to mount the camera on his Remote Control Unit (RCU). Apollo 13 training photo KSC-70PC-18 shows Fred Haise with a DAC mounted on his RCU. The character of the 16-mm film that Charlie shot - reasonably steady with John well centered - suggests that Charlie held the camera in his hands.]

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay. Now let me see. (As per LMP-26 ), you're suppose to drive 45 degrees to the Sun. Okay?

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Yep.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay. Let me get the 16(-mm camera) off.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: I'll do it from there up towards this way. Okay?

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Wait a minute. Okay, which way you gonna drive? From here, this way?

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Going over...

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Towards Stone (Mountain)?

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: You see where that white thing is?

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Yeah.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: I'll go over there toward a rock and drive up this way. Okay? 124:55:09 Duke: Okay. Well, wait. Why don't you just drive towards the LM. Let me move out here, and you just drive towards the LM, turn around, and then drive towards Stone.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay?

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Let me get the camera. Let me get it set here now. It's 24 (frames per second). Gonna be using the trigger, so (as per the notation at the top of LMP-26 ) it's 24 (pause) and f/8 at 250(th of a second).

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Hey, that LM makes a nice looking house. (Pause)

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Especially since it's about the only one there.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Yeah.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: You're right, Tony. It ain't nothing much up here but a lot of rocks.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Hope the (LM) door opens, Charlie.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Huh? What?

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: I said, I hope the door opens.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: It'll open. (Garbled) close it. (Grunting) This thing is stuck. I can't get it up. Let me move out. Okay. To start, I'm suppose to be about 50 meters or so from you.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay, Charlie. And what I'll do (as per CDR-36 ) is drive from A to B, standing start, max velocity readout. And (pause) then do some...I'm not going to do much steering control around here, other than to avoid regular craters. I'm going to have to do that anyway.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Yeah. Okay. I'm ready.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: And I'm not going to brake it, to amount to anything. 16-mm film clip (2 min 20 sec; 75 Mb) by Ken Glover from material provided courtesy Mark Gray, including synched audio. Mac users may need VLC ( free download ). Journal contributor Maksim Kakitsev has created a stabilized version of various Apollo 16 film clips, including the Grand Prix.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: DAC's on; Mark. (Pause) That max acceleration?!

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: No. (Pause)

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Man, you are really bouncing! (Pause)

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Is he on the ground at all...

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay; that's 10 kilometers (per hour). (Hearing Tony) Huh?

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: (To Tony) He's got about two wheels on the ground. There's a big rooster tail out of all four wheels. And as he turns, he skids. The back end breaks loose just like on snow. Come on back, John. (Pause) And the DAC is running. Man, I'll tell you, Indy (meaning the Indianapolis 500)'s never seen a driver like this. (Pause) Okay, when he hits the craters and starts bouncing is when he gets his rooster tail. He makes sharp turns. Hey, that was a good stop. Those wheels just locked.

a16a1244820.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1244820.text: (Singing) Dee-dum-dum-dee-dee-dum.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Mark, (the camera's) off.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Okay. [NASA photo S72-37002 is a frame from the 16-mm movie. It shows John driving in an easterly direction, toward the LM, with Smoky Mountain on the horizon on the right side of the picture. We can see the dust being thrown up by the wheels and can also see that the fenders are effective in keeping that dust from being thrown onto the vehicle. Not counting the turn John made before coming back on the return leg, John drove about 25 seconds in each direction. His average speed would ahve been less than 10 km/hr, so the distance he drove in each direction would have been less than 70 meters.]

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay, you want to do it one more time?

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Had about a minute and 5 seconds that time.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Yeah, (lost under Tony). 16-mm Film Clip (2.3Mb; mov) by Gordon Roxburgh 124:58:10 Duke: Okay. Mark; on. (Pause) Okay. You could have gone the other way, but go ahead. There's the big craters there, though, aren't they?

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Yeah. I don't want to run into those holes.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: They want 4 minutes' worth, John. That was a minute and five (seconds). Maybe you can do it twice more.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: (Lecturing) Charlie!

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay. Turn sharp.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: (Laughing) I have no desire to turn sharp. (Charlie laughs, too.) Okay, here's a sharpie.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Hey, that's great! (Pause) Man, those things...When those wheels really dig in, John...When you turn is when you get the rooster tail.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Charlie?

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: The suspension system on that thing is fantastic!

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: That sounds good. We sound like we probably got enough of the Grand Prix. We're willing to let you go on from here. Call that a (complete) Grand Prix.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay. (Pause) Man, that was all four wheels off the ground, there. Okay. Max stop.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay. I don't want to do that.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay. Excuse me.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: They say that's a no-no.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay, DAC off; Mark. Okay, John. DAC's off. [Each leg of John's second run as also about 25 seconds although, perhaps, his average speed was slower and he didn't go quite as far toward the LM.]

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay. I have a lot of confidence in the stability of this contraption.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Me, too.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Sounds great. [Young, from the 1972 Technical Debrief - "I didn't get up to any great speed - maybe 10 clicks at the most - but the terrain around there was too rough and too rocky for that kind of foolishness."] [Duke, from the 1972 Technical Debrief - "It was, to do that."] [Young, from the 1972 Technical Debrief - "I was driving around craters and a couple of times I did a breakout there on the turn to show them how it looked. Driving the Rover, when it breaks out, is no problem. All you have to do is cut back (meaning steer into the slide) like you do in snow when the back-end breaks out.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay. You got to dismount, arm the mortar pack...(Pause) 124:59:41 Young: Okay. Where's your core tubes at, Charlie?

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: I'll get them.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay. Well, I'll stop it...

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Go ahead. I'm going to run back in (to the LM).

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: I knew you'd rather get out and walk.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: That's right. (After) watching you in action.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: After he saw the way you drove.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Well, when Charlie's in here, it's a lot less bouncy. (Pause) And that's the truth. I should say "some" less bouncy. [Duke, from the 1972 Technical Debrief - "I'd left the core tube standing on the little tripod (that is, leaning on the drill stem rack, which he did at 122:30:56 ). I picked them up and ran back to the LM. I didn't bother getting back on the LRV - just put them in the bag. At first, they were a little bit too long for the bag and I couldn't get the Velcro down on the bag. But, once we got them inside (the LM) and tamped it in, the snaps snapped and the Velcro Velcroed. We broug

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Man, I can't believe mine's going through that much faster. Course, I sweat like crazy. Always have. [Charlie switched to Aux water at 123:31:50 . See the discussion there.]

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay, Tony, I'm jogging back in.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Okay. (Pause)

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Charlie, I can't get my seatbelt off.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Uh-oh. (Pause)

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: See if you can tell me what the problem is.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay. You don't have it...(Pause) You don't have it unlocked. Now let it go. No, you don't have it unlocked, John. Got it over center. Push it. Now let your hand go. (Pause) See. Wait; wait a minute. Now. You got to let this thing go...You're pushing...Here.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Oh, okay.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Okay; let it...

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay, I couldn't see it...

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Now...There you go.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Okay; fine.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: There you go.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: Thank you.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: You are filthy.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: (Laughing) I tell you, there's the pot calling the kettle black. (Pause)

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Man, there's a beautiful secondary, Tony.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Is it oblong or round?

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: Meter size. (Answering) It's round, with a very angular block in it.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: I guess we don't have time to look at it, Charlie.

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: And my purge valve (locking pin) is still in strong (meaning it is in firmly).

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: (Answering Tony) No, I'm going to press on.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Okay.

a16a1244820.speaker: Duke
a16a1244820.text: I didn't even stop.

a16a1244820.speaker: England
a16a1244820.text: Gee, we could have called that a Seatbelt stop. (Pause) [This is a reference to a surreptitious sampling stop Dave Scott made during the drive back to the LM at the end of the Apollo 15 EVA-1 traverse. He told Houston that his seatbelt had come loose but, in reality, he stopped to collect a visually-striking piece of rock, now known as the Seatbelt Basalt. See the dialog and discussion following 123:42:11 in the Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Journal.]

a16a1244820.speaker: Young
a16a1244820.text: That's what it was. (Long Pause) MP3 Audio Clip ( 8 min 19 sec )

a16a1250236.speaker: Duke
