And old La Perouse looks like a - looks like an old Langrenus with a big star in the center of it.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Boy, I'll tell you, you can hardly make out much of anything about Kapteyn, due to this high Sun.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: No, I'm afraid I won't be able to say anything about Kapteyn. We're past it now and at this high Sun, you can't make out much of anything. He's a little too far from the ground track in this attitude to comfortably do when you're scrunched up in the corner of the window. And I guess I'm looking almost straight south now. Boy, there's one set of peaks that stick up down there that are really huge. Stick up over the horizon, make it look like the Andes.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. We copy that, Ken.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Go, Flight [?]

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Say again, please.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay, Ken, this is just sort of a general question about the terraces in Stone Mountain and if you get a chance, why, look down around the south end of that EVA-2 traverse, down around Station 5, and just might look in the area and see if you can give any hints on how definite those terraces are. They're going to try to establish at Station 5 on the first terrace. And if you think it looks definite enough, why, that's a no-sweat operation or how easy it looks to determine between first, second terrace, and so forth.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. I kind of looked for that and - I - let me take another look specifically at that. It appeared to me that - probably on the ground you wouldn't know you're on the first terrace. But let me take another look at that - I'll check it out this time. And again - we're only guessing what - you know, trying to guess what it would look like if you indeed were that far down.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Roger. And this is sort of a no-sweat type question, Ken, so don't - don't worry too much about it, we just like to have you lamp that area again.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Did they get a chance to drive the Rover around very much?

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Ah - yeah. The Rover went real well. I think they had - got pretty much everything in on the first EVA that they'd planned on.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: I'll bet those are two tired guys by now, then.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Yes. I expect they are, Ken. They got in 56 pounds of rocks today.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: (Laughter) Oh - very good. We've got a place for them.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Did Hank tell you we got a couple of little Casperellos flying along with us?

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: No. No, I guess I don't get that one, Ken.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: (Laughter) Well, the first time I noticed it was - I guess it was yesterday evening. I think maybe you were on when I saw the little particles flying along with me - right after - after the ground goes into darkness and you're still in daylight, then you can see all these things against the ground. And they all flicker and speckle and they come tumbling along. And this morning we came out, and I guess we were going minus-X, and I looked out the center hatch and here was this little thing just flying formation on me and I - in the dark, I couldn't tell how far back it was, but it was just sitti

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Well, that sounds like a real live Casper to me, Ken.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Well, it's so small it's probably a Casperello.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: (Laughter) All right.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: I'm looking at the - down at the central peak at Theophilus. And it has all of that same crosshatched appearance on the shadowed side that we saw on Silver Spur and Hadley.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. I put Power on the Pan Camera and the barber pole's back to gray.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. I copy that. Standby, Stereo, and Power, and you're a minute and 20 seconds from T-start.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. Passing over Kant.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: I'll tell you, the old landing site stands out now. You couldn't miss that for anything. And it wasn't that obvious at the lower Sun. Unfortunately, I'm a little too far south to be able to give you a good answer on those terraces, but I'll give a hack at it.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. Copy that. And you're 45 seconds from T-start.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. And I'm just over here standing by.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: You're ten seconds from T-start.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: And she ought to be -

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Operate.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: I have a barber pole with gray.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. And you've got an Image Motion. You want barber pole.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Beg your pardon?

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay, You want to take your Image Motion to barber pole.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Do you want me to go back to the observation?

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Does that take priority over the observation?

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: No.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Yes or no.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: No.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Yes. I think that they will be able to recognize that they're on the first terrace.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Oh, I don't know, over by Cinco they're not that obvious. They are further around to the west, but I'm not sure that recognize the first terrace. They might recognize Cinco.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. I'll get the Image Motion now.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. You're ten seconds to a - T-stop.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Stand by.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Roger. Standing by for T-stop.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. Stand by. And we're barber pole on the Image Motion.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Thank you, sir.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Roger.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. And the lens is stowed; you can go PC off, Ken.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. Pan Camera power is off.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Got you.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Boy, these - these -

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: And we'd like High Gain, Auto, Ken.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: You'd swear that - Sure thing. You'd swear that you ought to be able to see the LM with these binoculars. I think if you knew where to look - exactly, you might be able to see it. But you couldn't hold anything in your hand any more sensitive. I'll tell you, the Cinco craters stand out very nicely and the Crest crater is very obvious from up here. But it looks like the path you've drawn that goes from Station 5 to 6 and 4 - that path looks to me like it runs down sort of a tongue of material. That you can drive up it - and that those white lines we've got drawn on Chart 9 Charlie - really aren

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: They got a good system; they should be able to find Cinco.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. Now I heard earlier that you could see Double Spot with binocs. Does that sound right, Ken?

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: That's affirmative.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: I'll tell you, it's - they're really neat.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. And I'm sure that they passed on to you that the LM should be 200 meters northwest of Double Spot.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Yeah. I just - Every time I've gone over, I've been looking for something that I thought was probably more worthwhile than just the gee whiz of my saying I saw the LM.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Yeah. I agree with that priority.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: I wish they - I really wish we'd gotten into North Ray - maybe they'll still get a chance, because it looks to me like a - that's a pretty interesting path up there. Interesting from the fact that it looks like it's constructional - the ridge that runs up to North Ray crater.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: You know that central peak that we've all been looking at in Albategnius and thinking it was so big? It can't be so terribly big because - at least, it can't be terribly tall because it is just now sticking its nose up in the daylight. And the terminator passed here a long time ago.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. Good observation, Ken.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Boy, that straight wall really shows up from here. Just so they know that's a pretty interesting thing. It's interesting enough to rate number 36.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. And I guess you're rocking on, ready for your terminator photos here of Guericke.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Yes. I'm sitting waiting to get a little closer to them. I got Lassell, Albategnius B all lined up and boresighted.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Golly.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: There's a lot more of these sharp depressions. I don't know whether to call them grabens or what, but these - these little sharp lines that run across - there's a lot more of them than I'd guessed you'd find.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: I suspect that they are showing...

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: And there's Lassell C.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: ...up now in the low Sun angle?

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Yes They really stand out in low Sun. One of the things - I'm looking at one right here that's next to Lassell C. I'm going to start my strip and talk a little while I'm doing it. And that's at a - one that's just to the north of Lassell C in that highlands clump that's next to it there. And - it looks like in the low Sun, on the outside of it, you see all kinds of craters. You know, the typical low Sun angle pictures of crater patterns. Oh, down in the floor of this thing it's just as smooth as a whistle. Like someone had drug a - something heavy through there and just made a deep impression.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. Got you.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: You know it's not real obvious whether I see the end point of that strip. The thing we've drawn I think I see - but it looks like an awful lot of other craters in this low Sun. We'll have to wait until a higher Sun to see if it really is different.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. Magazine SS is now reading 47.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Forty-seven on SS.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. It's time for a little Gamma Ray Deploy.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Roger.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Mark. It's coming out.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. We got your Mark.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. I'm - I'll turn it off. Well - it looked to me like in 12 seconds and I still had a barber pole. Let's say I retract it and try again.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Oh, wait a minute. That thing was already 15 inches out. That's what it is. Okay.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: All right.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Am I correct?

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: That's correct, Ken.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. I just - my tape in this dim light, I had the lights turned down, I didn't see the tape until it was already out.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: That sort of makes it Sim Bay 5 - Casper 0.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: And, Ken. Before you put your Flight Plan away there to exercise, I'd like to remind you of something here.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: All righty. Go ahead.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. If you want to turn over to 129:25, there abouts.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Got it.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. You'll see the - the write-in change there that may look funny to you, but we really want those steps done. And what we're doing is turning the Image Motion Off for that pass and that's why it's a little out of the ordinary.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Roger. I understand. This is - the purpose of this was so that they can get a calibration on just how much motion comes with that. They can tell where the zero point and smear comes on the film. Is that correct? That's just a gee-whiz thing.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay, Ken.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: The information is gee whiz to me; I guess it's important to the people who have to make maps out of the stuff.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Roger.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. And anything else before I do myself in?

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: No. About the only other thing I've got, Ken, is your - your temperature for the sleep period. I guess there are a couple of things we could do, like we could leave some power on to increase the load, or we could try to move the Temp In valve or we could - I guess you don't have any -

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: I'm sorry. I wasn't meaning to be complaining. I was merely wanting to record a remark that there was a significant change in the cabin. Sometime starting yesterday, sometime, and I don't know when - compared to what we had had. And that was not something that I was asking for relief on. It's very comfortable.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. Very good.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Sorry if somebody put any time on it.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: No. It's no problem and...

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: No, I just...

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: ...was just glad you're happy.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: I thought it was kind of interesting. Yeah, I thought it was kind of interesting and I don't know whether it's because I'm in a 60-mile orbit or whether it's because there is only one guy in here adding heat to the atmosphere. I guess we'll decide that when John and Charlie climb in.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: One explanation is that you lost two roommates; but, also, my cabin ran what I thought a little chilly, and do you notice it getting a - gets a little clammy going through dark pass?

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Well, it's not doing so bad today. Yesterday, in the dark passes, all the windows were fogging up and every time I'd breath I had to go wipe the window off. Looked like I was standing in front of a pet store. And I haven't had that trouble - today at all. And it looks like it's slowly drying itself out. We had an awful lot of condensation in here - showed up during - after LOI. All down in the suit bay was a great big puddle of water, and we had not been aware of any collection of water anywhere before that. But it had obviously been there. It didn't come out of the tunnel, but it just sort of

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. We got those. And I'll not talk to you for a while here. You can have at it.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. As a courtesy, I'll turn Vox off too.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Hey, Stu.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Go ahead.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Do you folks have any - if you don't have anything more to pass up on this pass, I'll set my alarm clock here to remind me just before LOS, but I'd kind of like to take my comm carrier off during the exercise period if that wouldn't bother anybody.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: No. That's - that's fine with us.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. I've got my tone booster hooked up. And if you want me, send a crew alert and I'll come talk to you.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. We can handle that. And looks like we have nothing else. And if you come up before LOS, fine; if not, we'll see you around.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Okay. See you in a little bit.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay. And if I miss you at LOS, I do want to remind you about - you've got to configure the DSE on this pass.

a16a1274548.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1274548.text: Roger. I've got my kitchen clock set for that.

a16a1274548.speaker: Roosa
a16a1274548.text: Okay.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Okay, Ken, if you'll give us Low Altitude on the V/H override.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: Okay, going Low Altitude...

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: Mark.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Okay.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Okay, Ken. You can go to Center, Off position on the V/H override, and you can go Auto on the High Gain.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: Okay, V/H override is Center, Off and High Gain is in - Auto.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Okay.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: And, Ken. Just for your info, the field geology team are in the final phase of making their plans for EVA-2 tomorrow. So, if you've got any additional comments, why, better make them this - this pass because they'll have to have it all firmed up.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: Oh, I think they're smarter than I am.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Well, now. Don't get too carried away up there.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: [Laughter.] No, I would really - I'd really hope they make it to North Ray though. I think that's going to be different than we expected it to be.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Roger.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Okay, Ken, we are ready for Pan Camera Power to Off at this time.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: Okay, Pan Camera Power is coming Off -

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: Mark.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Okay, we got it.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Hey, Ken. How did we make out in our discussion on North Ray low altitude there as far as being able to see the - the white albedo or not? Or, were you too far to the south?

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: Oh, I got ahead. It depends which rev you want to talk about. On - well, I looked at her on the first day, right after DOI, there wasn't any - there was two craters, but no rays. When I went back and looked at him on landing morning, there's a slight ray. But North Ray still doesn't stand out as being the bright guy that South Ray does.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Well, it's obvious I was talking about the - the landing day.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: (Laughter) I gathered that it would be the case.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Yeah, by all means.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: Right now I would agree with you on anything, Stu.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Yeah, I'll - I'll be quiet...

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: I'm [garble] here with my...

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: I'll be quiet...

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: ...potato soup and my - Ah! Ah!

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Yeah, I ought to - I'll be quiet here and let you concentrate on your eating.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: Oh, man. This is gourmet style. I got - I got the Modern Jazz Quartet playing "Porgy and Bess," and I got orange/grapefruit, some of it in the bag, some of it on the bulkheads, potato soup. Man, it's real gourmet style. Even got a Beta candle.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: Hey, Ken. With all of that, now while ago you talked about some Casperellos - with all that Beta Candle and all that food, you don't have any such thing as a Casperette, do you?

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: (Laughter) No, I'm afraid I left that at home.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Roosa
a16_131_45_33.text: (Laughter) All right.

a16_131_45_33.speaker: Mattingly
a16_131_45_33.text: That's about all this place is lacking, though. (Music in background)

a16_132_07_14.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_07_14.text: And, Ken, just another comment to close the loop on you on that P23s - the - like I said before, the marking data was very good, and you came up with an horizon of 33 and loaded is a value of 28. And after massaging all the data decided to not change it since we've shown on the other missions that coming back - the - has a tendency to have a lower horizon. So, looks like we're just swinging with what we got there.

a16_132_07_14.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_07_14.text: Couldn't pass up a chance to watch the landing site one more time, and so I took a quick break from chow and went and watched it. And had a couple of questions in mind and only got two of them answered. One of them is that counting the - the layers in North and South Ray and South Ray looks different than North in that South Ray shows three distinct light and dark sequences. I suspect they're slumps, but there's at least three bands. North Ray doesn't have any of that sort of thing. It's obvious from this altitude. I took another look for their terraces and the whole area - the thing that we t

a16_132_07_14.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_07_14.text: Okay, I'm - I'm looking there. Now, go straight for north of the - of the LM and a little to the west, there's three small craters there that are covered with what looks like by ray, now. Where are you talking from that?

a16_132_07_14.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_07_14.text: Okay, Ken. Did you fade out, or did you stop talking? How do you read?

a16_132_07_14.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_07_14.text: Oh, hey. I - I had you off of Vox and I forgot to push the key down, I had gotten so use to it. No, I - I gave you an 80 and about - oh, you were looking in the right area. And, let me see what I can give you for coordinates on that.

a16_132_07_14.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_07_14.text: Okay, and you know I'm - I'm not overhead long enough to be sure that that's what I'm looking at, but it looked to me like it had a - a different kind of glint to it.

a16_132_07_14.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_07_14.text: Okay. I'm sure they've got that.

a16_132_07_14.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_07_14.text: Well, I missed it. By the time I got the camera, it was gone. But that little - little buildup that we talked that was just to the west of Lassell, I had it spotted, and I was grabbing for the camera, and I couldn't find it again after I got back.

a16_132_07_14.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_07_14.text: Okay. And, Ken, if you want to go Accept we'll uplink the jet monitor load; and, it's your choice whether you want us to initiate it or you want to initiate it.

a16_132_07_14.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_07_14.text: All right, you guys can do that.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay, we've got - Copy that.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay, Ken. The computer is yours. Go to Block, and the EMP is running.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. Thank you very much. You guys are really helpful.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: And, Casper; Houston.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: Be with you in a second.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay, go ahead, Stu.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. We're showing the lower 14 minutes to LOS; but, we're going to lose data before that. And, we'd like to get that E-memory dump just any time you're ready. We're all configured.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: You got it.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: And, Ken, on the High Gain, we'd like a Reacq. We'd like Pitch, zero; Yaw, 170.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay, you have Reacq; Pitch, zero; Yaw, 170.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. Ken, we're going to lose comm, with you here shortly. And, we'd like to get your onboard readouts and if you would get your book to copy, we've got a TEI-41 PAD.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. Let's see. Okay, I'll give you some readouts first. Battery C is 36.7; Battery B, 36.3; Battery A, 36.8. I guess all you really needed out of that was Battery C though. Now, you'd like the pyros. Okay. They're - A is 36.7 and B is 36.7.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. We've got all of those. Give us your RCS.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: And, you'd like to have - you want the quantities?

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: That's affirmative.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. On A - 63 percent. Bravo shows 62 percent.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: And, Ken; let's go Auto now with the High Gain. We're going to lose you in Reacq.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. You've got Auto. Charlie is 66 and Delta is 67.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. We've got all of those and I'd like to give you a TEI-41 PAD.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: Standing by to copy.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay, it's TEI-41: SPS/G&N, 38709; plus 0.72, plus 1.33; 155:06:58.45; plus 3355.2, plus 1151.0, minus 0235.0; 181, 095, 020; rest of the PAD NA. The GDC align - same as circ. Ullage, two Jets, 17 seconds. Longitude at T IG . plus 173.29, assumes no LOPC-1.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. TEI-41: SPS/G&N 38709; plus 0.72, plus 1.33; 155:06:58.45; plus 3355.2, plus 1151.0, minus 0235.0; 181, 095, 020. Sirius and Rigel with the same numbers for circ; two jets, 17 seconds. Lambda plus 1732.9 and no LOPC-1.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. That's a good read-back and we'd like to bid you good night and remind you that your logic power for the SIM bay is still on.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I'll see you in the morning.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. And we'd like to have Reacq at LOS. And that will be Pitch, zero; Yaw, 170...

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay, I'll get it. I

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: I have Pitch, zero; and 170 set in.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. Get a good night's sleep.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay. Good night, Stu. Yes, sir. Thank you very much. You've been a big help.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Roosa
a16_132_16_49.text: We'll see you tomorrow.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mattingly
a16_132_16_49.text: Okay.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mission Control
a16_132_16_49.text: This is Apollo Control 132 hours 56 minutes Ground Elapsed Time [132:45 actual GET]. We've had Loss of Signal now with Command Service Module Casper. Ken Mattingly and Stu Roosa met [sic] each other good night about four minutes prior to LOS. Some six hours 28 minutes remaining in the sleep period for the crew of Orion at Hadley or as you were Descartes landing site. We're looking toward EVA 2 starting around 141 hours 43 minutes or possibly as late as 142 hours depending on what time the crew does indeed wake up. How much time it takes for EVA preparations, eating, getting suited up and we ma

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mission Control
a16_132_16_49.text: This is Apollo Control 134 hours, 47 minutes [134:36 actual GET] into the mission of Apollo 16. All three crewmen and Casper and Orion still asleep at this time. Casper nearing the end of its 31st Lunar orbit some five minutes and 56 seconds until Loss of Signal. No communications with Mattingly at all this rev. He said his final good night at the end of the previous revolution. Four and a half hours remaining in the scheduled sleep period for Duke and Young aboard Orion who will have a second 7-hour Extravehicular Activity period later in the day. All's well with both vehicles. No systems pro

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mission Control
a16_132_16_49.text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 135 hours, 35 minutes Ground Elapsed Time [ 135:24 actual GET]. The crew aboard Orion is - is sleeping as is Ken Mattingly aboard Casper. We show the Command Module presently in an orbit of 64.4 nautical miles by 55.2 nautical miles. Meanwhile in the Mission Control Center, we've had a change of shift. Gene Kranz's team of White flight controllers are now aboard. Our Capcom at this time [is] astronaut Don Peterson who has replaced Stu Roosa at this position. We expect no conversation with the crew of Apollo 16 but should one develop, we will pass that along. W

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mission Control
a16_132_16_49.text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 136 hours, 33 minutes Ground Elapsed Time [136:22 actual GET]. The crew of Apollo 16 still in their rest period. Our countdown clock in Mission Control shows two hours, 52 minutes of sleep time remaining. We've had no conversation with the crew over the past hour. We're at 136 hours 33 minutes, continuing to monitor the displays and conversations at Mission Control. This is Apollo Control Houston.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mission Control
a16_132_16_49.text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 137 hours, 33 minutes Ground Elapsed Time [137:22 actual GET]. We show one hour and 52 minutes remaining on the rest schedule of the [LM] crew of Apollo 16. Our present schedule calls for cabin depress for the start of EVA 2 at 143 hours, two minutes ground elapsed time. At 137 hours 33 minutes, this is Apollo Control Houston.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mission Control
a16_132_16_49.text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 138 hours and 32 minutes Ground Elapsed Time [138:21 actual GET]. We show 53 minutes until time of crew wake-up. Presently, Casper is in an orbit 64.1 nautical miles by 55.3 nautical miles and on its 33rd revolution around the Moon. At 138 hours 33 minutes, continuing to monitor.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mission Control
a16_132_16_49.text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 139 hours, 17 minutes Ground Elapsed Time [139:08 actual GET]. We're some 8 minutes away, now, from time of crew wake-up. We'll leave the release line up live at this time, in the event we should hear from the crew before the 8 minutes elapse. We're at 139 hours 17 minutes, continuing to monitor. This is Apollo Control Houston.

a16_132_16_49.speaker: Mission Control
a16_132_16_49.text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 140 hours, 22 minutes Ground Elapsed Time [140:11 actual GET]. We've had noisy communications thus far with Orion this morning. The crew aboard the Lunar Module, Charles Duke and John Young, however, passed along their post sleep status reports covering a range of subjects such as how much they had eaten and how much they had slept. They also were enthusiastic about the size of the meals provided. Our Capcom since crew wakeup has been Tony England, and in the course of the conversation he's given updates to the traverse plan for EVA 2. These are minor. It's ba

a16a1390526.speaker: Peterson
a16a1390526.text: Orion, Houston. How do you read?

a16a1390526.speaker: Young
a16a1390526.text: Rog. What time are we supposed to get up? Over.

a16a1390526.speaker: Peterson
a16a1390526.text: John, I can't understand you. We'd like, if you're reading, to go Down Voice Backup.

a16a1390526.speaker: Young
a16a1390526.text: Okay. What time is wake-up time? (Pause)

a16a1390526.speaker: Peterson
a16a1390526.text: You're about 3-1/2 minutes from nominal wake-up now.

a16a1390526.speaker: Young
a16a1390526.text: Okay, we timed it pretty good.

a16a1390526.speaker: Peterson
a16a1390526.text: Looks like you timed it just about right on your own. (Long Pause; static clears) Orion, Houston. Voice check.

a16a1390526.speaker: Young
a16a1390526.text: (Muddy, but improved) We're reading you loud and clear on Down Voice Backup. Over.

a16a1390526.speaker: Peterson
a16a1390526.text: Okay. We're reading you a little better, too. (Long Pause) [Because Houston is transmitting through at least an 85-foot dish, the signal reaching the Moon is quite strong and the comm in the LM cabin is much better than the comm being heard in Houston.]

a16a1390526.speaker: Young
a16a1390526.text: How did the systems look last night?

a16a1390526.speaker: Peterson
a16a1390526.text: Everything looked real good, John. [Very Long Comm Break] MP3 Audio Clip ( 9 min 58 sec ) (This clip starts with a 8 minute 54 second interval with no comm.)

a16a1391326.speaker: Duke
a16a1391326.text: Hello, Houston; 15 (sic). (Long Pause) Hello, Houston; 15. Over. 139:22:52 England: Good morning, Charlie. How are you?

a16a1391326.speaker: Duke
a16a1391326.text: I guess it's 16; excuse me. (Hearing Tony) Fine. I guess we're 16. How did the biomed look on me all night long, Tony?

a16a1391326.speaker: England
a16a1391326.text: Okay, Charlie. I guess the biomed looked good. How do you feel this morning?

a16a1391326.speaker: Duke
a16a1391326.text: I feel great. Why don't you have the docs tell me how much they think I slept? (Pause) MP3 Audio Clip ( 1 min 53 sec )

a16a1392327.speaker: England
a16a1392327.text: Charlie, they say they think you've slept 6 hours.

a16a1392327.speaker: Duke
a16a1392327.text: Okay, fine. I was going to say 7. Of course, I don't know exactly when we got started, but once we got started, it was just like a baby, except for...One time, I woke when I got cold, and had to put on my sleeping bag.

a16a1392327.speaker: England
a16a1392327.text: Outstanding. [Duke - "We had a little knitted thing that looked like cheesecloth, really, but it had wider pattern on it. We had 'em on the Command Module and the Lunar Module. You just climb into it and zip it up. It didn't look like it'd help you much, but it did. I was surprised, because it had a pretty wide weave to it. You could hold it up and see through it real easy. It might be called a Sleep Restraint."]

a16a1392327.speaker: Duke
a16a1392327.text: Okay; here we go with the crew status report. First, I'd like to say that we gorged ourselves, really, and still couldn't eat everything. I tell you, one of those meals would fill the whole Roman army on maneuvers for 2 days. But John, he ate, yesterday: Day 5 Meal C, and Day 6 Meal A. And on Day 5 Meal C, John ate everything, plus an EVA beverage. And the Day 6 meal A, which was breakfast yesterday, John ate everything except the ham steak. You can scratch the ham steak. He got 7 hours and 15 minutes sleep last night, and he took no medication. Over.

a16a1392327.speaker: England
a16a1392327.text: Okay; we got that, Charlie. (Long Pause)

a16a1392327.speaker: Duke
a16a1392327.text: Okay; turning to my page. On Day 5 Meal C, you can scratch the chocolate pudding, and I ate everything else plus the EVA beverage. And John, also, had an EVA beverage. On Day 6 Meal A, I ate everything but the ham steak. Over. 139:26:03 England: Okay; we copy. [Details for the meals can be found in the LM Menu given in the Apollo 16 Press Kit ( 5.6 Mb PDF ).] [I presume "an EVA beverage" means a drink bag full of potassium-fortified orange drink.] [Duke, from the 1972 Technical Debrief - "We had too much food. Dave (Scott) said they ate everything; but we couldn't have possibly eaten everythin

a16a1392327.speaker: Duke
a16a1392327.text: And I said I got 7 hours, but whatever you all say. I slept real good; feel great. (Pause)

a16a1392327.speaker: England
a16a1392327.text: Okay; before you all get too covered up (with the suit), we'd like you to check your biomed sensors. (Pause) And did you take any medication?

a16a1392327.speaker: Duke
a16a1392327.text: Yeah, I took another Seconal again, to start off. And I guess my biomed (sensor) is good; John's look firm as they can be.

a16a1392327.speaker: England
a16a1392327.text: Okay.

a16a1392327.speaker: Duke
a16a1392327.text: Now we're going to start the chow. And, well, I guess I'll copy the lift-off times first, if you have them.

a16a1392327.speaker: England
a16a1392327.text: Say again, Charlie.

a16a1392327.speaker: Duke
a16a1392327.text: Do you have those lift-off times for us?

a16a1392327.speaker: England
a16a1392327.text: Okay; stand by one. (Long Pause) Okay, Apollo 16. We don't have that block time yet. We'll get it to you in a minute. We have a couple of questions about the (ALSEP) heat flow (experiment) again, if you want to think about those.

a16a1392327.speaker: Duke
a16a1392327.text: Go ahead.

a16a1392327.speaker: England
a16a1392327.text: Okay. That heat flow cable that fits into the Central Station is connected to a printed circuit board inside the connector there. And we're curious about the end of the cable. Does it have any of that printed circuit board on it or is it just a free end of the ribbon cable?

a16a1392327.speaker: Duke
a16a1392327.text: Tony, I was thinking about that last night, and it looked like to me that it might have some of that printed circuit. All I can see is that the end of the cable is very smooth and it's silver and I think the printed circuit is partly silver, but I'm not really positive; that's something you can think about. And it is very smooth; and around the connector it is very smooth there, also. And as John kicked that thing out of there, it came right out of there without moving the Central Station at all! Over.

a16a1392327.speaker: England
a16a1392327.text: Okay. How about the PSE - the passive seismic cable? Is it tight? What we have to decide here is, if you move the Central Station, will it disturb the PSE? That thing (meaning the sensors in the seismometer) is uncaged now and you can't re-cage it. So we can't afford to move it. (Pause)

a16a1392327.speaker: Duke
a16a1392327.text: Well, he said he thinks it's pretty tight, John does; but I can't remember. How far do you want to move it?

a16a1392327.speaker: England
a16a1392327.text: Well, what we're thinking about is if we did ask you to take off that astroconnector on the heat flow experiment, you may have to lift the station up to get underneath to the little lever.

a16a1392327.speaker: Duke
a16a1392327.text: Yeah. But, Tony, everybody's told me it's serrated and once you got that little beauty on there, you can't get it off!

a16a1392327.speaker: England
a16a1392327.text: We're working on that now.

a16a1392327.speaker: Duke
a16a1392327.text: Yeah, I think there's a little pin or something in there you have to push in. And I don't know whether we got the tools for that. (Pause) Well, I think we could do that. It's not that tight. I think we could do that; pick it up.

a16a1392327.speaker: England
a16a1392327.text: Okay; understand. Fredo's (Fred Haise) been over running, suited, this heat flow experiment, to see if the procedure is effective. We don't have a decision yet. We don't want to get you all excited about it, but we'll have something - a yes or no - in about 45 minutes.

a16a1392327.speaker: Duke
a16a1392327.text: Well, I guess we'll still be here.

a16a1392327.speaker: England
a16a1392327.text: Okay. (Long Pause) [Fred Haise, the Apollo 16 Backup Commander, is testing procedures in a pressurized suit to see if a repair of the broken cable is possible.] MP3 Audio Clip ( 9 min 36 sec )

a16a1393212.speaker: Duke
a16a1393212.text: Tony, if I thought yesterday's meal was big, you ought to see this one. Man, there's a lot of chow here. (Pause)

a16a1393212.speaker: England
a16a1393212.text: Charlie, which meal did you say you're eating? (Pause)

a16a1393212.speaker: Duke
a16a1393212.text: It's breakfast. Day 7 meal A...

a16a1393212.speaker: England
a16a1393212.text: Okay. (Pause) We're just trying to put a little weight on you.

a16a1393212.speaker: Duke
a16a1393212.text: (Lost under Tony) Day 6, Meal B tonight. Man, I tell you, I feel "oink" right now. (Long Pause) [Details for the meals can be found in the LM Menu given in the Apollo 16 Press Kit ( 5.6 Mb PDF ).]

a16a1393212.speaker: England
a16a1393212.text: I can just sit here and talk a few words about the traverse today, if you like. I haven't really organized my notes on it, so it may ramble a little bit, but I've gotten a briefing by the planning team. It looks like an interesting plan here. The traverse is almost...Well, it's exactly like normal EVA-2.

a16a1393212.speaker: Young
a16a1393212.text: (The Approving Teacher) There you go. [The stations planned for the EVA-2 traverse are shown on the " Descartes EVA-II, 2 of 2 " map.]

a16a1393212.speaker: England
a16a1393212.text: (Chuckles) From Ken (Mattingly)'s words, he can see definite benches in Stone Mountain and thinks that you'll have a pretty good chance of identifying them. He can see layers in South Ray, which makes the rays at Station 8 a whole lot more interesting than we had even anticipated. So right now, we'd like you to do a normal (Stations) 4, 5, and 6. The main thing identifying 6 is being on the bottom of the slope of the lowest bench, Station 5 being on top of the first bench, and Station 4 being on top of the second bench. In fact, it may be even a little above. Right now, we're thinking that we

a16a1393212.speaker: Duke
a16a1393212.text: Okay, Tony, I think you'll be able to...From up on Stone there, it looks like to me you're gonna be able to see right into South Ray and right into Stubby and all those craters. The general topography here is a downslope. From North Ray, it leads from the ridge to our immediate right all the way down to South Ray, with the lowest point really being maybe south of Survey Ridge. Over. [Survey Ridge is shown on the "Descartes EVA-II, 1 of 2" map and runs northeast/southwest through BT/82. As indicated on the map, John and Charlie plan to travel along the ridge crest during the outbound traverse.

a16a1393212.speaker: England
a16a1393212.text: Okay, right. And we could see, or I think I could see, the bright area of South Ray on the TV pan. It really stands out down there. But our really exciting station looks like it may be Station 8, and we're really going to encourage you to scout around and see if you can get the samples of the different layers that we see in South Ray.

a16a1393212.speaker: Duke
a16a1393212.text: It looks to us like the base of Stone Mountain is really topographically lower than we are right now.

a16a1393212.speaker: England
a16a1393212.text: Okay. (Pause) And, also, on Station 9, it may turn out to be difficult to find a pristine area. We'll let you scout around a little bit, and pick your own Station 9 on whatever looks like isn't ray material. And on the location of Station 10, we'd like you to put it just about where you said it might go as you were driving back yesterday. It sounds like the contact between the ray and the non-ray material is just west of you there, and we'd like to run the penetrometer array along the contact but in the ray material; that is, the penetrometer array would now go in a northeast/southwest directi

a16a1393212.speaker: Young
a16a1393212.text: (Changing subjects) Okay, Houston. We're going to have to move the UV camera back. I think the front lens is starting to get into the Sun.

a16a1393212.speaker: England
a16a1393212.text: Say again, John. (Pause) [It is not easy to understand John's transmission because of the static and the fact that he has changed subjects. Somebody else in Houston apparently understood what John said and told Tony.]

a16a1393212.speaker: England
a16a1393212.text: Okay, we've got a plan here at the end of the EVA to move it back. Do you think it will stay out of the Sun until then?

a16a1393212.speaker: Young
a16a1393212.text: Did you get that, Houston? (Pause) Houston, 16. Over.

a16a1393212.speaker: England
a16a1393212.text: Go ahead. (Long Pause) [As we will discover in a moment, the LM crew is no longer able to hear Tony because of a problem with the communications link between Houston and the receiving station in Australia.]

a16a1393212.speaker: Duke
a16a1393212.text: Houston, did you copy John? Over.

a16a1393212.speaker: England
a16a1393212.text: We sure did there, Charlie. You copy us? (Long Pause) 139:40:04 Saxon: Orion, this is Honeysuckle (Australia). We have a comm outage with Houston at this time. Stand by one, please. [The speaker is the Operations Manager at NASA's Honeysuckle Creek Tracking Station near Canberra, Mr. John Saxon, an Australian. My thanks to Dean Davidson who located this information in the August 24, 1972 editions of the Sydney Morning Herald and the Canberra Times.]

a16a1393212.speaker: Young
a16a1393212.text: (Under heavy static) Okay, Honeysuckle. Nice to talk to you. How are y'all doing down there?

a16a1393212.speaker: Saxon
a16a1393212.text: We're doing great; nice to talk to you.

a16a1393212.speaker: Young
a16a1393212.text: Right; you sound good.

a16a1393212.speaker: Saxon
a16a1393212.text: Roger that; we'll be with you shortly. We're just getting some line (garbled). (Pause)

a16a1393212.speaker: Young
a16a1393212.text: Have a Swan for us. [Swan Lager is a West Australian beer.]

a16a1393212.speaker: Saxon
a16a1393212.text: Say again, Orion. You're pretty poor quality on this backup.

a16a1393212.speaker: Young
a16a1393212.text: I said 'quaff a Swan for us'.

a16a1393212.speaker: Saxon
a16a1393212.text: I still can't copy you, Orion. I'm sorry about this. The quality is very poor at the moment.

a16a1393212.speaker: Young
a16a1393212.text: Okay, you're loud and clear.

a16a1425645.text: Okay. Thank goodness, you said that. I was about to pick this thing up. Video Clip ( 2 min 49 sec 0.7 Mb RealVideo or 25 Mb MPEG )

a16a1425645.speaker: England
a16a1425645.text: Sorry about that, John. [Comm Break] [After Charlie attaches the bag to the gate, he puts in two core tubes. Figure 99 (S88-52671) in Judy Allton's Apollo Toolbook shows an SCB with two core tubes stowed in interior pockets.] [In Houston, the Flight Director is told that the UV experimenters want to change targets. Quite properly, he decides not to bother John and says that they will "press on" with the mission.]

a16a1425645.speaker: Duke
a16a1425645.text: (Working at the back of the Rover behind John's seat) There's no way to get that out (garbled). (Long Pause) [As per LMP-5 , Charlie is trying to get either a sample bag dispenser or a core cap dispenser. He then removes the two core tubes he just placed in the SCB.] [In Houston, the Flight Director tells the UV experimenters that he doesn't want them to select targets where there is any chance that the camera will be pointed at the LM. "We're wasting time, here."] [Charlie seems to get a sample bag dispenser out of the SCB and then re-stows the core tube.] MP3 Audio Clip ( 1 min 05 sec )

a16a1430103.speaker: Young
a16a1430103.text: Okay, Houston, I think we're (aimed) clear (of the LM) now.

a16a1430103.speaker: England
a16a1430103.text: Okay, good show. Hit reset, watch the film.

a16a1430103.speaker: Young
a16a1430103.text: But it's reading 080 (degrees azimuth), Houston. (Pause) Is that okay? [The camera is pointing slightly west of north and not northeast. If they stay with this pointing, in essence they will be looking at a random piece of sky.]

a16a1430103.speaker: England
a16a1430103.text: Stand by a second, John. Why don't you read that tempa-label to us (while a decision is made)?

a16a1430103.speaker: England
a16a1430103.text: No; that's on the film cassette.

a16a1430103.speaker: Young
a16a1430103.text: Okay. The tempa-label on the film cassette is black at a 100 degrees F. [In Houston, the Flight Director relents and allows the UV experimenters to pick a new target.]

a16a1430103.speaker: England
a16a1430103.text: Good show. That's good news. I hate to do this to you, John, but we're going to have to change targets. We'd like to go to azimuth 317. Video Clip ( 3 min 01 sec 0.8 Mb RealVideo or 27 Mb MPEG )

a16a1430103.speaker: Young
a16a1430103.text: Okay, 317. (Long Pause) MP3 Audio Clip ( 0 min 17 sec ) [Charlie comes around to the LMP seat and puts something down. Whatever it is, it is not large enough to be a bag dispenser.]

a16a1430205.speaker: England
a16a1430205.text: And elevation, 51. (Long Pause) [This target is in the southwest direction.] [Charlie returns to the back of the Rover, gets an SCB and takes it to the LMP seat. He then examines his checklist and goes to get the ETB, which has been hanging from the front edge of the MESA. During the following conversation between John and Tony, Charlie takes the ETB to the CDR seat. Note that, as per CDR-5 , John was supposed to have unloaded the ETB. Charlie does not have the details on his checklist ( LMP-5 )but, probably having watched John do it often enough in training, doesn't have to ask Tony for instr

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Okay, 317 at 51.

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Okay, hit reset and watch the film; if it advances, we're through with it for now.

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Oh, boy; it advanced! Over 120...Almost 180. (Lost under Tony)

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Good show. That's the way it should go. Now we'd like you to turn around and look at the cosmic ray for a second.

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Okay. (Hearing Tony's request) Get turned around and looked at the cosmic ray.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: (In his W.C. Fields voice) Turn around and lookit the cosmic ray. [John has turned to face east and walks to the cosmic ray experiment, which is out of our view on the south side of the spacecraft.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: That's a nice cosmic ray and... [Fendell starts panning counter-clockwise.]

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Okay. (Chuckles) In the top panel...

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Where's this...(Stops to listen)

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: ...in the top panel when you pulled that...

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Yes?

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: ...ring, (John laughs) a piece of tinfoil should have slid up so there's only a 2-by-2 flap in the upper left-hand corner. Can you see that tinfoil? [Before John and Charlie start the drive to Stone Mountain, one of them takes two pictures of the Cosmic Ray Experiment, AS16-107- 17441 and 17442 .]

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: (Mulling the question) There's only a 2 by 2 flap in the upper left-hand corner. Yeah, but it's more than 2 by 2; it's about...There's a hole that's covered up. There's a hole up there, and it's covered up in the upper left-hand corner, or almost covered up.

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Okay. Understand that. That should be right.

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: It's almost covered up.

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Could you describe how it's almost covered up? Which part isn't covered?

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: The bottom part of the hole is almost uncovered. I'd say the bottom one-fourth of the hole is not covered.

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Okay. That's good news, John. That means you deployed...(Choosing a more diplomatic phrasing) It deployed fine. We'll get a picture of it later from Charlie, and if you could go about your nominal work now. (Pause) Video Clip ( 3 min 03 sec 0.8 Mb RealVideo or 27 Mb MPEG )

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Ah, the old water bag is working super! This is going to be a good day, Charlie.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Good. (Pause) (Doing his W. C. Fields voice) Ah, the old commander's camera. Right down in the old dust. (Normal voice) That's on the floorboard; that's not onto the ground. (Pause)

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Okay. (Laughing) I wonder what my nominal workload is at this point.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: I don't know.

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: We're supposed to be at Station 4, Charlie. [Although John is aware that he lost a lot of time because of the UV camera, he sounds relaxed and, obviously, is not in a mood to complain.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Just like in training, John...

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Yeah.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: ...I'm licking the orange juice off (the inside of) my visor. [Fendell finds Charlie at the CDR seat. He is holding the ETB in his left hand and is reaching in with his right. He pulls something out - probably a film magazine - and stows it under the CDR seat.]

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: And, Charlie, when you're taking that pan, let me know. I have another picture for you.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: All righty! [John comes up behind Charlie from the back of the Rover but, during the following is out of view while he works on the right side of Charlie's PLSS.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Okay, Charlie, hold still a second and let me get your old PLSS strap tie-down on here a little bit.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Old PLSS strap tiedown.

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Man, that's really bad there. (Long Pause) (I) don't know how a growing boy could get his straps so messed up in one little EVA. (Pause) [John comes around to the left side of Charlie's PLSS to check that part of the harness.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Oh, the old dark slide. Coming out! Expose one picture. Okay. [Charlie has just withdrawn the dark slide from a film magazine, installed the magazine in the 500mm camera, and then advanced a frame so that the next picture will be on unexposed film. As Charlie works at the CDR seat, we get a glimpse of John as he examines his checklist.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Okay. (Looking at CDR-5 ) You got the ETB (unloaded). Right?

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Yeah. Just about finished with it.

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: (Looking at CDR-4 ) You got the LRV circuit breakers, Bus A, B, C, and D, and Nav closed?

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Yup. No, I didn't close...Yeah, Nav Power's closed. [Fendell starts to pan clockwise just as John walks toward the front of the Rover, looking at his checklist as he goes. One of the raised battery covers is visible in the foreground.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Okay. The dustbrush is on the LCRU. It is.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Amazing. [A detail from training photo KSC-71PC-777 shows the dustbrush stowed on the front of the training Rover.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: "Close LRV (batt) covers and press tight." Okay, Houston, the covers are still open, and they don't have any more dust on them than they did yesterday.

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Outstanding.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: (Joking) Therefore, you have to dust. (Pause) What we need is a dustbrush for the dustbrush.

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Don't say it, Charlie.

a16a1430222.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1430222.text: Sixty [garble].

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Say again?

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: I said, don't suggest it.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Yeah. Somebody will probably log that. [Tony is warning Charlie that somebody will take the suggestion seriously and design a dustbrush dustbrush for Apollo 17.] [Jones - "Were there people in the support rooms listening to this and writing things down that needed to be changed or added. Is that the implication of this?"] [Duke - "Well, the implication is that somebody might think, 'Oh, yeah, we do need that', and add something else to the stowage list when we were just kidding. But lot of times (in training), though, things you thought of, like that, would result in a change in the procedures

a16a1430222.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1430222.text: Another one we sneaked by.

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: (To Houston) Hey! Can you guys see that dust on there, with the TV?

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: We're not looking down far enough right now. [Charlie closes John's seat and takes the ETB to the MESA. Fendell shifts his aim down, giving us a view of the battery mirrors just as John pushes the cover closed.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Oh.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: John, make sure that I did all the things on (the ETB unload on CDR-5 )...The ETB is emptied, and magazine Lima is on the camera - (the) 500 - and all the other film is stowed. [A puff of dust flies off the battery cover as it falls shut. John then presses the cover with his right hand.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Whew. Okay. Down and pressed tight.

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Okay. [Fendell raises his aim. John is no longer in sight.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Man, that LPM (Lunar Portable Magnetometer) is a bucket of spaghetti!

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: You're not messing with it, are you?

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: No. I was just... [After John used the LPM at Station 2, he did his best to rewind the ribbon cable that connects the sensor to the gauge mounted on the back of the Rover. Obviously, he didn't get it wound very neatly.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: (To Houston) And as near as I can figure, Tony, what we've got to do now is load up the PLSSs (as per CDR-5 ) and go get 'em (meaning the rocks on Stone Mountain). (Pause) [Fendell starts a clockwise pan.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: (To Tony) Want me to reset the far UV again, or you just want to be happy with this? All we got to do now is a PLSS load-up.

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Okay; yes. We have one more target on it. I'm not sure they have enough time, yet. Hold on. [Tony is probably saying that the UV experimenters may not have been on the current target long enough to have good data.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Want a minute; I got to get a pan, John. So it'll be a few minutes. Why don't you run around and pick up a rock?

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Hey! Outstanding suggestion. Give me a rock bag, Charlie.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: The little ones or the big ones?

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Huh?

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Why don't you take your camera?

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: I will.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Okay. That...

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: That's yours, huh?

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Yeah. Well, I got some right here. You use those, and I'll put the old maps...(Rhetorically) Which way are we going today? Hmmm.

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: How about south?

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Let's see, (pretending to read) "Hadley Rille". (Pause) [During our mission review, Charlie told me that, before the Descartes maps were ready for training purposes, he and John used copies of the Apollo 15 maps. Those, of course, showed Hadley Rille.]

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Okay...

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Tony, this map says "Start at training building." [This is a reference to training exercises conducted at the Cape.]

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: (General laughter in Houston) Okay. Verify that your PLSS antennas are up, and could we have an EMU check first chance? And John, if you're out picking up a rock, you might...

a16a1430222.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1430222.text: [garble] now.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Our antennas aren't up. How's the comm?

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Comm sounds good.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Maybe we ought to leave them down. That way we won't break them off! (Pause) [On Apollo 15, Jim Irwin broke his antenna when he and Dave Scott forgot to stow it before he climbed back in the LM. In Houston, Flight is told that they need the antennas up because, if they bend over, the comm can deteriorate.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1430222.text: Thirty-six.

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: And John, if you're picking up a rock, could you get that...

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Always thought it would work...(Stops to listen)

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: ...the vesicular basalt underneath the engine bell?

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Yep. Sure could do that. [Fendell stops his pan with the MESA on the left side of the frame. Charlie is in view for a few seconds but then goes off-camera to the right.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1430222.text: Okay, now this little terminator should be out here at 60.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Tony, that is a "double" Muley, that rock. [Big Muley, the sample collected near the Rover at Plum crater is a 28x18x16 cm rock weighing 11.7 kilograms. A "double" Muley is clearly too big for John to collect, especially from under the spacecraft.]

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Uh-oh.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Come here, John. Let me get your antenna. (Pause) Well, I can't reach it. Why don't you get downslope and lean on the Rover. [Fendell completes the pan and finds Charlie at the back of the Rover. John is at the right edge of the picture he is facing Charlie and is bent at the waist to get the top of his OPS into reach. He has his left hand on the top of the gate for stability.] Video Clip ( 2 min 50 sec 0.7 Mb RealVideo or 25 Mb MPEG )

a16a1430222.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1430222.text: Must have been Mandel'shtam I was looking at. Yeah. That would change [garble

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: There we go. Camera's on. This is a...Guess what. The antenna's up, and the comm is still the same. There we go. [Charlie's cryptic comment about his camera is probably a reference to the fact that, with it on, he can't get very close to John.] [Young, from the 1972 Technical Debrief - "(During training) it had been easy for us to deploy our antennas when we were on the surface but, once we were in one-sixth gravity, the only way that I could reach up to deploy Charlie's antenna was to have him come over and grab hold of something like the ladder or the Rover and bend over so I could get my ha

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: And just forget that big rock for now. That's too big to handle.

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Well, it's inaccessible; (laughing) it's underneath the engine cover.

a16a1430222.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1430222.text: Okay, and the lighter areas seem to have fewer craters.

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Okay; fine.

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: You want me to crawl under the LM?

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: No. That's all right.

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Okay. But there's probably another nice rock. I'm sure there's another good rock around here that I've been eyeing out my window I wanted to get anyway. [Fendell pans left and finds Charlie at the LMP seat, just as he turns his checklist page to LMP-6 .]

a16a1430222.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1430222.text: Almost all these craters in the - let's see, can we say that the - I see no elongate craters at all. I'm just looking in the area just past Mandel'shtam. The dark areas seem to have more craters and more small craters. The light areas have - not so many craters.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Hey, John?

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Yes, Charlie.

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: I hate to tell you, but I need your camera for the (color pan)...Here, take mine with the black-and-white (film) and let me have yours for the pan.

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: (Admonishing) Charlie. [After taking the LMP Hasselblad off his RCU bracket, Charlie has run off-camera to the right to swap cameras with John. Fendell pans right to follow.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: I'm sorry. Little out of sequence here. (Garbled) (Pause) [Fendell finds John and Charlie beyond the Rover console.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: (It's) like running together in the Sahara Desert. (Pause) [The sequence of tasks had been designed, partly, to ensure that John and Charlie didn't get in each other's way. Consequently, they are used to working alone during this sequence of tasks and Charlie is amused that they - the only two people on the Moon - have bumped into each other.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Let me...(Pause) Okay; I got it. I got it.

a16a1430222.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1430222.text: Some bright halos and dark ones. And the darker areas look like Cayley, don't have as many bright craters on them, as a matter of fact. Let's see, can I - Yeah, there's one bright-rayed guy on - another Cayley type. Most of the Cayley types seem to have dark craters - generally rimless. Everything here is still - On the small scale, we have circular craters; on the large scale, we have crater chains and - and lineaments - they're on a very large scale. Both [garble] certainly.

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Got it?

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Yeah.

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Okay. (Pause) [Charlie goes off-camera to the left, going around the south side of the LM. John bobs down to pick an object - possibly a dropped bag - off the ground.] 143:12:12 Duke: Okay. Hmm. "Happy birthday", it says. [Charlie may be reading a note on his checklist, probably a reference to his intention to leave a medallion on the Moon to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the creation of the United States Air Force in 1947. The original flight plan had the start of EVA-2 at about 125 hours into the mission, or about 6 p.m. 21 April 1972, Central Standard Time . Charlie mentions the anniv

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: (H)EDC (Hasselblad Electric Data Camera). Let's see; "pan quad III". Well, guess what? I'm on the wrong side (of the LM). (Pause) [As is indicted in Figure 3.4-1 from the Apollo 16 Lunar Surface Procedures volume, Quad III is the northeast face of the LM. As Fendell pans left, Charlie comes into view, using a skipping stride as he goes clockwise around the spacecraft.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: Ah, me. (Pause) Works better for me, Tony, if skip out here rather than (use another stride)...(Pause) If you want some of this blackish rock, John, a small one that's bag-able; there's a bunch right out here that look just like what I call that basalt. In fact, there's hundreds of them. [Fendell has panned left until the plus-Y (north) and minus-Z (east) footpads are at the right side of the TV picture. As indicated in Figure 6-13 in the Preliminary Science Report , Charlie is about 60 feet north of the LM and, consequently, is not in sight. Fendell reverses direction.]

a16a1430222.speaker: Young
a16a1430222.text: Yeah. They're out from that little impact crater we just landed beyond. And I want to get this nice white one right here. 143:13:18 Duke: Okay. The old pan...

a16a1430222.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1430222.text: Now, there's places out here in this Cayley now where you find smooth areas that interweave with the - the more pitted areas. Then these smoother bands seem to be just like these thin bands at [garble]. Then some of these bands seem to cross both the white and the Cayley-looking materials. Now then, here comes - this must be Mandel'shtam that I'm coming up on now.

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: And...

a16a1430222.speaker: Duke
a16a1430222.text: ...starts at f/11 at 250. Okay. Exactly 60 feet to the left, Tony! Video Clip ( 3 min 39 sec 0.9 Mb RealVideo or 32 Mb MPEG )

a16a1430222.speaker: England
a16a1430222.text: Okay. (Pause) [Fendell reaches the clockwise pan limit and finds John, who is visible beyond the console as he collects samples. Although most of our view is blocked by the console, it looks like he is just south of the LM shadow.] MP3 Audio Clip ( 11 min 50 sec )

a16a1431346.speaker: Duke
a16a1431346.text: The best pan. (Pause) [Charlie's 4 o'clock pan consists of frames AS16-107- 17419 to 17440 .] [Frame 17419 is a down-Sun photo of the Solar Wind Collector (SWC) and 17431 shows some Rover tracks.] [Frame 17435 is a good portrait of the LM, the MESA, the SEQ Bay, the Rover, and John beyond it.] [Frames 17436 , 17437 , and 17438 also show John.] [Frame 17440 shows the U.S. flag and the SWC.] [Adam Bootle has assembled the portion of the pan showing the LM and Stone Mountain.] [The f-stop settings used relative to the direction of the Sun are shown on decals mounted on the tops of the film magazi

a16a1431346.speaker: Duke
a16a1431346.text: Boy, it sure looks different looking up-Sun. (Pause) You can still see those lineations in Stone Mountain, Tony. In fact, they're maybe a little bit more pronounced (with the Sun higher than it was during EVA-1). 143:14:14 England: Okay. Do you feel like they're the same angle? [The Sun has risen about 8 degrees in the sixteen hours since the end of EVA-1. If the pattern of lineations is a lighting effect, it would be expected to change as the Sun rises.] [John is taking a cross-Sun stereopair of "before" photos from the south of sample 60025. These are AS16-110- 17866 and 17867 . Sample 60025

a16a1431346.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1431346.text: No, I guess not. Rather, this must be - our old friend, the Cayley floor.

a16a1431346.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1431346.text: That stuff is all so subdued, it's just like someone stretched a cold cream over it up from underneath to hide it. Like it was a thick paint, and it - it just barely reflects all the things that are underneath it. And every now and then there's a little old bubble in it that popped.

a16a1431346.speaker: England
a16a1431346.text: Okay. Why don't we catch that as you drive out... [Tony is suggesting that Charlie wait to describe the lineations during the drive to Station 4.]

a16a1431346.speaker: Duke

a16a1431346.speaker: England

As shown in photos taken from the Command Module, the soil around the LM is lighter than the normal surface. Although the precise mechanism that causes the surface to be more reflective isn't known, it is undoubtedly caused by the Descent Engine plume during the landing. When the astronauts disturb the surface near the LM, it returns to its normal color. Down-Sun photos taken on various missions show darkened soil in that direction. See, for example, AS17-140 21355 .]
