a16a1541126.speaker: Young
a16a1541126.text: I would be interested in what our EVA is gonna look like for tomorrow. Maybe I was off comm and you told Charlie or something.

a16a1541126.speaker: Roosa
a16a1541126.text: Well, that's - that's the one thing you've always got to watch out for. That and Check 6.

a16a1541126.speaker: England
a16a1541126.text: No. We haven't said anything about it. The planners will be back working on it. I can tell you what it looked like before EVA-2. It was a 5-hour EVA with about an hour up on North Ray and about 20 minutes at Station 13 and essentially the rest of the time back in the LM/ALSEP area, especially east of the LM, there.

a16a1541126.speaker: Roosa
a16a1541126.text: And, Ken, a reminder on your Waste Stowage Vent valve.

a16a1541126.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1541126.text: Gee, thank you. Is it that time? It sure is.

a16a1541126.speaker: Young
a16a1541126.text: Okay. It's probably subject to a change, huh?

a16a1541126.speaker: England
a16a1541126.text: Yeah, it probably is. You got a lot of good data today, and that'll make them think about it overnight, anyway. But I'm sure everybody's sort of drooling about North Ray.

a16a1541126.speaker: Young
a16a1541126.text: Yeah. I kind of feel like if we're ever going to be able to sort this out, North Ray's probably the place. Personally, to be able to get down 200 meters is something we probably ought to do to see just how complicated this thing really is. [The North Ray impact dug out rocks from a depth of at least 200 meters and, because it is 10 km from South Ray, may have sampled a different formation. Similarities and differences between samples collected from the two impacts will say a lot about the site.] 154:21:26 England: Right. You're sure right. But let's not think geology, let's go to bed. Incident

a16a1541126.speaker: Young
a16a1541126.text: Okay, Lo Bit Rate and Down Voice Backup. You got it.

a16a1541126.speaker: England
a16a1541126.text: Okay. 154:21:47 Duke: Okay. Tony, whose arrhythmias y'all want to look at tonight? [This is a reference to the heart irregularities seen in both members of the Apollo 15 crew, a condition believed to have been caused by potassium deficiencies. Because John and Charlie are getting plenty of potassium, they are not showing abnormalities. Journal Contributor Garry Kennedy notes that occasional problems with arrhythmias crop up in the Shuttle/Mir era. In July 1997, during the days following the collision of an unmanned Progress supply ship with Russia's Mir Space Station, the mission commander exp

a16a1541126.speaker: England
a16a1541126.text: Okay. Biomed, Left.

a16a1541126.speaker: Duke
a16a1541126.text: Yea! (Static) [This means that the Flight Surgeon wants to look at John's heart and that Charlie can take his sensors off.]

a16a1541126.speaker: Roosa
a16a1541126.text: Ken, have you got any bright planets in your view in that double umbra? Isn't that something - really a beautiful sight, isn't it?

a16a1541126.speaker: England
a16a1541126.text: Charlie...(Pause) MP3 Audio Clip ( 1 min 50 sec )

a16a1542213.speaker: Duke
a16a1542213.text: Okay. We still put in a strong vote for North Ray. It looks accessible, and there's a tremendous block up there we'd like to look at. [This is House Rock.] [Jones - "If I'm remembering right, you saw House Rock during the landing. Could you see it from the spacecraft, here at the landing site?"] [Duke - "No, not from...I couldn't look out the window and see it. When we pitched over and I looked up there, that's when I was talking about it."]

a16a1542213.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16a1542213.text: Hey, you know, I haven't - hadn't gotten around to looking for planets. That's what I was doing the other night when - when things went to worms, and I decided they're probably trying to tell me something. It really is pretty out there, the way you can see all those stars. They - they really stand out. Looks like a planetarium, there's so many.

a16a1542213.speaker: England
a16a1542213.text: Okay. We heard you talk about that. I vote for it, too. I'm gonna go back and talk to them before I go home. We'll see y'all in the morning. Good night.

a16a1542213.speaker: Young
a16a1542213.text: Okay. Take it easy, Tony. Thank you, now. That was a good day's work for yourself.

a16a1542213.speaker: Duke
a16a1542213.text: Hey, Tony, one final comment. We've been talking about that crater that we took a pan of as we spun around and...I said, looked like Big Sag. John and I are leaning towards endogenic on that, and hopefully from the films that we got you might be able to sort that out. [This is the feature they encountered at 148:39:07 during the drive back to the LM. Charlie is suggesting that it was created by some process having to do with the Moon, itself, as opposed to being an impact feature.]

a16a1542213.speaker: England
a16a1542213.text: Okay. We'll sure take that in consideration. I don't know whether it'll affect tomorrow, but I think it's a good observation. We'll see you. (Pause) And, Charlie, we still have a Hi bit rate. We'd like to go to Lo.

a16a1542213.speaker: Young
a16a1542213.text: Okay, Lo bit rate. And Charlie's changing the (ECS) LiOH canister right now.

a16a1542213.speaker: England
a16a1542213.text: Okay. [Very Long Comm Break] MP3 Audio Clip at 154:24 ( 1 min 00 sec ) MP3 Audio Clip at 154:51 ( 0 min 18 sec ) [Astronaut Stu Roosa, who flew as the Apollo 14 Command Module Pilot, has taken over as CapCom.] MP3 Audio Clip ( 4 min 46 sec )

a16a1542400.speaker: Roosa
a16a1542400.text: And, Casper, we're about 2 minutes to LOS, and we'll see you on the other side.

a16_155_14.speaker: Mattingly (CM onboard)
a16_155_14.text: All righty. See you in a little bit.

a16_155_14.speaker: Mission Control
a16_155_14.text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 155 hours, 25 minutes [155:13]. We're coming up on acquisition with Casper in less than one minute, approximately. We'll open our line to Air [to] Ground [Channel] 2 and monitor for conversations that may very well take place between CapCom Stu Roosa here in Mission Control and Ken Mattingly aboard Casper. Mattingly is not scheduled to start his sleep period until about midway through this front side pass on the 42nd revolution around the Moon. We're at 155 hours 26 minutes. This is Apollo Control Houston standing by. We're now acquiring telemetry data on Casp

a16a1543613.speaker: Duke
a16a1543613.text: Houston, 16. Over.

a16a1543613.speaker: Roosa
a16a1543613.text: Yup.

a16a1543613.speaker: Duke
a16a1543613.text: Hello, Houston. Houston, Orion. Over. (No answer) Houston, Orion. If you're reading me, you have a lot of static on the up-link. Over.

a16a1543613.speaker: Roosa
a16a1543613.text: Okay, Percy Precision. Sorry about that, and we had the up-link turned down. Now I guess somebody...Did you hear us comment? ["Percy Precision" is what Charlie called John at 104:31:06 , Shortly after the landing.]

a16a1543613.speaker: Duke
a16a1543613.text: Somebody was blasting us out of the cockpit. I turned the Squelch, Off, but now whoever...Who's that talking, is that Stu?

a16a1543613.speaker: Roosa
a16a1543613.text: Yeah, Charlie! Boy, you're sure looking good up there.

a16a1543613.speaker: Duke
a16a1543613.text: Hey, babe, how you doing?! Nice to talk to you.

a16a1543613.speaker: Roosa
a16a1543613.text: Yeah...

a16a1543613.speaker: Duke
a16a1543613.text: Hey, you were right. Greatest thrill of my whole life. Really big. Really a thrill, really great.

a16a1543613.speaker: Roosa
a16a1543613.text: Oh, man, you're really swinging. (Pause) Okay. Charlie, we'll do something about that uplink, and we're working maybe the switch configuration now. (Pause)

a16a1543613.speaker: Duke
a16a1543613.text: Okay, this is beautiful right now, Stu.

a16a1543613.speaker: Roosa
a16a1543613.text: There would be an old saying that would apply to that, then, wouldn't there?

a16a1543613.speaker: Duke
a16a1543613.text: That's right. [Duke - "Probably something like 'that calls for a cool one'. I would imagine."]

a16a1543613.speaker: Roosa
a16a1543613.text: Hey, Charlie, could we have you check your uplink Squelch. Is that Off?

a16a1543613.speaker: Duke
a16a1543613.text: Yeah, it's Off right now. (Pause)

a16a1543613.speaker: Roosa
a16a1543613.text: Okay, Charlie. We're going to kill the uplink. I'll be standing by. If you hear the noise, give us a call back. And have a good night's rest, boy; we'll have a cool one (meaning a cold beer) for you.

a16a1543613.speaker: Duke
a16a1543613.text: That sounds good. Hey, we haven't gotten to the pre-sleep checklist part. If it calls for Squelch, Enable, I can turn it on, and we'll be okay. (Long Pause)

a16a1543613.speaker: Roosa
a16a1543613.text: Okay, Charlie. Looks like we wanted you to go to sleep a little early, and we got ahead of you. Could you call us just when you finish your pre-sleep checklist, and at that time we'll have the right configuration. [Houston had assumed that John and Charlie were ready to go to sleep and had changed comm configurations to match the presumed, rest-period configuration in the LM.]

a16a1543613.speaker: Duke
a16a1543613.text: Okay, Houston...Stu. And, hey, since we only got a watch on Houston time, could you give us a time...what time we're supposed to be up in the morning?

a16a1543613.speaker: Roosa
a16a1543613.text: Okay. Stand by. (Long Pause)

a16a1543613.speaker: Roosa
a16a1543613.text: Okay, Charlie. We're going to wake you up 8 hours from now. I'm showing around 10:35 (p.m. Central Standard Time , April 22, 1972), so you'll be getting a call around 06:35, in the morning.

a16a1543613.speaker: Young
a16a1543613.text: Okay, but we're about a half hour away from being asleep. (Pause) We're still gonna get up at 08:35, right? 06:35?

a16a1543613.speaker: Roosa
a16a1543613.text: Okay, John. We'll give you a call at 7 o'clock. (Pause)

a16a1543613.speaker: Young
a16a1543613.text: Okay. (Long Pause) Hey, only with the understanding that that doesn't take a half hour off our EVA, huh? (Pause)

a16a1543613.speaker: Roosa
a16a1543613.text: Okay. Flight says that since they got all those good up-links changes to you this evening, everything looks real clean. And he feels that you can get into the EVA on time. 154:43:07 Young: Okay. [Houston will make the wake-up call at a Ground Elapsed time of 162:38:32 or 6:32 a.m. Houston time and not 7 a.m. as Roosa indicates here.] [Jones - "I don't remember if you talked about it in 'Moonwalker' or not, but I'd be interested to hear your thoughts on the mysterious thing about how Deke picked people to be on crews."] [Duke - "I think we mentioned it. Just to recap, to me it's a mystery how c

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Casper, Houston standing by.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: Hello there.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Greetings.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Well, how did old Kohlschuetter look, Ken?

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: Like a big mountain.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Ah so.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: This is one of these things where that - that strip was planned for the - the ground track post plane change. And, of course, we were further south at the time than was intended, so it didn't fit very well. It was really scrunched up in the corner. I don't know whether that's really going to be any help or not. But there is - Try it and maybe it'll come out okay.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: There can't be any bad pictures of the Moon.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: (Laughter) That's right. When you've got nothing, a little goes a long ways.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay. We're about to wind it down, Ken. Only two things I have for you is to go over the rendezvous procedures and I'll let you get on through your pre-sleep checklist and - and wipe it out for the day.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: Sounds like a good plan. Why don't we go through your - your little plan first?

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay. If you're ready, go over to 171:40 and you'll have your pro - procedures there.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay, 100 and let's - 140 - let's see, before I get over there, you want me to - Oh, you'll remind me to come back to the shift the deadband. Okay. Okay, I'm at 171:40.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay. And in that space in between that update and the LM lift-off is a nice place to write. Let's put in there first, "Optics Mode, CMC, verify." Underneath that, let's write a note. "Spacecraft Control must be in SCS prior to Optics Mode, Manual." I'm just reminding you of the note that - that we passed on the other night, Ken.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: That's just fine.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay. And then come on down after LM lift-off, and where you have P34, delete the "CMC Mode, Hold." And delete the next line, "Set Noun 79," et cetera. Okay, and we'd like to add in here, and it will be four lines, so you might start out kind of small, "Spacecraft Control, SCS; BMAG Mode, 3, Att 1/Rate 2."

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: All righty. And then, next line, "Attitude Deadband, Max; Rate, Low; and Limit Cycle, On." That's all on that page.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay. Let me read that back to you, then. Between the update and lift-off, I've got "Optics Mode to SMC, verify." And the note that "Spacecraft Control must be in SCS prior to Optics Mode going to Manual. Following lift-off, next to the Verb 88, "Spacecraft Control, SCS; BMAG Mode, 3, Att 1/ Rate 2; Deadband, Max; Limit Cycle, On; and Rate, Low."

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay, that's affirmative.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay. Go to the next page, Ken.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: All set.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay. Down here at 172:10, delete "CMC Mode Auto."

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay, now, Ken. This is just a couple of words on dealer's choice. Now as you recall from running this in your attitude, right here at about 172:13, your trunion is down through about 22 degrees. And, of course, there you were going Auto. Now they tell me the way you had been flying the SCS rendezvous, that you'd just stay in an Att Hold and let the trunion. If you want to here, you could put the Pitch BMAG to Rate 2 and just bang it once. But I - I'm not gonna give you any - any changes of Flight Plan on that. That's just your option on how you want to keep the trunion angle.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay. I'll write a note here to watch for that, at that point.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Yeah, your trunion will be - if you're right on nominal - will be 22 degrees right around - oh, somewhere in the order of 172:12 there.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay, and then down at the bottom there, prior to - in between the "MSFN disables" and the "P34 final comp," I want you to write in, "Optics Mode, CMC." And this is just a reminder.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay, between "MSFN disables" and "final comp," we'll write in, "Optics Mode to CMC." I've added the note at the top - at 172:10 - to watch for trunion increasing greater than 22 and BMAG, at least the Pitch one, can go to Rate and give it a blip.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay, that's just - that's just one way of doing it, and it - it works real good and it does not take a large rate in there, just - just about 1 or 2 at the most of what would be a minimum impulse fire.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay, the only reason I had been using Att Hold before was because we were simulating loss of - of the IMU; and, in that case, I wanted to use the attitude gyros because they had less drift. And it made the marking simpler; but, in this case, I might as well let it - give it a burp and let it track along.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay, that's the way I ran them and the - the line of sight rates are - are pretty low, and it's just sort of one of these no-sweat things. Just about one fast blip and then it - it just hangs right there.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: Very good.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay, and you've got your Optics Mode, CMC, down here toward the bottom. We'll turn the page.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: All right, I'm with you.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay, now, Ken, here's - It - This gets kind of messy through here so you might try to write small. And the only thing we're trying to do is, of course, get into P40 and take the auto maneuver, set up for the SCS burn, get back into track attitude, and then back to SCS. And the way we'll do that is we'll take the first line, "Cycle CMC Mode, Free, Auto," and delete it.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay. And then, after P40, write "Spacecraft Control, CMC." And next line, "BMAG Mode, parenthesis 3, Rate 2." And I want to make a note there, Ken. I mean this is not for you to write down, unless you want to, but you'll be tracking along here, and you might be a little out of the preferred track attitude. And if you go into Spacecraft Control to CMC before you get to the burn program, the CMC will try to take you back to the preferred attitude, and you're just wasting an RCS maneuver. So wait until after you're in the burn program to go to CMC, and that's - that's true also of P41 for the mi

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay, that's a good note.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay, and down here where it says "SPS checklist," we're deleting that only because your SPS cue card is - is marked up so bad. And so, the - the reason why - Let's - let's at least say you don't use the cue card as written, which you wouldn't, but we just want to make that point. And in the space in there between "Compare solution in TPI," I've got three lines for you. The first one is, "Spacecraft Control, SCS, after auto manoeuvre." The next line is, and here again this is sort of superfluous, but it's "BMAG Mode, 3, Att 1/Rate 2." And then, just to sum it all up, could we add a note, "Use

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: And here again, I'll - this is not for you to write down null - unless you want to, Ken. It's a personal reminder that we talked about before, that, if you Enter on that 204 display before going to SCS, you have activated the - the relay.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay. I think I will just put another little note out here.

a16_155_14_23.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_14_23.text: Okay.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay. If I am in SCS control, though, I can - I can afford to do an Enter on 204?

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: That's affirmative. If you're in SCS control, you have no power to that relay. It comes through the Spacecraft Control switch, and it...

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay. That was my impression.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: ...and it must be in CMC, so you cannot get the activation of the relay as long as you're in SCS.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: All righty.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: I can still have good navigation through the CMC.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: That's - that's affirmative. You mean - you mean - you mean the navigation programs?

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Onboard state vector, in the event that you did a burn?

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: Oh. What you want to do is - is go on into P40 and stay in P40, and then trim - trim your residuals under - out on the G&N.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Roger. That's what I was - that's what I wanted to get at.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: Yeah. And then here's...

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: The only thing I have to do is make the actual burn itself under SCS control.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: What we want you to do is be in SCS control when you respond to that 204 display and make the burn in SCS. And now, here again, I'm going to bring up another little pitfall. You want - down after TPI, you want to wait until the flashing 16 85 comes up before you go back to CMC. Now, you know, TPI is a short burn and you could very well burn in SCS on time and have a 99 flashing up there. Go on, get through that, and get into your flashing 16 85 before you return the - the Spacecraft Control to CMC. At least, by that, is what I'm trying to say, Ken.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay. And that summarizes my next line, it just was "Flashing 16 85," then "Spacecraft Control to CMC" and it was just trying to get across what I just told you in words; and, if you made the burn, why, null your residuals.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay. And the - if it's all nominal, there really shouldn't be any manoeuvre there at all for - to attitude for the first midcourse.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: That - that's affirmative. It's - it's generally not. And what - the way the procedures show it, if you want to be technically correct is, prior to P35, reminding you of your BMAGs again - BMAG Mode, 3, to Rate 2. Then go ahead into P35 and - generally, I don't come up with a - with a greater-than-10-degree maneuver, but sometimes it - it dresses up the - the preferred track, there. So...

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Roger.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay. Then after P35, we have "BMAG Mode, 3, Att 1/Rate 2 after manoeuvre."

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay. "Attitude Deadband, Max" is next line. And the next line after that is "Spacecraft Control to SCS." And if you want to write you down a little note beside that "Before Optics Manual."

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: And stand by one - That's okay, Ken. Okay, let's come on down here to P35, and delete "Cycle CMC Mode, Free to Auto."

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay. And let's - Just before that P35 final comp, just because it's an easy place to write it, let's put it down "Optics Mode, CMC."

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay. Got that.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay, then after P41, we'll put "Spacecraft Control, CMC." And now here, Ken, since it's - We never take the manoeuvre, but just to cover all cases on the - on the P41, after "Spacecraft Control, CMC," we can put down "BMAG MODE, 3, Rate 2," since we are running a little out of configuration.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay. Then, Ken, after - after the Midcourse 1 through P76, P35, and we're just about through with these. We'll have "BMAG Mode, 3, Att 1/Rate 2 after manoeuvre." And the next line is "Spacecraft Control, SCS, before Optics, Manual." And that takes care of that page.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: All right. If you want to turn the page, we're just about home. Right before the P35 final comp, we'll put "Optics Mode, CMC." And after the P35 final comp, we'll delete the line, "Cycle CMC Mode, Free, Auto." And then after P41, "Spacecraft Control, CMC." And our last entry then, "BMAG Mode, 3, Rate 2." And that was a lot of talking, Ken, but that will keep the BMAGs where they're supposed to be and the relay where it's supposed to be.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: And it was all worth it. Okay, suppose - suppose I read that all back to you?

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay, we already covered the...

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: Ken, about...

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: And I'll go to Attitude - Yes, go ahead.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay. Could we interrupt here before your readback, and we've got your jet-on monitor loads but - Stand by one. Yeah, what we'd like for you to do is go to the 2&frac12 degree deadband - there's that change that we had, and then they can be uplinking while you're reading back.

a16_155_27_46.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_27_46.text: Okay, I'll do that. Just a second here.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_37_36.text: Okay, we're in the 2½-degree deadband and you've got Accept.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_37_36.text: Okay, jolly good, and I'm ready for the readback.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_37_36.text: Okay, let me mark off what I did here. Okay, before lift-off, we'll end up with - making sure that the CMC has control of the optics; we'll fly with the CMC to the initial attitude, then we'll go to SCS Control; BMAGS, 3, Att 1/Rate 2; Max, Deadband; Limit Cycle, On; and Rate, Low. Then we'll do our initial tracking there. And we'll stay with that and 172:10 when the normal auto manoeuvres would be enabled, I - I'll probably take the Pitch BMAG to Rates and start a small rate in there.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_37_36.text: Yeah, that'll be just one small blip.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_37_36.text: Roger.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_37_36.text: Okay, and just before the final comp on P34, we put the Optics Mode to CMC. Let the P34 finish and once I'm in P40, I give the Spacecraft Control to CMC; BMAGs, 3, to Rate 2; and accept the manoeuvre. When I'm in Attitude, I can go back and do SCS control; BMAGs, 3, Att 1/Rate 2; and, should a burn be required, I'll make an SCS auto burn. I'll null the G&N residuals, still remaining in SCS control. I'll proceed past the Noun 85 before returning control to G&N. And it'll be BMAGs, three, to RATE 2 when I get - I think the safest place is when I get in - all the way into P35. When I get it - the

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_37_36.text: Okay, Ken. Couple of comments there, now. I guess how you trim the residuals is sort of dealer's choice. Once you're in that flashing 16 85 display, why, you can go to CMC freely. So you can play that any way you want.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_37_36.text: Okay, but I might just as well stay in SCS. That's a simpler - and one less number that I'm likely to confuse.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_37_36.text: Okay, now let me - and your - your readback was - was okay. There is something now that I'll say - after the P35 where you have BMAG Mode, 3, Att 1/Rate 2; okay, if the - the CMC will start you on a good track rate; I just didn't want to get the procedures too clowned up; but, you know if you put your Pitch BMAG to Rate 2 there, before you go to SCS, you'll keep in your CMC track. Now you'll be below the rate at which you're maneuvreing, but you - between TPI and Midcourse 1, you'll exceed your - your attitude deadband. So, since you did say you were going to go - to go on the track method, pe

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_37_36.text: Okay. That sounds like a good plan. Yes, sir; I understand you.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_37_36.text: Okay. And that would also be true after the other P35.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_37_36.text: Roger.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_37_36.text: And just so we make sure that all procedures showing the same - I'm - I'm changing mine to show that, Ken.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_37_36.text: Okay. I have mine changed, too.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_37_36.text: Okay. And I think that's it. I thought before the rendezvous, we'd - we'd give you a swinging Delta tail off just for your weight even though you've got a chart. Just so you wouldn't have to do any figuring out. Of course, 11 is always a good number, but, just to be professional, we'll give you a good one - and since you are making an SCS burn.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_37_36.text: Thank you. I was going to ask you for that. It's really not quite the same as if you had SCS only because you got the information there what's the right thing; but it sure helped to - be a lot cheaper about your RCS.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_37_36.text: Roger. We might as well be professional about this whole show, since you're doing such a good job up there.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_37_36.text: Hey, there's one other thing I was going to ask you. Yeah. About the Mapping Camera. Are we going to leave it out or we going to try and retract it?

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_37_36.text: Stand by.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_37_36.text: Ken, the SIM Bay is configured for sleep. As of right now.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_37_36.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I - I'm - I'm still thinking about rendezvous.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_37_36.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Okay. Stand by.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_37_36.text: Okay, Ken, we're going to retract the camera for rendezvous, extend it again, and then we'll retract it for TEI.

a16_155_37_36.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_37_36.text: Okay. I guess since we're a little down on the RCS that might be a prudent plan. Looks like we're holding our own, if it hadn't been for that practice in formation flying.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_46_55.text: Ken, as far as the Flight Plan now - the - the new revised version, we're 15 pounds ahead of the - of the Flight Plan. And we're fat on the - on the rescue redline.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_46_55.text: Okay. That sounds a little bit like changing the specs.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_46_55.text: (Laughter) Well, you got to - you got to be fast on your feet. And we're 168 (pounds) above the rescue redline.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_46_55.text: Okay. I will continue to be miserly.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_46_55.text: By all means, and we are minus 139 on the other Flight Plan.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_46_55.text: Okay. And I guess that takes care of our - of our rendezvous procedures. And sounds like you got them all copied in good order and I feel certain that'll go real easy for you. That's a - that's a smooth procedure even though it takes a lot of talking. And I guess I might remind you about your Waste Storage Vent valve at this time - if you haven't already got it.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_46_55.text: I've already turned it Off, Stuart.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_46_55.text: Okay. I thought maybe if I talked to you long enough you might - you might miss that; but I didn't catch you.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_46_55.text: Okay. Well, I think I'm gonna configure myself to sleep.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_46_55.text: Okay. That's - that's all we have and we'll - Well, I guess we got maybe a couple of things there on the onboard read-outs and after that it'll be - we're through.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_46_55.text: Okay. Let me give you those little guys right now. Start with the RCS: quad A, 61 percent; quad Bravo, 59; Charlie, 66; Delta, 67; Battery C is 36.5, Pyro Battery A is 36.7, Battery B is 36.7.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_46_55.text: Okay. We've got all those, and the computer is yours; you can go back to Block.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_46_55.text: Okay. And, let's see, did you start the - Yes, you've got my monitor running. Thank you, sir.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_46_55.text: Okay, I'm going to hush and leave you with the Flight Plan and let you get some rest; and tomorrow's going to be a big day. And we'll see you around.

a16_155_46_55.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_46_55.text: Okay, Stu. Thanks a lot. Good night.

a16_155_51.speaker: Mission Control
a16_155_51.text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 156 hours, 03 minutes [155:51] Ground Elapsed Time. The long exchange between CapComs Stu Roosa and Ken Mattingly was principally involved with Flight Plan updates for tomorrow's rendezvous and docking. Mattingly now readying himself for the - for a night's sleep prior to rejoining his fellow crewmembers tomorrow. We're at 156 hours and 03 minutes. This is Apollo Control Houston.

a16_155_56_22.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_56_22.text: Stu, would you folks like to have E-memory dump?

a16_155_56_22.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_56_22.text: Could you stand by one for us, Ken?

a16_155_56_22.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_56_22.text: Okay. Ken, we're ready for the E-memory dump, and Big Brother is looking over your shoulder. We notice...

a16_155_56_22.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_56_22.text: Okay, somebody's moved the secular point on us, Ken, and we'd like to verify the VHF in the Right Antenna; and, if it is, we'd like to go to the Left Antenna for 3 minutes. And you give me a mark and I'll give you a call.

a16_155_56_22.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_56_22.text: Okay, it is in the Right. I'm going to move it to the Left. Stand by.

a16_155_56_22.speaker: Mattingly
a16_155_56_22.text: I can't imagine who'd do something like move something like that.

a16_155_56_22.speaker: Roosa
a16_155_56_22.text: You know, it's getting where you can't trust anybody these days, not even Newton.

a16_155_56_22.speaker: Mission Control
a16_155_56_22.text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 156 hours, 13 minutes [156:01] Ground Elapsed Time. In the mission control center we're in the process of having a shift change over. Gerry Griffin, whose team of gold flight controllers now taking over - Griffin's team of Gold flight controllers are now taking over from Gene Kranz's White Team of flight controllers. There will be no change of shift briefing or news conference following this change over. We're at 156 hours 14 minutes [156:02] Ground Elapsed Time and this is Apollo Control Houston.

a16_156_03_07.speaker: Roosa
a16_156_03_07.text: Okay, Casper, if you'd give us VHF Right Antenna and we are going to leave it in Right Antenna.

a16_156_03_07.speaker: Mission Control
a16_156_03_07.text: This is Apollo Control, 157:12 minutes [157:00] into the mission of Apollo 16. All three crewmen aboard both Casper and Orion [are] tucked in for the night, on what should be about 8 hours sleep period on both spacecraft, for both sets of crews. Ken Mattingly signed off during the 42nd lunar rev and he and Casper are some ten minutes away from Acquisition of Signal coming around on lunar orbit number 43. [The] Gold Team of Flight Controllers came on at midnight Central Time here at [the] Control Center, and are fine tuning the flight plan items; sorting out systems status and so on for the Lun

a16_156_03_07.speaker: Mission Control
a16_156_03_07.text: This is Apollo Control, [at] 158 hours and 12 minutes [158:00] Ground Elapsed Time. Command Service Module Casper [is] more than midway across the front - face of the Moon in revolution number 43, 23 minutes away from Loss of Signal. Meanwhile, Young and Duke are still asleep at Descartes Landing Site. The Apollo Lunar Surface Experiment Package that has been erected at Descartes Landing Site by Young and Duke continues to operate normally at this time. 149 commands have been uplinked to the station scientific station. The input power from the thermoelectric generator is steady at 70.4 Watts.

a16_156_03_07.speaker: Mission Control
a16_156_03_07.text: This is Apollo Control at 159 hours, 12 minutes [159:00] Ground Elapsed Time. About 4 hours remaining in the sleep period for Duke and Young aboard ORION, in as much as they'll probably sleep about 30 minutes past the normal wake up time - the pre planned wakeup time. Casper meanwhile, the Command Service Module is in a 56.2 by 63.5 nautical mile lunar orbit coming up on the front side pass for Rev 44 in about 9 minutes. Gold Team, flight control team here in Mission Control [are] watching a playback of the video tape [of] EVA number 2. At any rate those members of the team who were not involv

a16_156_03_07.speaker: Mission Control
a16_156_03_07.text: This is Apollo Control [at] 160 hours, 12 minutes [160:00] Ground Elapsed Time into the Mission of Apollo 16. Command Service Module, Casper, [is] nearing the end of the 44th revolution on side pass. Two and a half hours showing in the sleep period clock for Duke and Young aboard Orion. However, likely [that it] will run closer to 3 hours before the crews is waked [sic] up. Twenty-one minutes to Command Service Module LOS [on] Rev 44. [A] Rather quiet night here in Mission Control. Some of the console positions doing a little homework study for the day's activities, straightening out the accum

a16_156_03_07.speaker: Mission Control
a16_156_03_07.text: This is Apollo Control [at] 162 hours, 12 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. About 37 minutes showing on the wakeup clock until the crew of Orion is called for the start of their final days activity at Descartes landing site. Briefly summarized the EVA 3 activities will begin with some 45 minutes after depressurization being spent in the immediate area of the Lunar Module. Getting the LRV loaded with all the gear for the geological sampling. Getting everything prepared for the trek out to North Ray Crater. The arrival at North Ray Crater at what's called Stations 11 and 12 will be at 1 hour and 25 m

a16a1623832.speaker: Peterson
a16a1623832.text: Roger. How are you doing this morning?

a16a1623832.speaker: Duke
a16a1623832.text: Super. Is it time to get up?

a16a1623832.speaker: Duke
a16a1623832.text: Okay, reveille, reveille. (Long Pause) Okay, Pete, we're stirring; we'll be up in a minute.

a16a1623832.speaker: Peterson
a16a1623832.text: Roger. (Long Pause) Okay, Orion. You're Stay for EVA-3.

a16a1623832.speaker: Duke
a16a1623832.text: Hey, that's mighty nice of you. And we were looking for reveille for about 7 o'clock, but we'll get going right now.

a16a1623832.speaker: Peterson
a16a1623832.text: Roger. (Pause) These flight directors are slave drivers. [Comm Break]

a16a1623832.speaker: Peterson
a16a1623832.text: And, Orion, would you give us Voice, Normal, and Hi Bit Rate, please? [Long Comm Break] [After getting out of the hammocks, John and Charlie are stowing hammocks and the sleep restraints in the jettison bag , as per the handwritten note on Surface 5-7. Originally, John and Charlie had planned to have three sleep periods while they were on the Moon, one after each of the EVAs. However, because of the six-hour landing delay, they had their first sleep period before EVA-1, the second before EVA-2, and have just completed the third. They will return to lunar orbit after EVA-3 and will not have ano

a16a1623832.speaker: Peterson
a16a1623832.text: Orion, Houston. Let's go back to Lo Bit Rate, please. [Comm Break] MP3 Audio Clip ( 10 min 43 sec )

a16a1624800.speaker: Duke
a16a1624800.text: Houston, Orion. We have a crew status report for you.

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: Okay, Orion. Go ahead. (Long Pause)

a16a1624800.speaker: Duke
a16a1624800.text: Okay. For John, yesterday he had Day 7, Meal A; and Day 7 - Stand by - and Day 7, Meal B. On day 7 Meal A, he ate everything but the beef steak. On Meal B, he ate everything but the romaine soup and the butterscotch pudding. He had no medication, and he'd like for the docs to guess how much sleep he had to start with, and then we'll give you our estimate. For me, we had Day...(the) same two meals; I ate everything on meal A except the bacon squares and on meal B everything but the romaine soup and the butterscotch pudding. I had no medication, and I slept for 7 hours. Over. [Details for the me

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: Roger. And we estimate John slept 6 and a half to 7 hours.

a16a1624800.speaker: Duke
a16a1624800.text: Okay. He was going to say 7. That's great.

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: Roger. (Pause) Okay. And, Orion, I've got block data and a note from the Surgeon and a battery-management procedure at about 164 hours any time you're ready to copy. (Pause)

a16a1624800.speaker: Duke
a16a1624800.text: Okay. You can go with the block data. [These are launch times for upcoming Command Module passes over the landing site. Each of the launch times is followed by the TPI, Terminal Phase Initiation, time at which they will start the final rendezvous maneuvers. T46 is the launch time for the 46th Command Module pass.]

a16a1624800.speaker: Duke
a16a1624800.text: Give me number 50 again, please.

a16a1624800.speaker: Duke
a16a1624800.text: Okay. I'll just read you back the lift-off times, starting with 46, (reading quickly) 163 plus 54 plus 55; 165 plus 53 plus 25; 167 plus 51 plus 55; 169 plus 56 (sic) plus 26; 171 plus 48 plus 57; and 173 plus 47 plus 29. Over.

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: Let's verify T49 as 169:50:26.

a16a1624800.speaker: Duke
a16a1624800.text: That's a "Charlie". (Pause) [Journal Contributor Larry Turoski writes, " When I was in the Air Force, the phrase 'That's Charlie' or 'That's a Charlie' was synonymous with 'Affirmative' or 'That's correct.' Most of us didn't use it, though, because it was too cumbersome a phrase, especially when "Roger" would do. I don't recall ever using it myself. It was used enough, though, to remain in my memory. I believe Pete Conrad uses it somewhere in the Apollo 12 transcript. "] [Among other places, Pete used 'That's Charlie' at 109:45:05 during the Apollo 12 landing.

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: Okay. And the battery management (listed on Surface 5-10) is at 164:45.

a16a1624800.speaker: Duke
a16a1624800.text: Okay, Pete. What time is it now?

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: It's 163:05. (Long Pause) [The difference between the Journal time and the Mission Time being kept in Houston represents an 11 minute 48 seconds clock update that was done at about 118 hours to simplify operations at the new lift-off time. See the discussion at 115:55:23 .]

a16a1624800.speaker: Duke
a16a1624800.text: Okay, Pete. On that battery management, when we get to that time, just give me a call, if you will. Over. [To conserve power, John and Charlie turned off the Mission Timer and their only time pieces are their watches, which are set to Houston time.]

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: Will do. (Pause) Okay, and the note from the Flight Surgeon requests that you have the crew check the Biomed harness prior to suit-up for EVA-3. And if you have the PRD readouts handy, we'd like them; otherwise, we'll skip them. [Although both John and Charlie are wearing biomed sensors, only one is transmitted to Houston while they are in the cabin. Houston is asking Charlie to change a switch setting so the Flight Surgeon can look at the data from Charlie's sensors to make sure they are still functioning properly.]

a16a1624800.speaker: Duke
a16a1624800.text: Okay. I'll give you (my) Biomed in just a second, and John's was on all night, so I guess his is okay. And we'll give you the PRDs like we always do when we get suited up.

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: Rog. That's fine, Charlie. And John's Biomed data did look good all night.

a16a1624800.speaker: Duke
a16a1624800.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay. You're looking at my Biomed now, Pete.

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: Okay. Stand by a minute. (Pause) Looks good, Charlie.

a16a1624800.speaker: Duke
a16a1624800.text: Okay. (Switching) back to John.

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: Okay. (Long Pause) Okay. Both the Biomeds look real good. [Comm Break] [After checking their Liquid Cooled Garments (LCGs) as per Surface 5-7, John and Charlie will have breakfast.]

a16a1624800.speaker: Young
a16a1624800.text: Okay, Houston. How do you read? Over.

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: Okay, you're loud and clear.

a16a1624800.speaker: Young
a16a1624800.text: Okay. And we're going on with the PLSS top-off right now (as per the third item under "Eat Period" on Surface 5-8).

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: Say again, John. (Pause) Okay. Copy PLSS top-off.

a16a1624800.speaker: Young
a16a1624800.text: (Not having heard Peterson) Topping off the PLSSs right now.

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: Roger. (Long Pause) And, Orion, we just want to remind you again that we want to put the Commander's OPS on the LMP PLSS.

a16a1624800.speaker: Young
a16a1624800.text: Okay. The EVC(S)'s not in the OPS? [The EVCS is the Extravehicular Communications System.]

a16a1624800.speaker: Peterson
a16a1624800.text: We didn't copy the question, John.

a16a1624800.speaker: Young
a16a1624800.text: I say I thought there was something about a radio transmitter that had to be...Is the radio transmitter located out on the PLSS? Is that the answer to that?

a16a1625827.speaker: Peterson
a16a1625827.text: That's affirmative, John. [Long Comm Break] [The tip of John's OPS antenna broke off when he climbed into the LM at the end of EVA-2. His PLSS is the one which contains the EVCS radio gear capable of transmitting both his and Charlie's voice and data to the LM or the Rover and Houston wants him to have the good OPS antenna. See Figure 1-3 in the LCRU Operations Manual.] [EVA CapCom Tony England takes over from Peterson.] MP3 Audio Clip ( 9 min 58 sec ) (This clip starts with a 5 minute 45 second interval without comm.)

a16a1625827.speaker: Young
a16a1625827.text: Okay, Houston. I'm going off Biomed for about 10 minutes. Over.

a16a1625827.speaker: England
a16a1625827.text: Okay, John. [Very Long Comm Break while they have breakfast, adjust the Biomed harnesses, and do other prep work before donning the suits.] MP3 Audio Clip ( 10 min 50 sec )

a16a1634519.speaker: Young
a16a1634519.text: Okay, Houston. How does that Biomed look to you now?

a16a1634519.speaker: England
a16a1634519.text: Okay. It looks good here, John.

a16a1634519.speaker: Young
a16a1634519.text: Okay. Fine. (Pause) [As per checklist pages Surface 5-7 and 5-9, John and Charlie are supposed to start suit donning 1 hour 25 minutes after wake-up. Wake-up was at 162:38:32 , so only 1 hour 7 minutes have elapsed. Tony's next transmission may be just a "hello", but may also be a subtle inquiry as to where John and Charlie are in the checklist.]

a16a1634519.speaker: England
a16a1634519.text: How are you doing up there?

a16a1634519.speaker: Duke
a16a1634519.text: Oh, just fine. We finished eating, and we're ready to don suits now (as per Surface 5-9).

a16a1634519.speaker: England
a16a1634519.text: Okay. Fine. Do you want a quick briefing on the traverse today (as per Surface 5-8)?

a16a1634519.speaker: Duke
a16a1634519.text: Okay. One comment, Tony, that we were talking about last night that we didn't pass on, that the feeling we got from all the crystalline rocks was that they had a sugary texture to them. [This observation suggests that the crystalline rocks they found - and there weren't very many - were all highly shocked, probably in the South Ray impact.]

a16a1634519.speaker: England
a16a1634519.text: Okay. We copy that. The changes for the traverse today are pretty simple. We've got changes to your Cuff Checklist if you want them, or I can real-time them (during the traverse). I think we can real-time them if that's okay with you. But I'll outline them now. The only change on egress...

a16a1634519.speaker: Young
a16a1634519.text: Yeah, summarize it for us, please. 163:46:46 England: Okay. Fine. The only change right after egress (on cuff checklist page LMP-28), Charlie, (on cuff checklist page LMP-28) instead of putting on mag L, I'll ask you to put mag M on the 500 millimeter. That will give you a full mag, and that would be all you need. That will save a change up at Station 11. And at the LM site there, we'd like you to shoot off a pan of Stone Mountain, but I'll call you on that when you get out; otherwise, the LM area is nominal. And you go up to Station 11 slash 12 (meaning "11/12"), which will be just one statio

a16a1634519.speaker: England
a16a1634519.text: We're going to drop the near-field polarimetry up there (which is listed on CDR-32 and CDR-33), and we'll concentrate on big boulder samples, a permanently-shadowed sample, and the padded bag sample on the special samples area. We'll still like a stereo pan...a far-field polarimetry of the crater interior; we'll try to get about an 80-meter base on that; and, when you get up there, Charlie, I'll brief you on what looks like the best way to do that. And we'll return along the same route you went up, and about one-half to one kilometer off the rim when you still feel you're on the continuous eje

a16a1634519.speaker: England
a16a1634519.text: We'll make a Station 10 Prime which is about 50 meters west of your Station 10. So it makes a triangle with the deep core, which would be south of it, and the Station 10 which would be northeast of it, and then Station 10 Prime which makes that northwest corner of the triangle, and we'll ask for a rake soil at Station 10 Prime, a double core at that station, a rake soil at Station 10; and then whatever time is left to 35 minutes (prior to repress) will be documented samples.

a16a1634519.speaker: England
a16a1634519.text: Now, the end of the EVA is pretty much nominal except, John, when you go out to the permanent parking location of the Rover (as per CDR-48 and 49), we'd like you to make sure you take a camera along, and we'll do an LPM measurement there after you've parked it, and we'll also ask you to try to find us a dense crystalline rock if you can find it. If you can't find a crystalline one, then at least a dense breccia, and we'll do the rock-on-top-of-the-LPM measurement (which is indicated on CDR-42 and CDR-45). And that's pretty much it. I'm going to try to keep you to the timeline as much as possib

Just when you do the Nav update, try to park in a level area. And the Backroom is hoping that the Nav problem was a temporary one; that'll be okay for your EVA-3. Either way, you shouldn't really have any problem because you can probably see the area you're going to, and you're going to go right back al

Also, they mentioned that if you have a dust problem from that missing fender - (right) rear fender - there is a way of putting one of the front fenders on the back; but, golly, I don't know whether you really want to do that.

a16a1634519.speaker: Young
a16a1634519.text: Yeah, I don't either, Tony. We'd get the dust from the front fender, then, probably. 163:51:50 England: Yeah, you're probably right. I don't understand it, but that's what they said. (Pause) And that's all I've got if you want to go ahead and get dressed. The streaks up the side of the craters are basically the same. But (with) the North Ray you got to guess at it a little bit more; and that might be totally what my guess is. It could be wrong, but I kinda think they're at least a similar rock. (Pause; no response from Houston)

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: That stumped them. (Pause) So crazy (a suggestion) they didn't even answer me. (Pause) [Jones - "(Chuckling) Did you get a silent response sometimes during training?"] [Duke - "Yeah."]

a16a1684720.speaker: Young
a16a1684720.text: Houston, do you read? Over.

a16a1684720.speaker: England
a16a1684720.text: Oh, we sure do. Sorry, Charlie. We copy that.

a16a1684720.speaker: Young
a16a1684720.text: Okay. Fine.

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: (To Tony; Laughing) That's okay.

a16a1684720.speaker: England
a16a1684720.text: It was just mind boggling, as Freddo says here. [Fred Haise, the backup Commander, is sitting with Tony. NASA photo S72-38433 shows Haise and Deke Slayton sitting with Tony earlier in the missions at 145:38:32.]

a16a1684720.speaker: Young
a16a1684720.text: Sure is. (Pause) I'll tell you one thing...

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: Okay, I think you...I think we could make it up over there, John, if you broke (meaning "turned") right here, but I guess you want to follow the old (outbound) tracks. We were pretty close to the rim there for one time.

a16a1684720.speaker: Young
a16a1684720.text: Yeah, we'll get there.

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: Yeah. (Pause) We know this way works.

a16a1684720.speaker: Young
a16a1684720.text: Yes, sir. Let's not do any R&D (Research and Development). Unnecessarily, that is.

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: But, Tony, if we sample one of these very fresh craters with the indurated regolith that to me look like they're maybe the freshest thing around, can y'all date that just from the regolith? The glassy shards or whatever is in there? [Very fresh, small craters often have a glass-coating in the bottom - made during the impact if the projectile velocity was high enough - and numerous clumps of compressed soil. The latter is called "indurated regolith" or, more colorfully, "instant rock". Charlie is asking if it would be possible to use samples of the glass and/or instant rock to date impacts that

a16a1684720.speaker: England
a16a1684720.text: Say again, Charlie.

a16a1684720.speaker: Young
a16a1684720.text: (Garbled)

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: I was just asking a question about whether you could date a fresh crater with the indurated regolith?

a16a1684720.speaker: England
a16a1684720.text: Ah, we'll work on an answer on that. I don't know, off-hand.

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: Okay. There's a lot of them around the (Palmetto) rim, and I'd like to at least pick up some of that and see what y'all could do with it.

a16a1684720.speaker: England
a16a1684720.text: That sounds like a good idea. We've...

a16a1684720.speaker: Young
a16a1684720.text: (Lost under Tony)

a16a1684720.speaker: England
a16a1684720.text: ...got a definite "maybe" from the Backroom there.

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: Okay. And, Tony, we're looking into End Crater, and it's a blocky crater. There are blocks inside of it, and there's some on the rim, half-meter size.

a16a1684720.speaker: England
a16a1684720.text: Right. [They have not reached End and will not do so until 168:59:04 . Charlie's comment about "looking into End" suggests that, at least for the moment, they are above End.]

a16a1684720.speaker: England
a16a1684720.text: And you were asking about a stop (to collect a sample from a small, fresh crater)...

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: And maybe 10 percent of it...(Correcting himself) Naw, let's make it...(Stops to listen)

a16a1684720.speaker: England
a16a1684720.text: ...we don't want to stop. We want to go on to (Station) 10-Prime.

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: Naw, we weren't talking about a stop. I was just describing End Crater there. It is a blocky-rim crater.

a16a1684720.speaker: England
a16a1684720.text: Okay, fine.

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: As we suspected. (Pause) [This is probably a reference to a pre-flight discussion. The activities planned for Station 17 at End Crater and shown on checklist pages LMP-40 and LMP-41 include a radial sample. Radial sampling starts with a rock sample at the rim of a crater and then continues with samples taken at successively greater distances as the astronaut walks radially away from the rim.]

a16a1684720.speaker: Young
a16a1684720.text: How do you like this (ride), Charlie?

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: It's great.

a16a1684720.speaker: Young
a16a1684720.text: We're doing 14 clicks. [On flat ground, John's usual speed is about 10 km/hr. A speed of 14 km/hr strongly suggests that, since Charlie said they were "looking into End", they have been dropping down into a depression.]

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: This is smooth going. (Pause) Boy, not having that fender really sprays it up there over you, doesn't it?

a16a1684720.speaker: Young
a16a1684720.text: Yeah. It does.

a16a1684720.speaker: England
a16a1684720.text: And could we have an amp-hour reading...(Correcting himself) An amp reading ...

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: Tony, occasionally, when we hit a big bump...(Stops to listen) 40. Between 30 and 40.

a16a1684720.speaker: England
a16a1684720.text: Okay. (Pause)

a16a1684720.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1684720.text: Servo Power 1, AC1, Servo Power 2, AC2. Rotation Control Power Normal, Number 2, AC; Direct, two are Off. BMAGs are uncaged; 2, 3 uncaged. Going to SCS. RHC number 2 is armed. Here comes Gimbal Motor Number 1. Pitch 1 -

a16a1684720.speaker: Duke
a16a1684720.text: When we hit a bump, Tony, and bounce down, that rear wheel that lost the fender showers dirt all over the front of us, and that's what gets the LCRU and the (TV) camera so dirty.

a16a1684720.speaker: England
a16a1684720.text: Okay. We copy that. (Long Pause) MP3 Audio Clip ( 9 min 02 sec ) [Charlie's traverse photos taken during the approach to End Crater are AS16-117- 18759 to 18765 .]

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Mark. Good start. Yaw 1 -

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Mark. That's a good start. The trim thumbwheels work - both directions - on Pitch, 7.48, 1.5. I can tell the difference. Yaw thumbwheel works in both directions set on plus 1 - 02. Okay. Pitch, MTVC; Yaw, MTVC is good. Okay; back to CMC; then go back to zero. Going clockwise. Start, Pitch 2. It trims, and MTVC. Back to neutral. I have no MTVC, Pitch and Yaw. Then back to zero. Rotation Power Number 2 is AC/DC. Direct Number 2 is Main A/Main B. Let's see. We'll take a manoeuvre and see if it gives us one. It does not. The gyros - I'll just sort of cage them to bring them up to speed and back to

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: (To John) Man, I'll give you...You earned your driver's license on this thing, John, I tell you.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: Either that or lose it.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: You know, it takes just about any terrain. It's really a remarkable machine.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: Sure is climbing a slope right now, Charlie.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Yeah.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: We're only doing...Got a v-max (that is, John is applying maximum throttle), and we're only doing 8 clicks. So you know this has got to be steep. [Now they are climbing out of the depression and, in a moment, will reach the rim of End. Frames AS16-117- 18762 to 18765 may show the area around End Crater.]

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: We're pulling a little over 40 amps, Tony.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: Okay. (Pause)

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Don't anybody tell Ken (Mattingly, the Command Module Pilot) how dirty we are.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: Yeah, he won't let us in the hatch. 168:59:04 Duke: I know it. (pause) Okay, Tony, we're at End. Just passing End Crater; and the rocks appear to be the same as we sampled, in texture. They may be not as shocked as the ones up on the rim. I could grab you one in about a minute.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: No, we'd better press on.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Let's go over and look at the (Palmetto) rim, John, here. (Stops to listen) Okay.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: Incidentally, we were able to track you in the Rover on the way out with the PSE and they are able to see you now on the way back with the active seismic geophones. We'd like to be sure that you are in the same tracks you were going out.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: That's true.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: Okay.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: True, that's true. 169:00:08 Duke: And we're at 192 at 1.9 . [These readouts give a location of CL.4/82.2. As can be seen in the " Descartes EVA-I, III 1 of 3 " map, this location is on the west rim of End Crater. It has been about a minute since Charlie reported they were passing End which, assuming a speed of 9 km/hr, suggests they are about 150 meters south of End, in reasonable agreement with the estimated 180-m error of their Station 13 position. Charlie's next transmission indicates that they are looking into Palmetto.]

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Hey, John. (Turn) right, babe. Look at that! Hook a right, please. Get this old pick-a-chur (sic). (Pause) Okay, Tony. We're gonna to drive over to the rim of Palmetto, which is a pretty good sight.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: Okay. [Charlie's photos taken on the rim of Palmetto are AS16-117- 18766 to 18772 . All but the last of these show the interior of the crater.]

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: And, we see some blocks on the inner rim; but nothing that really appears to be outcrop. But it's really a deep crater, Tony. It's...

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: I don't see the bottom.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: We can't see the bottom, and we're right on the rim. It must be a 100 meters or so deep.

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: And it's time to strap in my trusty machine. A piece of bread I don't need in my face.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: Pictures of it, Charlie?

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: No, I didn't get it. I thought we were going to do a 1...3...180... [Charlie is trying to say "360", meaning a full circle.]

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: Okay. Here we go. 169:01:07 Duke: Okay. (Pause) Okay, starting now: click - click - click - click - click - click. Okay, that's about a four-shotter. It might not be completely overlapped, but I think it will be good enough.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: Okay. [Charlie's six pictures are part of the sequence AS16-117- 18765 to 18771 .] [Frame 18765 shows South Ray Crater in the background. Palmetto Crater fills most of the frame but is largely washed out in this down-Sun photo. Part of the inner slope can be seen to the left of the TV camera.] [Frame 18768 is a down-Sun picture.] [Frame 18770 shows the south and east rims.] [By the time Charlie takes frame 18771 , John is driving south again.]

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Okay. We're heading out, Tony.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: Okay.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: And the rim here is cobbly. I wouldn't say it's blocky, but it's cobbly.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: I think we've been averaging 11 kilometers (per hour), Houston.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: Okay. (Pause) [They have driven a straight-line distance of about 2 km since leaving Station 13 and, at the time they started the Rover pan, had been underway for about 15 minutes. The implied straight-line speed is 8 km/hr. although an allowance for weaving around craters might increase the vehicle speed to 9 km/hr.]

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: (To John) Look at that view back towards South Ray, isn't that spectacular? [This view is shown in AS16-117- 18771 .]

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: Looking ahead...

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: (There's) Baby Ray.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: ...at your tracks, could you tell when you picked up the softer regolith? On the tracks that you came out?

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Do not yet have Yaw Gimbal Number 2 on. But I will bring it on in just a minute.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: They've all looked the same. Haven't they to you, John?

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: Softer regolith coming out from the LM?

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: Right, you...

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: We're keeping up on it, Charlie.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: ...mentioned up on North Ray that you only went in...

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Yeah.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: ...an eighth of an inch or so. [Tony is asking if, during the return trip, the outbound tracks show any indications of deeper penetration as they get closer to the LM.]

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: (To Tony) Naw, the regolith does change character right past the LM, and it's a lot less blocky, you know? I think this ray (material) right here...

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Okay; I'm going to bring Yaw Gimbal Number 2 on.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: I think this is probably...Yeah, it's probably ray (material). Yeah. (Pause) Either that or it came out of Palmetto. [Charlie's next seven traverse photos are AS16-117- 18773 to 18779 .]

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Mask. Direct Ullage breakers are 2, In. Okay, we're at 3 minutes and 9 seconds. I'll go to Vox at - 2 minutes. Let's see, it should have Houston here in another minute or 2.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: (To Tony) This would have been a good choice for a walking traverse (in the event of a Rover failure). See over there in the west, (pause) over there in the far rim over there? Don't you see something that looks like...Down in that ledge down there.

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: I am indeed going sideways, so I must be doing it right.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Yeah. There are two spots over there that might be outcrop, Tony. There's...

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: Well, that's probably a secondary from...That's probably a big block clot (sic) from...

a16a1685810.speaker: LM Crew
a16a1685810.text: From North Ray.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Yeah.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: Yeah. That's what it is. See there...

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: I don't...

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: It's hit in there and...

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Yeah. There's one further around, though on the southwest rim, John, that sticks out like it's eroded away from underneath it.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: Yeah.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: That has a hint of bedrock. But it's...And that's about on the southwest rim, about 20 percent down from the upper rim of Palmetto, Tony.

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Hello, Houston. How you doing?

a16a1685810.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1685810.text: Hello, Casper. How's it going? Are you all set up?

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: Okay. We copy that.

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: All set to go. 509 is out, I'm in attitude, and we must be right, I'm going sideways.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: But it's just one little isolated block. And I don't really think it means much. Still can't see the LM. We're on the...

a16a1685810.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1685810.text: Roger.

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Counting down at 155. I'm on Vox, and I'll give you the final couple of steps on Vox.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: See South Ray, though. Get a picture.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: I'm getting them; as fast as I can pull the trigger. a16a1685810.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1685810.text: Okay, Ken. We got data and everything looks good. You're still go.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: We thought we'd be able to see the rim (means the LM) from here, Tony, but you can't do it...(Correcting himself) I mean (see) the LM, but you can't do it. (Pause) That thing says 194 for 1.4 . I bet you that's right. (Pause) We came farther east (than planned).

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: Yeah. We're way east. [The readouts indicate a location near CH.9/82.3 . They are actually very near the planned traverse and are seeing higher LM bearings than expected because John landed about 200 meters NNW of the planned landing site.]

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Yeah. (To Houston) Okay, Tony. Between Gator and Palmetto ...

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: Uh-oh. [John has seen a rock just ahead that is taller than the Rover's 14-inch (35-cm) clearance. This could be the rock in AS16-117- 18786 .]

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Uh-oh. Ah! We missed it.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: Ahh, good suspension.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Yeah.

a16a1685810.text: In one minute, the EMS is going to Normal. Translation Control Power is on. Translation Controller and Rotation Controllers are Armed.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: Well, we're all holding on to our chairs.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: (To Houston) Between Gator and Palmetto...(Stops to listen) We almost hit a great big rock, but old Percy (Precision), here, avoided it. (To John) Look at that. (A LM bearing of) 194, John, takes us right out our (outbound) tracks. (To Houston) Between Gator and Palmetto, Tony, there's a swale - a depression - that runs east-west that is apparently more cratered and (has) fresher craters there than what we've been driving on between Palmetto and North Ray.

a16a1685810.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1685810.text: Got it.

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: The Arm light is out; the SPS Delta-V Thrust A is coming on -

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Mark.

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Average g is on. IPS [?] look good.

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Ullage. Good ullage. Attitude's good. Engine enable.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: Roger.

a16a1685810.text: I just finished my 2 pounds of potassium (meaning the potassium-fortified orange drink in his drink bag ). I would have guessed it woul

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: You finished your 2 pounds already?

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: Yeah. I don't know whether I'm driving or sloshing. (Charlie laughs)

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: There's ignition.

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: (Laughing) Okay. We copy that.

a16a1685810.text: Don't let's go unstable with a fuel slosh mode.

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Auto shutdown.

Or both?"] [Duke - "It could be both. Yeah: big airplanes. They baffle the tanks, usually; but it is not much of a problem any more with big airplanes. But, in the spacecraft

a16a1685810.speaker: England
a16a1685810.text: And the Command Module just did their plane change burn, and it's a good burn.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Good.

a16a1685810.speaker: Young
a16a1685810.text: (Garbled) (Pause) [During the 65 hours since John and Charlie landed, the Moon has rotated under the plane of the Command Module's orbit and the displacement is now about 33 degrees in longitude. a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Okay, residuals, I have - on Y is minus 0.1. I'll get you the Verb 6 Noun 20s, and you can watch that while I turn the Gimbal Motors, Off.

a16a1685810.speaker: Duke
a16a1685810.text: Ah, the old (garbled) (Pause) Man; we are showered (by dust thrown up by the fenderless rear-wheel).

a16a1685810.text: Yeah. (Long Pause) MP3 Audio Clip ( 9 min 07 sec )

a16a1685810.text: That's affirmative.

a16a1685810.speaker: Mattingly
a16a1685810.text: Okay; I see that is no trim.

a16a1690707.text: (To Houston) How many gammas did you say that LSM (Lunar Surface Magnetometer) was, Tony? 300 and some?

a16a1690707.text: Yeah. That's what I thought. Well, the magnetic field of the Moon, in places, is a lot more than anybody ever believed it would be.

a16a1690707.speaker: Hartsfield
a16a1690707.text: Roger; 9.1.
